A trade war between Canada and the US deepens rupture in what had been a close and durable alliance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
15:23:01 UTC
00:23:01 KST

A trade war between Canada and the US deepens rupture in what had been a close and durable alliance
TORONTO (AP) — For decades, Canada built much of its prosperity on privileged access to the United States. Now, after the collapse of trade talks, one of the world’s closest and most durable alliances has been fundamentally altered, with both countries facing the risk of a full-scale trade war.
Prime Minister Mark Carney acknowledged the break after last-ditch negotiations failed Friday, saying Canada had recognized that “America has changed” and that the countries would “not return to our old relationship.”
The United States imposed 50% tariffs on about $20 billion worth of Canadian goods early Saturday. Canada promised to match the import taxes dollar for dollar. Carney suspended negotiations and ordered Canada’s trade team home after accusing Washington of last-minute changes that were “unfair, uneconomic, and called into question the reliability of any deal.”
Carney foreshadowed the shift at the World Economic Forum in Davos in January, declaring that the world was experiencing “a rupture, not a transition” and urging countries such as Canada to reduce their vulnerability to economic coercion by strengthening their economies at home and diversifying abroad.
“The collapse of the tariff talks points to the fact that the old Canada-U.S. relationship is over and, for many Canadians, it also confirms the perception that Canada can’t trust the Trump administration,” said Daniel Béland, a political science professor at McGill University in Montreal.
The pressure from Republican President Donald Trump has gone well beyond tariffs.
He has questioned Canada’s economic viability, repeatedly talked about making it the 51st U.S. state and used trade measures to press for more production in the United States. The threats and economic pressure have angered many Canadians and fueled a sense of betrayal in a country that had long regarded the U.S. as its closest ally.
Travel to the U.S. remains sharply below levels before the dispute, with Canadian-resident return trips in July down nearly 29% by car and 27% by air from July 2024, Statistics Canada said.
The failed trade negotiations underscored how far the relationship had shifted. Canada had been prepared to accept some U.S. tariffs in exchange for broader market access and greater certainty — a sharp break from decades of continental trade policy built around eliminating barriers and increasing integration.
Washington has portrayed its proposed terms as especially favorable to Canada. But for Canadians accustomed to preferential access under the 1989 Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement, the North American Free Trade Agreement and its successor, even reduced tariffs would mark a fundamental retreat from the old relationship.
The collapse also puts Carney’s approach to Trump to the test.
The prime minister’s “elbows up” posture — hockey shorthand for playing aggressively and refusing to be pushed around — has helped keep him popular at home. His decision to resist U.S. pressure could also resonate abroad with those impressed by his Davos call for countries to resist economic coercion and reduce dependence on great powers.
Provincial leaders had already been preparing Canadians for a permanent change. Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe said “the old status quo is not possible.”
Ontario Premier Doug Ford, who leads Canada’s most populous province, said Carney had his “full support” for retaliation “tariff for tariff, dollar for dollar.”
Former Alberta Premier Jason Kenney, a prominent conservative and former federal Cabinet minister, said Canada was “not cravenly surrendering in the face of constant economic and political aggression” from Trump. Kenney noted that Canada, along with China, was among the few countries to retaliate against U.S. tariffs. “Damn right we are,” Kenney wrote.
The economic risks of fighting back and a shift seen as perhaps lasting beyond Trump
Nearly three-quarters of Canada’s goods exports go to the United States. The U.S. economy is roughly 10 times larger than Canada’s, limiting Ottawa’s ability to retaliate dollar for dollar without inflicting disproportionate damage at home.
Royal Bank of Canada economists estimate the tariffs directly affect about 0.4% of Canada’s gross domestic product and jobs because the trade penalties cover only about 5% of Canadian exports to America. The damage could grow significantly, however, if retaliation broadens, more sectors are pulled into the dispute or the standoff persists long enough to curb investment and disrupt integrated supply chains.
Béland said the countries were witnessing “the beginning of a full-scale trade war,” though he cautioned that the situation could change rapidly.
The dependence is not one-sided.
Canada supplies roughly two-thirds of U.S. crude oil imports, making Canadian energy critical to large parts of the U.S. economy. Trump has focused much of his pressure instead on autos, steel and aluminum, sectors where he wants more production moved to the U.S. That push has fueled resentment in Canada, where many see it as an effort to hollow out key industries.
Goldy Hyder, president and CEO of the Business Council of Canada, said businesses still view the U.S. as Canada’s most important trading partner but increasingly see the shift as lasting beyond Trump.
“There is a new trade and investment model, one that could well be kept in place by future U.S. administrations whether Democrat or Republican,” Hyder said.
Canada looks beyond the United States because ‘things will never be the same’
The breakdown adds urgency to Carney’s push to diversify beyond the United States. He has traveled abroad seeking investment and new trade ties, aiming to attract $1 trillion Canadian (US$730 billion) by 2030 and to double non-U.S. investment over the next decade.
In July, Ottawa and Alberta advanced plans for a new Pacific Coast oil pipeline to give Canadian crude greater access to Asian markets and reduce reliance on U.S. buyers.
In recent days, Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew had urged Canada to keep fighting rather than accept a weaker deal. He argued that Trump was vulnerable because the cost of living was the top election-year issue for U.S. voters and that America had grown weaker internationally, pointing in part to the confrontation with Iran.
“I think we should fight. I think we’ve got the upper hand,” Kinew said.
Kinew also questioned whether Canada should make lasting concessions to tariffs that may not outlive Trump’s presidency.
“I just wonder if accepting the idea of the Trump tariffs are here forever is the move,” he said.
The immediate question is how long the latest tariff confrontation will last.
Béland said the deeper change probably will, partly because U.S. protectionism is likely to remain influential under future administrations.
“The idea that things will return to ‘normal’ once Donald Trump leaves the White House is probably just wishful thinking,” Béland said. “It doesn’t mean the relationship might not improve in the future but that things will never be the same.”

The kippah in his pocket: Don’t hide your Judaism, you never know who needs to see it - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
15:22:27 UTC
00:22:27 KST

Four loaves of challah, a Friday afternoon in Australia, and the long reach of one Jew who refused to be embarrassed.
I am currently in Perth, Australia, celebrating my granddaughter’s bat mitzvah. When I arrived, I was shown a photograph. It is not a picture of my family, or of Israel, or of anything a stranger would think worth saving.
It is a photograph of four loaves of challah, slightly lopsided, still steaming on a wire rack in a kitchen somewhere in Australia. It was sent by a young man I have never met, to my son, whom he had known for only three weeks.
Let me explain how it got there.
My son is a rabbi. Recently, he spent three weeks on an intensive residential course in Australia – long days outdoors, very little sleep, and a great deal of mud. The organizers made sure he had kosher food. This meant airline meals. Anyone who has eaten a long-life kosher airline meal will tell you it is less of a lunch than an act of faith.
So there he sat one afternoon in the dining hall, with his tray of foil-sealed devotion in front of him and his kippah on his head. Another participant sat down beside him. He mentioned, quietly, that he too was Jewish. Then he reached into his pocket and pulled out a kippah of his own.
He did not normally wear it. He had not felt comfortable wearing it there. But now that somebody else was wearing one, he said, he would wear his too. He wore it for the rest of the course.
I have thought about that pocket a great deal since. A young Jewish man, capable and committed, carrying his Judaism folded up where nobody could see it. Waiting. Not for permission, exactly. Waiting for company.
The program did not pause for Shabbat. There were activities on Saturday, as there had to be. My son kept Shabbat, of course, but in somewhat difficult circumstances, as Jews have done in every generation. And as the two of them walked, they sang “Lecha Dodi,” the song that welcomes the Shabbat. Two Jews walking through the Australian bush, welcoming the Shabbat bride in the only way available to them. I cannot think of a purer act of Jewish defiance in a long time.
My son told me that something else extraordinary also happened. The non-Jewish participants noticed. They watched this young rabbi stay committed to the strictures of Shabbat observance and, instead of mockery, they offered to assist him by, for instance, carrying the bags he was not permitted to carry.
During the rest of the week, my son did the same for them. Christians, Muslims, and people of no faith whatsoever quietly worked out between themselves how to make room for one man’s covenant.
The bond that formed between them was not built on anybody pretending to be less than they were. It was built on the opposite.
On the Friday after they came home, the young man baked challah. And he sent my son the photograph, with a message thanking him for giving him back his Jewish identity.
Nobody preached. Nobody argued. Nobody won a debate. One man simply ate his terrible airline schnitzel with his head covered, and the ripples reached a kitchen he will never stand in.
Same pocket, different setting
Now for the uncomfortable half of this article, because I am not writing a feel-good story. I am writing a warning wrapped in one.
We are living through the ugliest wave of open Jew-hatred most of us have known, and the Jewish response, in too many places, has been to get smaller.
The baseball cap over the kippah (I admit that I did just that on my Emirates flight this week). The Star of David tucked inside the shirt on the train. The mezuzah taken down from the door of the apartment. The Hebrew name shortened on the office directory. The hesitation before saying where you spent the summer.
I wrote recently about a statistic that stopped me cold: requests for kosher meals in some British hospitals have reportedly halved in two years. Not because British Jews stopped keeping kosher, but because, at the moment they were most frightened and most dependent, they hesitated to tick a box that said, “I am Jewish.”
That is the same pocket. It is simply a different setting.
I understand the instinct completely. It is not cowardice; it is arithmetic, done quickly, by frightened people: Why invite the risk? And in genuinely dangerous situations, discretion is no sin. Our tradition has never demanded martyrdom over a hat.
But we should be honest about the price. A kippah that goes into a pocket does not merely make one Jew invisible. It withdraws the permission that another Jew was waiting for.
That young man was not converted by an argument. He was released by an example. Had my son quietly accepted the standard meal and left his head bare – which might have been entirely understandable, even defensible – there would have been no conversation in that dining hall, no singing on that walk, no challah on that Friday.
The absence would have cost nothing anyone could measure, which is exactly what makes it so dangerous. We can never see the ripples we fail to make.
The late Rabbi Jonathan Sacks put it with characteristic bluntness: non-Jews respect Jews who respect Judaism, and they are embarrassed by Jews who are embarrassed by Judaism.
Forty years in medicine have taught me he was right about something deeper still. Patients, colleagues, and strangers all take their cue from your posture. Apologize for your existence, and you invite others to audit it. Stand comfortably inside your own skin and, in the overwhelming majority of cases, the world simply makes room. The people around my son did not respect him despite his Shabbat. They respected him because of it. Nobody is inspired by a person hiding.
Our oldest story says the same thing. The midrash teaches that our ancestors were redeemed from Egypt because they did not change their names, their language, or their dress. Not because they out-argued Pharaoh, but because in the middle of an empire built to erase them, they remained visibly, stubbornly, unmistakably themselves.
I am not asking anyone to be reckless. I am asking us to notice what is at stake when we shrink.
Wear it, or don’t – that is between you and your own courage on any given morning. But understand what you are carrying.
Somewhere in your office, your ward, your lecture auditorium, or your neighborhood, there is a Jew with something folded up in a pocket, waiting to find out whether it is safe to be who they are. You may never meet them. You may never know it happened.
But three weeks later, somebody bakes challah.
The writer is a rabbi and physician. He writes and teaches on Jewish ethics, leadership, and resilience. His work appears on rabbidrjonathanlieberman.substack.com and youtube.com. @rabbidrjonathanlieberman.

Zagreb to Opatija: Discovering Croatia’s northern Adriatic treasures
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
15:22:22 UTC
00:22:22 KST

Surprisingly, 2026 has been a landmark year for direct flights to Croatia’s capital, making Zagreb more accessible than ever for Israeli travelers.
For many years, however, Zagreb and northern Croatia remained an underrated destination, often overshadowed by Croatia’s famous Adriatic destinations, with Dubrovnik in the south as the crown jewel.
For me, the city became something far more personal. While my daughter, Lihi, studied medicine at the University of Zagreb, it became a home away from home during my many visits. Those trips opened the door to discovering the hidden gems of northern Croatia, an enchanting region of elegant towns, breathtaking landscapes, and rich cultural heritage.
This summer marked a particularly meaningful journey. As Lihi graduated, adding another Israeli doctor of medicine to the healthcare system, I returned to Croatia to help her pack and to celebrate this special milestone.
Seaside town of Opatija
From there, I set my sights on the aristocratic seaside town of Opatija, where timeless elegance, grand Habsburg architecture, and the sparkling Adriatic create one of Croatia’s most captivating destinations.
Opatija is the closest Adriatic seaside destination to Zagreb, just a two-hour drive from the Croatian capital or an easy three-hour bus journey, with comfortable services starting from around €14. Its convenient location makes it the perfect escape, whether for a weekend getaway or as the gateway to exploring northern Croatia.
A coastal gem that has enchanted travelers for more than 180 years, Opatija is where historic elegance meets the shimmering Adriatic.
Often referred to as the riviera of northern Croatia, the town is renowned for its grand Austro-Hungarian villas, elegant seaside promenades, lush gardens, and refined atmosphere, which has attracted royalty, artists, and distinguished visitors since the 19th century.
Standing proudly on the shoreline is Opatija’s most recognizable symbol, the iconic Maiden with the Seagull. Gazing across Kvarner Bay, the graceful statue has become the town’s enduring emblem, embodying its maritime heritage and romantic spirit.
Visitors are drawn to Opatija by the calm, crystal-clear waters of Kvarner Bay, its Mediterranean climate, sophisticated coastal charm, and rich cultural heritage. The famous 12-kilometer Lungomare promenade reveals one breathtaking panorama after another.
One of Opatija’s greatest pleasures is the scenic walk to the neighboring village of Icici along the famous trail-promenade. Stretching beside the Adriatic, this leisurely rocky pedestrian route takes around an hour at an easy pace, with breathtaking views accompanying you every step of the way.
For my money, this is one of the most beautiful sceneries I have ever experienced. Not to be missed. The path winds past elegant Austro-Hungarian villas, grand historic hotels, charming cafés, and beautifully landscaped gardens, while the turquoise waters of Kvarner Bay remain constantly in view.
Along the way, countless swimming platforms and ladders invite you to pause for a refreshing dip before continuing your stroll.
One of Opatija’s most delightful features is how effortlessly the sea becomes part of everyday life. Nearly every stretch of the waterfront is equipped with these inviting ladders, allowing visitors to step directly into the refreshing Adriatic whenever temptation strikes.
Israelis, accustomed to sandy beaches, will be puzzled to see both locals and travelers spreading towels on hard concrete surfaces or endless rocks. I was intrigued as well. However, surprisingly, it was an interesting, pleasant experience, as the Kravner beaches here are similar to swimming pools – only wider, saltier and cleaner.
Postcard-worthy views
And then there is the scenery. Every turn reveals another postcard-worthy view. Elegant architecture framed by palm trees, sailboats gently gliding across the bay, the green slopes of Mount Ucka rising behind the town, and the endless blue horizon stretching toward the Adriatic.
At the heart of Opatija lies the magnificent Villa Angiolina Park, widely regarded as the birthplace of tourism in the town. It was here, in the mid-19th century, that Villa Angiolina welcomed European aristocracy, transforming Opatija into one of the continent’s first fashionable seaside resorts.
Today, the beautifully preserved botanical park remains a tranquil oasis, where centuries-old trees, exotic plants collected from around the world, elegant pathways, and seasonal blooms tell the story of the town’s remarkable heritage. Surrounded by impressive marinas, it continues to capture the refined character that has defined Opatija for generations.
As a backdrop to the iconic Slatina Fountain stands the newly opened Keight Opatija, a boutique-style luxury hotel and Croatia’s first international property. Perfectly positioned in the heart of Opatija, the hotel blends effortlessly into the town’s elegant streetscape while introducing a fresh, contemporary energy to this historic seaside resort.
Keight stands apart as Opatija’s first true lifestyle luxury hotel. Rather than recreating the grandeur of the Austro-Hungarian era, it embraces bold modern design, sophisticated interiors, and an intimate boutique atmosphere that appeals to today’s luxury traveler while respecting the town’s rich heritage.
Unlike the grand historic hotels that have defined Opatija for generations, Keight delivers beautifully appointed guest rooms, thoughtfully designed wellness facilities, and personalized hospitality.
Davor Kovcalija, cluster hotel manager of Curio Collection by Hilton, is especially proud of the hotel’s unique highlight – the rooftop bar.
“Here, guests sip handcrafted cocktails, unwind beside the infinity-style outdoor pool, and soak in sweeping views of Kvarner Bay as the sun slowly sets behind the surrounding islands and mountains,” he rightly says.
With Croatia's beaches ranked among the most beautiful in Europe, our journey continued northwest to the enchanting Istrian Peninsula, the largest peninsula in the Adriatic Sea.
Shared by Croatia, Slovenia, and Italy, Istria is a fascinating blend of cultures, cuisines, and architectural influences.
While all three countries lay claim to part of the peninsula, Croatia encompasses the largest and most diverse stretch, where medieval hilltop villages, Roman heritage, crystal-clear coves, vineyards, and olive groves come together in one unforgettable destination.
At Istria, within easy driving distance from Opatija (even a day trip would be rewarding), magical surprises await.
Rovinj, a feast for the senses
One of its undisputed jewels is Rovinj, a town that effortlessly captures the romance of the Adriatic. Rising from a small peninsula, its pastel-colored houses, winding cobblestone alleys, lively harbor, and charming squares create one of Croatia’s most photographed settings.
Beyond its beauty, Rovinj is a feast for the senses, with boutique galleries, waterfront cafés, artisan shops, and elegant restaurants. Don’t miss dishes with the local finest white and black truffles. Enjoying lunch in one of the narrow streets, while fishing boats gently sway in the picturesque marina, is an experience.
Heading south brought us to Pula, the largest city in Istria and one of the Adriatic’s greatest historical treasures.
Located at the peninsula’s southern tip, Pula combines a relaxed Mediterranean atmosphere with over 3,000 years of history.
Unlike many historic cities that feel like open-air museums, Pula remains a vibrant, lived-in destination where Roman monuments blend naturally into everyday life.
Its compact historic center is filled with reminders of the Roman Empire, highlighted by the city’s crowning glory – the magnificent Pula Arena, one of the world’s largest surviving Roman amphitheaters and among the best-preserved anywhere outside Rome. Once the stage for gladiator contests, it today hosts concerts, film festivals, and cultural events, creating a remarkable connection between ancient history and modern Croatia.
Indeed, Opatija is far more than an elegant seaside resort. It’s the perfect gateway to Croatia’s northern Adriatic.
Yet after every adventure, there’s something special about returning to Opatija as a base. Here, sunset strolls along the Lungomare, refined waterfront dining, and the timeless charm of Kvarner Bay guarantee evenings as memorable as the day itself.
The writer is the publisher of Travel Flash Tips.

Tracing roots: Why every Jew should reclaim family histories disrupted by the Holocaust - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
15:22:09 UTC
00:22:09 KST

This year is the 50th anniversary of the publication of Alex Haley’s widely acclaimed, best-selling book Roots – The Saga of an American Family.
Roots, which was also made into a miniseries, set off an ongoing global trend of tracing family origins.
Not all such searches are for positive reasons. Many German citizens want to know if their grandparents or great-grandparents were Nazis. Now, with access to the US National Archives catalog, they can find out.
In some cases, it’s merely curiosity about a long-held family secret and a desire to know the truth. In others, it’s fear that they may have inherited the evil DNA.
Among Jews, tracing ancestry is a voyage of discovery. Many Jews of European background grew up believing that all their relatives on both sides of their families had been murdered during the Holocaust.
Nonetheless, some such Jews join genealogical societies to seek pre-Holocaust information about their forebears.
Many have discovered through DNA tests and other means that some of their relatives survived the Holocaust and, together with their progeny, are living in another country or even close by.
In Israel, a long-overdue family reunion is taking place this month. Facilitated by MyHeritage, one of the myriad Jewish genealogical organizations, its key players are Adrianna Turk, 74, from Australia, and Raanan Gidron, 73, from Israel.
The two are second cousins. Her grandmother and his grandfather were siblings.
Turk and Gidron have more than 50 other relatives around the world. Turk, the daughter of a Jewish father, grew up in New Zealand believing that no one from her father’s family was left.
Gidron’s mother had miraculously survived Theresienstadt and Auschwitz.
After learning from her DNA test that she had relatives abroad, Turk reached out to some of them through social media. She met Gidron virtually several months ago and met him face-to-face in Israel earlier this month.
Countless similar reunions have taken place in Israel and around the world since the Holocaust.
In Israel, there was a special office dedicated to searching for relatives of Holocaust survivors. The searches were broadcast on the radio and often published in newspapers.
That was long before the founding of the International Association of Jewish Genealogical Societies (IAJGS) in 1988. There were Jewish genealogical societies before that, but they operated without an international roof body.
There are an abundance of stories about family reunions and the tracing of family histories.
One heart-warming Israeli story is about two elderly men who shared a bench in a shopping center. They began a conversation. It transpired that both were Holocaust survivors from Romania. Each thought that he was the sole survivor of his family.
As the conversation progressed, each spoke of the place in which he was born and raised. It happened to be the same village.
Both had adopted Hebrew surnames. Then each stated his original name.
They found out they were brothers who had lived around the corner from each other for years. Their appearances had radically changed with time, which is why they had not recognized each other.
But the most amazing story is that of Genie Milgrom, a Cuban-born American woman of Spanish ancestry, who was raised Catholic but did not feel comfortable as a Christian. Her family kept certain Jewish customs without knowing their background.
Curiosity drove Milgrom to begin exploring her ancestry.
She learned that she was descended from conversos. More important was the discovery that she was descended from a 22-generation maternal line of women that went back to pre-Inquisition Spain and Portugal.
Milgrom has spoken at many genealogical gatherings and has won awards for her research. To help other descendants of Jews from Spain and Portugal, Milgrom has written books with guidelines for the accessibility of birth, marriage, death, and Inquisition documents.
From the past to looking toward the future
The major obstacles for researchers are the different spellings, abbreviations, and translations of surnames.
For instance, Cohen can also be Cohn, Kohn, or Cowen. In my own family, my maternal grandmother’s maiden name, Joskowitz, had been abbreviated to Joske and Joss.
In Israel, someone whose last name is Shahor may have previously been called Schwartz or Black.
IAJGS has published extensive material on surnames.
The umbrella organization was founded with the help of Sallyann Sack, a veteran genealogist, clinical psychologist, and editor of Avotasynu, a journal on Jewish genealogy, and the late Rabbi Malcolm Stern, a long-time genealogist with the American Jewish Archives,
IAJGS collects, preserves, disseminates, and researches Jewish ancestry and promotes public access to records containing genealogical data relevant to Jews.
Some 90 societies now come together under the IAJGS banner.
Current IAJGS president Susan Weinberg of Minnesota is in the planning stages of the organization’s 46th annual conference, which will run from April 4-6, 2027. The planning committee is calling for new ideas and for people to present papers, tell stories, or run workshops.
The best-known Jewish genealogical societies are JewishGen, MyHeritage, IGRA, LitvakSIG, and JRI Poland. Most genealogical societies are non-profits.
One of the world’s largest, which does operate for profit, is Ancestry, which boasts more than 70 billion records, including those of Jews.
Genealogy dates back to ancient Jewish times.
The Bible is full of details of who begat whom, plus the names of all the important members of the 12 tribes, and before that – Adam and Eve and their children, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob and their wives and offspring, and later the family of Moses.
Interest waned in the post-biblical centuries. Families in which distinguished positions were passed on from generation to generation were among the rare exceptions, and some of their family trees can be found in Israel’s National Library in Jerusalem.
The Holocaust, with its enormity of family tragedies, rekindled interest in the desire to know about past generations from which individual Jews were spawned.
Young children nowadays know both their grandparents and their great-grandparents. Few Jews born between 1930 and 1950 knew their grandparents, and in many cases were not even aware of their great-grandparents’ names.
Longevity now enables in-the-flesh connections between young people and their great-grandparents. Young members of four-generation families not only know the names of their great-grandparents but also how they look and how they sound.
Yet for all that, and the significant number of professional and amateur genealogists, if one were to stop people at random, in the street or on public transport, and ask them to name all of their great-grandparents, it’s doubtful that anyone would be able to.
That is likely to change in the future.
According to the Central Bureau of Statistics, there are more than 3,300 people in Israel who are over the age of 100.
There are many more nonagenarians, so it stands to reason that many more future generations will have relationships with their great-grandparents at family gatherings.
Until recent years, IAJGS held its annual conferences in a different city every year. Most conferences were in the US, but have also been in Jerusalem, London, Warsaw, Paris, and Toronto.
Epidemics and travel restrictions prompted virtual conferences, allowing for many more participants.
Next year’s conference will also be virtual.
Detailed information is available from the Program Committee at Program@IAJGS.org

US imposes 50% tariffs on Canadian goods after deal fails, USTR Greer says no new talks planned
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
15:21:44 UTC
00:21:44 KST

The US imposed 50% tariffs on some Canadian goods on Saturday after the two longstanding allies failed to reach a trade deal, with each side accusing the other of derailing days of talks.
The tariffs that came into effect just after midnight (0400 GMT) on some $20 billion of Canadian goods - things like wooden ice hockey sticks that are rarely used anymore - are far from an economic game-changer for the largest US trading partner after Mexico. That represents just over 5% of Canada's exports to the US.
But the new tariffs mark an increase in tensions between President Donald Trump and Prime Minister Mark Carney, and will likely make broader talks to renew the US-Mexico-Canada free trade agreement more difficult.
Carney said he had suspended trade negotiations and Canada would retaliate "dollar for dollar" on the new tariffs.
"I have decided to suspend trade negotiations with the US and have directed Canada’s negotiators to return to Ottawa," Carney said in a statement.
"They (negotiators) have worked hard, in good faith, to defend the interests of Canadians throughout these negotiations up until the very last minute," he said. "However, last-minute changes in the US proposed terms were unfair, uneconomic, and called into question the reliability of any deal."
Polls show Canadians oppose making any concessions to Trump
Carney, the only person to ever run the central banks of two major economies, was elected last year on promises to stand up to Trump, and remains broadly popular. Polls show most Canadians oppose making any concessions to Trump.
Hours earlier, the two sides had seemed close to an agreement that sources said would have lowered tariffs on steel, aluminum and autos and potentially brought American alcohol back to Canadian liquor stores.
"Tonight, Canada declined to finalize the trade deal under the terms agreed earlier this week," US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said during a White House briefing.
"This is a missed opportunity for Canada to partner with the United States, which is the fastest-growing economy in the G7," Greer said.
A senior Trump administration official said the US offer would have put Canada in the best tariff position of any major exporter to the US, but that Canada had sought additional concessions, especially on steel, aluminum, autos and softwood lumber.
No new US-Canada talks have been scheduled
No additional talks are scheduled as the US implements the new duties, the official said.
Trump last month threatened to impose a raft of duties on a range of Canadian imports, including wine, furniture, dairy products, cement, clothing, fishing rods, and hockey equipment.
The tariffs, which do not qualify for preferential treatment under the US-Mexico-Canada free-trade agreement, open up some already vulnerable sectors to potential severe damage that could lead to job losses and business closures, trade experts have said.
 
The decision by the US administration followed three days of talks in Washington between Canada's minister for trade with the US, Dominic LeBlanc, and Greer.
The new duties add to existing US tariffs on steel, lumber and autos, which have taken a major hit in the last 18 months, although the malaise has been largely contained within these sectors.

Intl. construction expo: A showcase of resilience, untapped cooperative potential

Intl. construction expo: A showcase of resilience, untapped cooperative potential
TEHRAN- The 26th International Exhibition of the Construction Industry was held during August 18-21 in various sectors, including building materials, equipment and machinery, doors and windows, elevators and escalators, mechanical and electrical installations, smart systems, safety equipment, architecture and modern designs, and knowledge-based products.
The exhibition was held in 20 halls and part of the open spaces of Tehran International Exhibition Center, organized by the Iran Chamber of Cooperatives.
As reported, over 600 domestic and foreign companies participated in this International event.
The head of Iran's Cooperative Chamber announced that organizers of the exhibition reported approximately $800 million in export contracts were signed at the previous edition of the event, and it is expected that this year will also provide a suitable capacity for expanding trade interactions and exporting domestic products.
Also, Fatemeh Mohajerani, the government spokesperson, stated on the sidelines of her visit to the exhibition: "The more actively the private and cooperative sectors can play a role in production and business, the smoother the path to economic growth will be."
The government spokesperson described the cooperative sector as inherently people-oriented and said: "The private sector is a strategic partner of the government, and we welcome its growth. Now that the country needs to utilize all capacities, the cooperative capacity must be harnessed, and we in the government are prepared to do so."
Mohajerani emphasized: "The Cooperative Chamber is a well-established and deeply-rooted institution, and the most important message that should emerge from this exhibition is that despite all pressures, the private sector remains steadfast and continues striving to meet the needs of all segments of society."
* More effective utilization of cooperative capacity in supplying essential goods, border economy required
During this visit, the head of Iran's Cooperative Chamber met with the government spokesperson and reported on the increased presence of manufacturers, knowledge-based companies, and foreign guests at the 26th Building Industry Exhibition. He stressed the necessity of more effectively utilizing the neglected capacities of cooperatives in supplying essential goods, market regulation, transportation networks, and border economy.
During the government spokesperson's tour of the exhibition, the Cooperative Chamber chief presented a report on the status of cooperative activities across the country.
Referring to the broader presence of domestic manufacturers, knowledge-based companies, renewable energy sector activists, and foreign trade delegations at this year's exhibition, he compared it to the previous edition and stated: "This year's exhibition was far better than last year—both in terms of manufacturer participation and the number of foreign guests, as well as visitor turnout."
According to the Cooperative Chamber head, the building industry exhibition not only showcases products and services related to this sector but also provides a platform for direct connections among manufacturers, investors, mass builders, and foreign market players.
Abdollahi added: "Despite the country's conditions and numerous difficulties, we decided to hold the exhibition, believing there is no reason for national activities to cease. Following this period, Iran's Cooperative Chamber is the first organization to voluntarily host an exhibition, and we wanted to convey the message that the country is in a state of stability and economic actors continue their work. We are grateful that our colleagues' efforts in this edition bore fruit, and aside from domestic reception, international and global reflection was also positive."
* Effective role of construction industry exhibition in developing export markets
The head of Iran's Cooperative Chamber continued: "In the past two days, numerous B2B meetings were held with foreign guests and participants, which can help introduce the capabilities of Iranian manufacturers and develop export markets."
Referring to the exhibition's focus on knowledge-based companies and renewable energy, he said: "A significant portion of this year's exhibition space was dedicated to knowledge-based companies and energy sector activists, and two axes were particularly pursued. First, the presence of knowledge-based companies, which participated prominently with support in costs and placement; second, the field of new and renewable energy, especially solar energy."
Abdollahi also noted the participation of companies involved in clean energy technologies and said: "Introducing new achievements in this field can be effective in developing energy infrastructure and reducing dependence on traditional sources."
Alongside the exhibition section, specialized panels related to housing were also held. Topics such as public housing development, rental housing, and professional leasing were examined with representatives from the Ministry of Transport and Urban Development, Bank Maskan, builders, and activists from the cooperative and private sectors.
He also reported on export contracts signed during the exhibition and said: "Organizers announced that in the previous edition, approximately $800 million in export contracts were signed at this event, and it is expected that this year will also provide suitable capacity for expanding trade interactions and exporting domestic products."
Emphasis on the neglected capacity of the cooperative sector was another focal point of the Cooperative Chamber chief's remarks, and referring to Article 44 of the Constitution, he described cooperatives as one of the pillars of the national economy.
The head of Iran's Cooperative Chamber continued: "Despite the vastness of this sector, its neglected capacities are not fully utilized in many policies and implementation programs. According to statistics, over 18 million people in the country are cooperative members, and more than 30 million benefit from cooperative services. Additionally, approximately 105,000 active cooperatives operate in various fields including agriculture, industry, mining, services, healthcare, transportation, and distribution."
Abdollahi further rejected the notion that cooperatives are only active in housing and consumer sectors, stating: "Cooperatives play a role in important areas such as agricultural production, fisheries, transportation, healthcare, and goods distribution; however, these capabilities are still not properly reflected in executive decision-making. We currently have a vast network of distribution cooperatives and essential goods supply that can be harnessed."
Referring to over 4,500 consumer cooperative stores, he described this network as one of the largest goods distribution capacities in the country and emphasized: "Entrusting a greater portion of the essential goods distribution process to cooperative networks can help increase transparency, strengthen oversight, and reduce intermediation."
Abdollahi added: "The cooperative structure, due to its membership-based nature and accountability to members, has suitable capacity for cooperation with executive bodies."
The head of Iran's Cooperative Chamber also pointed to the significant capacity of border cooperatives, describing it as a foundation for linking local economy and sustainable security in the country.
He also said: "According to available statistics, 453 border cooperatives operate in 17 border provinces, with approximately 7 million residents of border areas being members of these cooperatives. These cooperatives exported about $2.3 billion last year and can play a more prominent role in meeting the needs of border provinces, developing legal trade, and strengthening local employment."
The official emphasized: "Supporting the livelihoods of border residents is not merely an economic issue; by preventing migration, reducing marginalization, and maintaining the vitality of border regions, it can also have significant social and security implications."
It is worth noting that during this visit, Mohajerani toured various exhibition halls and booths of domestic and foreign companies, engaging in dialogue with building industry activists about production capacities, new technologies, and the role of this industry in the country's economic development.
This year's Construction Industry Exhibition was not merely a commercial event for displaying construction products; it became a platform for raising broader issues including export development, the presence of knowledge-based companies, renewable energy, smart housing, and the effective role of cooperatives in the national economy.
What was most emphasized at this event was the necessity of transforming the actual capacities of the cooperative sector into a more effective role in production, distribution, trade, and border area development policies—a capacity that activists in this field believe, with greater attention and support, could become one of the key pillars of economic growth and public participation in the economy.

Russian President Vladimir Putin said on Saturday that his country’s upcoming legislative elections next month will confirm the stability of the Russian state.

Moscow and Kyiv have increasingly targeted each other's logistics centers, as well as port and energy infrastructure, in recent months.
Both sides deny deliberately targeting civilian infrastructure, maintaining that their strikes are directed at military targets or facilities linked to military activities.

Discounts no longer work: how service and emotions are overcoming price-cutting in an oversaturated flower market
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
18:16:47 EEST
00:16:47 KST

Discounts no longer work: how service and emotions are overcoming price-cutting in an oversaturated flower market
Kyiv • UNN
Discounts no longer work: how service and emotions are overcoming price-cutting in an oversaturated flower market.
The modern floristry market in Ukraine is characterized by an exceptionally low barrier to entry. Every day, dozens of new local Instagram shops appear, trying to quickly capture an audience. Their main, and often only, weapon is drastically cutting prices. However, sharing their marketing experience, established industry players unequivocally state: competing solely on price in 2026 is a dead end. Dumping destroys business economics, since flowers are perishable goods with a high write-off rate. An attempt to sell more cheaply inevitably leads to savings on flower quality, the florist's qualifications, or delivery reliability.
After having a celebration ruined by a wilted bouquet from a no-name seller, consumers quickly return to established services. The experience of companies such as flori1.com, Flowers.ua, 7roses.com, pandafl.com.ua, kamelia-shop.com.ua, and flowers-city.com.ua shows that retaining customers sustainably amid fierce competition from Instagram shops is possible by focusing on Lifetime Value metrics, a well-designed loyalty program, and deep service personalization. The long-term profitability of a business is based not on a one-time transaction, but on building trust, so that customers choose one service for all important occasions over many years.
The economics of emotions works differently from the market for consumer goods. When a man orders a bouquet for his wedding anniversary, he is not buying 25 roses, but a guarantee of his wife's wonderful mood and his own peace of mind. If a delivery service guarantees that the bouquet will fully match the photograph on the website, that it will include a branded card with a personal message from the sender, and that the courier will be polite and punctual, the customer chooses reliability over questionable savings. That is why marketing budgets are now being reallocated from discount campaigns to improving the customer experience, developing convenient mobile interfaces, and providing systematic staff training.

Father leaves 7-year-old alone on Mount Fuji to keep climbing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
15:16:44 UTC
00:16:44 KST

A father in Japan was reprimanded by police after leaving his 7-year-old son alone on Mount Fuji in rain and fog so he could continue climbing toward the summit with his older child, Japanese media reported.
The incident happened Thursday morning on Japan’s highest mountain, where rapidly changing weather can make climbing conditions dangerous. The 48-year-old father, a tourist from Nagoya, had set out to climb the 3,776-meter mountain with his two sons, ages 7 and 12 or 13, according to Japan Today.
The three were climbing the Fujinomiya Trail, where many hikers begin near the fifth station at roughly 2,400 meters. Near the sixth station, at an altitude of about 2,490 meters, the younger boy reportedly became restless and complained that he was tired.
Instead of waiting for him to recover or abandoning the attempt to reach the summit, the father reportedly told him, “Wait here,” gave him snacks and a soft drink, and continued uphill with the older boy.
At around 7:30 a.m., a worker at one of the mountain stations found the child sitting alone on a bench as rain fell and fog began to build.
The worker brought him inside and contacted police. Officers then reached the father, who had already made it to the eighth station, at approximately 3,250 meters, and ordered him to return.
It is not clear exactly how long the child had been left unsupervised. Japan Today noted that the official Mount Fuji climbing website estimates it takes about three hours to climb from the sixth station to the eighth, meaning the boy may have been left alone at around 4:30 a.m.
Had the child not been found, he potentially could have remained alone for many more hours. The climb from the sixth station to the summit takes a little more than five hours, with another roughly two and a half hours needed for the descent.
Police reprimanded the father after he reunited with his son. “Leaving a child behind is unacceptable,” officers reportedly told him. No additional punishment or referral to welfare authorities was reported.
The father apologized, saying: “I made a reckless decision, and I deeply regret it.” Police later warned Mount Fuji climbers about the dangers of leaving members of their group behind and urged hikers to match their pace and ambitions to the stamina of everyone traveling with them.
Mount Fuji is known for highly unpredictable weather, with visibility and ground conditions capable of deteriorating quickly. More than 220,000 people climb the mountain during the July-to-September season, with many hiking overnight in hopes of watching the sunrise from the summit.
The mountain also holds deep cultural and religious significance in Japan and has been regarded as sacred for centuries. Authorities in recent years have introduced entrance fees and limits on visitor numbers in an effort to reduce overcrowding.
Mount Fuji remains an active volcano. It has erupted around 20 times in recorded Japanese history, most recently between December 1707 and January 1708.
The mountain has also seen several recent rescue incidents. Last month, a 99-year-old woman was rescued after falling and injuring her pelvis and back. Last year, a 27-year-old climber had to be rescued twice within four days after returning to the mountain to search for a phone he had lost.

Ukrainian Drones Rip Into Ozon Logistics Center and Novokuybyshevsk Oil Refinery
Ukrainian defense forces struck an Ozon logistics complex for the first time while also hitting the Novokuybyshevsk Oil Refinery in Russia’s Samara region, triggering major fires at both facilities, according to Ukrainian defense technology company Fire Point who confirmed the strike on August 22.
Russian media outlet ASTRA also reported the attacks after analyzing footage and other open-source material from the area.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The Ozon logistics center in Chapayevsk was engulfed in a large fire following the drone strike. By around 7:30 a.m., flames had reportedly spread across much of the sprawling warehouse complex.
The facility covers roughly 135,000 square meters and opened in late October 2022, making it one of Ozon’s newer major logistics hubs.
Ozon is one of Russia’s largest online marketplaces, operating on a model similar to Amazon and selling everything from everyday consumer goods to electronics and industrial equipment.
The platform also carries products with potential dual-use or military applications, including drones and components, communications equipment, thermal-imaging devices and tactical gear, some of which have been purchased for Russian troops fighting against Ukraine.
The complex is located near two facilities linked to Russia’s defense industry, including Promsintez, which manufactures industrial explosives, and another defense-related plant in the Chapayevsk industrial area.
Footage from the scene showed a towering column of dark smoke rising above the Ozon facility as the fire continued to spread.
Ukrainian drones also targeted the Novokuybyshevsk Oil Refinery elsewhere in the Samara region. Images and videos circulating online showed several areas of fire and thick smoke over the industrial site following the attack.
The refinery, part of Russia’s Rosneft group, is one of the major oil-processing facilities in the Volga region and has repeatedly come under Ukrainian drone attacks during Kyiv’s campaign against infrastructure supporting Russia’s war effort.
Ukraine already put seven of the ten largest logistics centers operated by Russian e-commerce company Wildberries, OZON rival, out of operation.
Wildberries facilities in Domodedovo and at the Koledino industrial park were among the sites affected. The Koledino facility, covering approximately 250,000 square meters, was the company’s largest warehouse by area.

ICC head decries US sanctions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
15:12:41 UTC
00:12:41 KST

ICC head decries US sanctions
International Criminal Court President Tomoko Akane has warned of what she described as the erosion of international law after US authorities imposed sanctions on her and another senior ICC official.
The Hague-based institution was created in 2002 under the Rome Statute to prosecute genocide, war crimes, and crimes against humanity. So far, 123 countries have ratified the treaty and are full members of the court. However, major global powers including Russia, China, India and the US have either not signed or not ratified the agreement.
“I had anticipated these sanctions against me to some extent, so I am not surprised,” she said in a comment included in a social media post on Friday by Japanese publisher Bungei Shunju, which had published her book. “What is important is not to let this become the beginning of the end of the international rule of law.”
On Tuesday, Washington sanctioned Akane and senior trial lawyer Abdoulaye Seye. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio described the institution as a “corrupt and fatally politicized supranational court that has maliciously abused its authority and exceeded its mandate.”
The designations are part of a campaign announced by Rubio last month to “systematically dismantle the threat posed” by the ICC to US sovereignty.
The ICC said on Wednesday that it “strongly rejects” the new designations, calling them “a flagrant attack against the independence of an impartial judicial institution.”
The White House has accused the court of targeting citizens of states that have neither consented to its jurisdiction nor ratified the Rome Statute. The ICC previously investigated alleged crimes by US military and intelligence personnel in Afghanistan despite Washington not being a member.
Israel has also rejected the court’s jurisdiction. Nevertheless, in 2024 the ICC issued arrest warrants for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and then-Defense Minister Yoav Gallant over alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza. US President Donald Trump later condemned the warrants in an executive order signed in February 2025.
The court has also faced criticism elsewhere, with Burkina Faso, Mali, Niger and Chad moving to withdraw from the ICC this summer, accusing it of disproportionately targeting African countries.
The Philippines withdrew from the ICC in 2019, but the court retained jurisdiction over alleged crimes committed while it was a member. Former President Rodrigo Duterte was arrested under an ICC warrant and transferred to The Hague in March 2025 over alleged crimes against humanity linked to his anti-drug campaign.
Russia has likewise rejected the court’s authority. The ICC issued arrest warrants for Russian President Vladimir Putin and Children’s Rights Commissioner Maria Lvova-Belova in March 2023 over the alleged unlawful deportation of Ukrainian children. Moscow called the warrants legally void, rejected the allegations and said it had evacuated unaccompanied minors from the war zone while taking steps to return them to their legal guardians upon request.

Iran's trade diplomacy surges with expansion of commercial attaché network
TEHRAN- The Director General of the West Asia Office at Iran's Trade Promotion Organization (TPO), elaborating on the organization's major achievements in the years 1403 and 1404 (2024–2025) announced unprecedented records in attracting trade delegations and developing export infrastructure.
He stated that Expo 1403 was one of the country's most successful trade events, yielding significant accomplishments through precise targeting and the strong presence of government officials and the private sector from various countries.

He continued: "In countries where we had only one trade center, the number was increased to two or three to maximize support services for Iranian exporters."

Israel conducts fresh strike in Syria after US criticism
DAMASCUS – Israel carried out a fresh strike in Syria on Aug 22 and lambasted US envoy Tom Barrack for criticising an earlier attack on an air base in the north-west, which Israel has accused Turkey of seeking to use.
US envoy for Syria Tom Barrack on Aug 18 slammed Israel’s attack on the disused military air base that day as an “unnecessary escalation that does not advance regional stability”.
On Aug 21, in an interview with influencer Mario Nawfal, Barrack said the strike may have been intended to provoke a conflict with Turkey, prompting Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz to hit back on Aug 22, calling the remarks “full of inaccuracies”.
Since the December 2024 overthrow of long-time ruler Bashar al-Assad, Israel has carried out hundreds of strikes in Syria and has sent troops into a UN-patrolled buffer zone that for decades had separated Israeli from Syrian forces in the Golan Heights.
Katz wrote on social media platform X on Aug 22 that Israel had passed on “intelligence information to the authorised parties in the United States” before the strike on Aug 18.
He added that Barrack’s comments were “full of inaccuracies and positions that contradict the stance of US President (Donald) Trump himself regarding the Golan Heights”, after Barrack called the territory “occupied”.
Israel captured most of the Golan Heights from Syria in the 1967 Arab-Israeli War and later annexed the areas under its control in a move recognised by only the US and, in August, also Colombia.
‘Flagrant violation’
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, commenting on the Aug 18 strike, said Turkey, an ally of the new authorities in Damascus, had been looking to establish a military presence on the airbase.
Ankara has denied any visit to the site.
Netanyahu and Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan have traded barbs since the incident, and Ankara announced it was seeking an Interpol red notice for Netanyahu, accusing him of “genocide” linked to the interception of a Gaza-bound aid flotilla.
Netanyahu’s office called Erdogan an “anti-Semitic dictator”, while Erdogan’s office called the remarks “outrageous ravings” and accused Netanyahu’s government of “seeking to evade accountability”.
Also on Aug 22, Syrian state television said a man was wounded when an “Israeli occupation drone” targeted a vehicle in the village of Beit Jinn, located south-west of Damascus near the Israeli-annexed Golan Heights, with the Foreign Ministry calling it a “flagrant violation” of its sovereignty.
Israel’s military acknowledged the strike, saying that its forces “fired in southern Syria towards a terrorist who advanced terror attacks in the final stages of preparation”, without identifying the target.
Israel has carried out repeated incursions into Syrian territory and has vowed to keep troops in a so-called “security zone” in southern Syria, where it seeks a broader demilitarised area.
This week, Israeli army chief Lieutenant General Eyal Zamir told troops in southern Syria: “We are monitoring the changes on the Syrian front. We will not allow hostile forces to establish themselves on our borders.” AFP

It was Ozon’s turn: the Ministry of Defense commented on the strike against a Russian logistics hub

Ukraine’s Defense Forces have begun striking logistics hubs of the Russian company Ozon, complicating the logistics of Russian troops and negatively affecting the economy of the russian federation. This was reported by the Ministry of Defense of Ukraine, writes UNN.
Details
"The Defense Forces have opened the account of destroyed logistics hubs belonging to the Russian company Ozon. Systematic strikes on storage centers for dual-use goods are complicating the enemy’s logistics and negatively affecting the economy of the russian federation as a whole. After Ukrainian units struck the 15 largest logistics hubs of Wildberries, it was Ozon’s turn. Our long-range sanctions are working—spectacularly and effectively," the ministry said in a post.
We remind you
Ukraine’s Defense Forces, using long-range FP-1 drones manufactured by the Ukrainian company Fire Point, struck the Novokuybyshevsk oil refinery and a logistics hub of the Russian marketplace Ozon in the Samara region of the russian federation overnight.
Fire Point noted that the refinery struck is one of the largest oil refineries in the region. Its capacity is approximately 8.3 million tonnes of oil per year.
The enterprise is part of the structure of "Rosneft" and produces gasoline, diesel and jet fuel, as well as other petroleum products.
The Ozon logistics hub struck in Chapayevsk is one of the company’s largest fulfillment centers in the Volga region. Its total area, after all phases are launched, is approximately 135,000 square meters, and its capacity is more than 40 million items. The hub processes more than 215,000 orders per day.
Earlier, Ukraine’s Defense Forces put out of operation most of the large logistics centers of the Russian marketplace Wildberries. One of the latest targets was the company’s logistics hub in the "Koledino" industrial park. It was Wildberries’ largest warehouse by area—250,000 square meters.
According to analysts, Wildberries’ direct losses alone, after it lost approximately 20% of its warehouse capacity within a few weeks, could exceed 100 billion rubles (US$1.24 billion), and in the worst-case scenario reach 200 billion (US$2.45 billion). In addition, because of the exodus of sellers, many of whom instantly lost their businesses and goods worth hundreds of billions of rubles, Wildberries’ turnover has already declined by a quarter.
The Bell reports that Wildberries’ overall need for funds could reach 1.3 trillion rubles (US$16.36 billion). The company will have to increase its debt by at least that amount. The marketplace has requested assistance from the state, but it is not yet clear how much financing will be provided, as the federal budget deficit has already reached 5.7 trillion rubles—1.5 times the full-year target.
Fire Point CEO and CTO Iryna Terekh said that Ukraine is capable of exerting a real impact on the enemy, while Russians understand only the language of force.

Japan’s leader Takaichi explains why she spends long hours in seclusion at her official residence
TOKYO (AP) — Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, who is increasingly seen secluding herself at home, said on Saturday that she is using her official residence next to her office more for work to maximize efficiency.
In December, Takaichi moved into the official residence, a brick-and-stone mansion that opened in 1929 used to be the original prime minister’s office until its replacement was built right next to it.
Takaichi said on X that living in the official residence, or “kotei,” is good because its proximity requires no commute and lets her immediately get down to work in time of an emergency.
Takaichi said she has reinforced office functions at the residence so she can work and have meetings there remotely or in person with her staff whenever needed, even after office hours. She also takes home documents to read.
“To me, the official residence is also a workplace,” she said.
But Takaichi, whose work mantra and her recent revelation on X of zero to three hours of sleep at night because of her homemaking burden on top of her heavy workload as prime minister, triggered criticisms that Japan’s first female leader was setting a wrong example for a work-life balance and gender-equality.
Takaichi has seen her support ratings rapidly drop as she pushed unpopular policies such as a revision to the Imperial House Law to reinforce a male-only succession system, while delaying economic measures to address rising prices.
Media reports have said that Takaichi was avoiding parliamentary sessions and largely holed up at the residence at night and on weekends, saying that she’s having significantly less interactions and communication with other lawmakers and officials than her predecessors. Takaichi frequently posts comments and policies on X instead of talking to the media.
The official residence was the site of two bloody coup attempts in the 1930s, and legend has it that the building is haunted by ghosts.
Takaichi apparently doesn’t mind spending long hours at the residence despite that.
“I’ve never seen a ghost, but I have often screamed because of my encounters with cockroaches,” she said. “I was shocked when a cockroach ran past my feet.”

EU sends helicopters, firefighters to Serbia to tackle wildfires
BELGRADE, Aug 22 - The European Union’s Civil Protection Mechanism sent helicopters and firefighters to help Serbia fight a massive wildfire in a nature reserve in the northeast of the country, the head of the EU mission to Belgrade said on Saturday.
Serbia activated the mechanism on Friday after struggling for weeks with a wildfire in Deliblatska Pescara, a unique mixture of sand dunes and woods about 80 km (50 miles) from the capital Belgrade, as well as other blazes in the southwest of the country.
“We stand with Serbia in protecting lives, livelihoods and the unique natural heritage of Deliblatska Sands,” Andreas Beckerath, the head of the EU mission to Belgrade, wrote on X.
Luka Causic, the head of the Serbian Department for Emergencies, said that European aid consists of four Black Hawk firefighting helicopters from Romania, Slovakia and the Czech Republic, 55 firefighters and 24 vehicles from Germany, and 69 firefighters and 15 vehicles from Romania.
One helicopter from Romania and one from Slovakia joined firefighting efforts on Saturday, while two others from the Czech Republic will be engaged on Sunday, Serbia's Interior Ministry said in a statement.
Romanian firefighters and vehicles have also arrived in the town od Bela Crkva, near the fire. A German team is expected to arrive on August 24, it said.
Serbia is not a member of the EU but has access to emergency EU help under its Civil Protection Mechanism.
This summer, Belgrade sent a firefighting helicopter and emergency response team to help Spain combat wildfires after repeated blazes across Europe sapped EU resources.
A Russian Emergencies Ministry IL-76P firefighting plane landed in the southern Serbian city of Nis on Wednesday to tackle the Deliblatska Pescara wildfire, which has gutted thousands of hectares of pine forest since late July.
Causic said the situation was more stable on Saturday, but that strong winds were expected and the priority is to protect settlements and human lives.
Other major wildfires were also active in the rugged Stolovi mountain range in the southwest of the country.
In neighbouring North Macedonia, a major wildfire was raging in the municipality of Strumica, south of the capital Skopje. According to media reports, at least one house caught fire in the village of Sofilar. REUTERS

It stressed the importance of preventing mountain torrents and small and medium-sized river floods, ensuring reservoir safety during the flood season, and implementing safety measures for tourists and construction workers.
Authorities should dynamically update high-risk area catalogs, evacuate residents from hazardous areas in a timely manner, and make every effort to safeguard people's lives and property, the ministry added.
Also on Saturday, the State Flood Control and Drought Relief Headquarters and the Ministry of Emergency Management jointly activated a Level-IV emergency response for typhoon and flood control in southeastern Fujian Province.
China has a four-tier flood-control emergency response system, with Level I being the most severe. ■

Xinhua Headlines: East China's Anhui eyes on strategic planning to foster future industries
China

* In the first half of 2026, Anhui's high-tech manufacturing added value surged 44.6 percent year on year, with sectors like electronic information and automobiles contributing over 70 percent of industrial growth.
* While supporting private tech companies through the full cycle, Anhui is also accelerating the commercialization of technologies derived from large scientific facilities.
* In Anhui, long-term planning and funding at both provincial and municipal levels ensure differentiated competition, which prevents redundant construction and enables cities to collaborate.
HEFEI, Aug. 22 (Xinhua) -- Along the "Quantum Avenue" in Hefei, provincial capital of Anhui, futuristic glass buildings house companies in quantum technology and digital services. Within the same vicinity sit facilities dedicated to voice recognition and deep-space exploration.
Two decades ago, populous and less-developed Anhui in east China used to be an inland province with large labor outflow, but in the past years it has drawn a growing number of researchers and entrepreneurs who boast cutting-edge technologies.
The province's long-term commitment to advanced technology has turned things around. In the first half of 2026, Anhui's high-tech manufacturing added value surged 44.6 percent year on year, with sectors like electronic information and automobiles contributing over 70 percent of industrial growth.
CULTIVATING FUTURE GROWTH
Early planning and sustained institutional support have advanced pioneering industries.
Lu'an, a small city renowned for its tea production and picturesque mountains, is now home to China's first megawatt-class hydrogen energy demonstration station, which converts electricity into hydrogen and vice versa to regulate grid peaks and troughs. The station is expected to save around 1,091 tonnes of standard coal equivalent and reduce about 1,889 tonnes of carbon dioxide emissions annually.
Mingtian Hydrogen Energy Co., Ltd. is one of such operators. Since its founding in Lu'an in 2017, the company has proactively aligned itself with the provincial and municipal development framework. Backed by long-term policies, the company has partnered with the State Grid to establish the power station.
For Wang Chaoyun, chairman of Mingtian Hydrogen Energy, the decision to set up in Lu'an was based on the city's diverse application scenarios for heavy freight and steel transport. "But what mattered more was that when some local officials mistook hydrogen energy for 'hydrogen bomb energy,' Anhui had already issued a clear hydrogen industry plan and set up dedicated industrial funds," Wang recalled.
Wang and his team overcame numerous technical hurdles, at a time when China lacked a complete hydrogen supply chain. Some key components, such as air compressors, had to be imported at high costs and with lead times of at least four months.
The city government stepped in to connect enterprises with research institutes. A physical sciences institute under the Chinese Academy of Sciences eventually developed a centrifugal air compressor, removing a critical bottleneck for local manufacturers.
To mitigate the financial risks of heavy R&D investment, the city government partnered with insurers to provide partial compensation if the project failed. After the company moved into full-scale production, Lu'an pioneered hydrogen fuel cells in its public bus fleet, with about a quarter of the buses now hydrogen-powered. The move not only helped the company gain operational experience but also served as a strong commercial endorsement.
Today, Mingtian Hydrogen Energy has built a complete industrial chain covering fuel cell manufacturing and hydrogen-electricity storage, and its hydrogen-powered marine systems have obtained certification from the China Classification Society.
"Anhui embraces new thinking, new technologies and new industries. The government here has a long-term vision and the courage to break new ground and take responsibility," said Wang.
FROM LAB TO MARKET
While supporting private tech companies through the full cycle, Anhui is also accelerating the commercialization of technologies derived from large scientific facilities. These spinoffs not only serve the public but also generate economic returns that are reinvested into long-term R&D.
At Hefei Ion Medical Center, a domestically developed superconducting proton therapy system is undergoing clinical preparations and is expected to treat patients this year. It grew directly out of core technologies accumulated during the development of the Experimental Advanced Superconducting Tokamak (EAST), dubbed China's "artificial sun," which aims to create nuclear fusion like the sun. These technologies include superconducting magnets, radiofrequency systems and ion sources.
Compared with conventional radiotherapy, the proton system precisely targets tumors while significantly reducing radiation damage to surrounding vital organs. This drastically lowers long-term complications and improves patients' quality of life.
This is far from unique. In Hefei, subway passengers pass through terahertz scanners, another innovation derived from the EAST fusion project. The technology outperforms conventional security devices by detecting prohibited objects previously overlooked, such as ceramic knives, liquid hazardous chemicals, and powdered drugs.
For companies seeking business opportunities in big science spinoffs, the Anhui Innovation Hall offers a one-stop hub that showcases more than 2,700 high-level international achievements and provides transaction and matchmaking services.
The Anhui Innovation Hall has trained over 5,100 "technology managers." With expertise in technology, industry and finance, these professionals offer end-to-end services from scouting to deal-making. The service network has facilitated the commercialization of more than 4,000 research results over the past six years.
This incubator is adopting a more proactive approach. "We have regularly stationed our managers on campus at the University of Science and Technology of China to engage with research teams at the earliest stage, connecting their work with provincial funding and applications, turning breakthroughs into tangible outcomes," said Li Wenxin, deputy director of the hall.
INVESTING IN CHAINS
With Hefei's stake in ChangXin Memory Technologies, China's leading memory chipmaker now worth over one trillion yuan (about 140 billion U.S. dollars), Hefei is called China's boldest "venture capital city." But its investment does not aim to bet on individual companies for financial returns, but aims to extend and strengthen industrial chains based on regional strengths.
In 2008, Hefei invested approximately 6 billion yuan in the sixth-generation production line of BOE Technology Group Co., Ltd. The move shored up a shortfall in local home appliance production and created China's first homegrown liquid crystal display supply. In 2020, it injected 7 billion yuan into NIO China, anchoring the electric vehicle maker's headquarters and R&D center locally and expanding its Anhui-based suppliers from about 60 to nearly 150.
Through these anchor companies, Hefei has cultivated national-level strategic emerging industrial clusters in new display technology, integrated circuits and AI. Quantum information, fusion energy and deep-space exploration are now its next frontiers.
Beyond Hefei, cities across Anhui are also nurturing their own signature industries. As of the first quarter of 2026, Anhui's first 10 provincial-level future-industry pilot zones had already generated over 93 billion yuan in total industrial-chain output.
Bengbu City, leveraging its core competencies in integrated circuits and new materials, has achieved a breakthrough in brain-computer interface (BCI) technology. A local hospital can carry out clinical work for both semi-invasive BCI surgeries and non-invasive BCI systems, offering patients with paralysis a path to restored independence in daily living.
"In Anhui, each city builds on its local strengths and supports leading enterprises to drive industrial chain development. Long-term planning and funding at both provincial and municipal levels ensure differentiated competition, which prevents redundant construction and enables cities to collaborate," said Cui Shihua, deputy director of the Bengbu high-tech zone's management committee.

Chinese customs official calls for more APEC efforts to remove trade barriers
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
22:46:50 CST
23:46:50 KST

DALIAN, Aug. 22 (Xinhua) -- APEC economies should step up efforts to eliminate trade barriers and take more concrete measures to address cross-border trade bottlenecks, so as to make supply chains in the Asia-Pacific region safer, more stable and more efficient, a Chinese customs official said on Saturday.
"Security and facilitation are eternal themes of customs governance," Zhang Baofeng, deputy chief of the General Administration of Customs, said at the ongoing second plenary meeting of the 2026 APEC Sub-Committee on Customs Procedures (SCCP) in Dalian, northeast China's Liaoning Province.
Amid growing fragmentation of global supply chains, adjusting rules and standards and strengthening supply chain resilience have never been more urgent, Zhang noted.
He expressed hope that all parties will take the meeting as an opportunity to deepen alignment of rules and standards, strengthen coordination on risk management and supervision, reduce transaction costs, improve customs clearance efficiency, and provide businesses with a safer, more transparent and more predictable business environment.
The Asia-Pacific region, home to one-third of the world's population, accounts for over 60 percent of the global economy and nearly half of global trade, serving as a key engine of global economic growth.
China's trade with other APEC economies totaled 18 trillion yuan (about 2.65 trillion U.S. dollars) in the first seven months of this year, up 21 percent year on year, outpacing overall growth in China's foreign trade in goods and demonstrating strong potential for regional cooperation.
During the meeting, participants observed smart devices, exchanged experience and ideas, and built consensus. China's customs shared the latest progress of the smart customs partnership program and held an exhibition showcasing achievements in smart customs development.
Zhang also put forward a three-point proposal to further deepen APEC customs cooperation -- upholding true multilateralism and jointly building a new pattern of open and inclusive Asia-Pacific cooperation; riding the wave of the digital era and reshaping new paradigms of customs governance with technological innovation; balancing security and facilitation, and underpinning lasting prosperity in the Asia-Pacific region with a resilient and stable supply chain system.
The meeting also approved an APEC customs cooperation document on promoting technology and innovation for trade security and facilitation.
The APEC SCCP was established in 1994. China's customs holds the SCCP chairmanship for 2026. This meeting, following the first plenary in Guangzhou in February this year, featured in-depth discussions on cutting-edge topics such as artificial intelligence, smart customs and cross-border e-commerce.
Over 100 delegates, including customs representatives from all 21 APEC economies and officials from relevant government departments, international organizations, and business communities, attended the meeting. ■
