US President Donald Trump says the project is being funded by private donors and companies.
US President Donald Trump announced that a new White House ballroom will cost nearly $400 million, funded entirely by private donors and corporations.
"We're spending hundreds of millions of dollars on the ballroom, and it's all from people like me and great companies that are putting it up. It's going to be close to $400 million, and it's all paid for by patriots and patriotic companies, big companies. I'll name the companies probably over the next couple of weeks, but I want to ask if they mind. But and really, most of them have said you could use my name gladly. So that's all money. No, no taxpayer money for the ballroom at all," Trump said.
Meanwhile, the Supreme Court has cleared the way for construction to continue for the time being.
The temporary order was issued just hours before lower-court rulings were set to halt above-ground work on the project due to a lack of congressional approval.
Trump thanked the high court and the chief justice during his remarks later Friday during a political appearance in South Carolina.
“When they say proceed, I think that's a good thing. That's a good thing,” Trump said.
The test of the limits of presidential power
The case reaches the nation's highest court as Trump exercises unprecedented assertions of executive power, increasingly seeking to reshape the capital to reflect his own vision.
The administration contends that the president holds absolute authority to alter the White House and other federal properties at his discretion, maintaining that the ballroom construction must proceed on national security grounds.
However, when Trump initially unveiled plans for the new facility, he made no mention of national security, instead framing it as a privately funded project supported by himself and other donors.
The National Trust for Historic Preservation counters that the president lacks the unilateral authority to carry out the work, which involved razing the East Wing. Legal counsel for the organisation accused the White House of attempting to "outrun the courts" by speeding up construction.
The full Supreme Court is expected to deliberate next on whether building work can proceed as the broader legal battle plays out.
Trump expressed appreciation for Friday's development, claiming in a social media update that the project remains "under budget and ahead of schedule."

The International Criminal Court issued an arrest warrant for Netanyahu on Nov. 21, 2024, over war crimes and crimes against humanity committed in Gaza.

Under Netanyahu, Israel launched two separate attacks on Lebanon, one in 2024 and another in 2026.
He also opened two wars against Iran, one in 2025 and the other in 2026.
Netanyahu was also behind attacks on Yemen and Qatar, which mediated ceasefire talks between Hamas and Israel.
After the fall of the Bashar al-Assad regime, Israel under Netanyahu carried out many attacks on Syria’s military infrastructure in 2024 and occupied some areas in southern Syria.
Netanyahu, who has maintained power through attacks and wars, first ended attacks on Iran reluctantly under US pressure after an agreement between Washington and Tehran.
The decision drew sharp criticism from his coalition partners and opposition leaders.
Former Israeli Prime Minister Yair Lapid, leader of the main opposition Yesh Atid party, criticized the US-Iran agreement and said Netanyahu had “lost the war.”
Netanyahu’s image as a “strong leader” weakened after he was forced to end the war with Iran under US pressure.
He was later forced to stop attacks on Lebanon, again at Washington’s request.
The decision pushed Netanyahu further into a corner in Israel.
Former Defense Minister Avigdor Lieberman criticized the ceasefire reached in Lebanon, targeting Netanyahu by saying: “Not a prime minister, but a puppet.”

“You said a strong prime minister says ‘yes’ to the US president when possible and ‘no’ when necessary. Now is the time to say ‘no’ to our friend, President Trump,” Ben-Gvir said.
Netanyahu’s Likud party is currently the largest party in Israel’s 120-seat parliament with 32 seats.
But opinion polls for elections scheduled for Oct. 27 show Likud falling from 32 seats to 23 and becoming the second-largest party.
Polls also show Likud and Netanyahu’s far-right and ultra-Orthodox coalition partners far below the 61 seats needed to form a government.
A poll published by Israel’s Channel 13 on Aug. 19 showed Netanyahu and his coalition partners winning a total of 51 seats.
Netanyahu and his team turned to anti-Türkiye rhetoric after being forced by US pressure to end the attacks on Iran and Lebanon.
The signals came weeks before Israel’s Aug. 18 attack on the inactive Abu al-Duhur military air base in Syria’s Idlib province.
Amichai Chikli, a Likud lawmaker and diaspora minister, claimed in a radio interview in June that Israel would “sooner or later enter a war with Syria.”
“Türkiye and Syria are far more disturbing developments than Iran,” Chikli said.
Chikli, who often draws attention with anti-Türkiye posts, also voiced unease over the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement signed by Türkiye, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan.
He said Saudi Arabia’s move to act with Türkiye was a “very bad development” for Israel.
Defense Minister Yisrael Katz, one of Netanyahu’s closest figures, has also emerged as a leading figure using anti-Türkiye rhetoric against Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan in the election campaign.
Katz frequently targets Türkiye and Erdogan on social media, and many of his posts are in Turkish.

“If Türkiye establishes a base in Syria, we will establish one too,” Cohen told a local radio station.
Netanyahu and his team have visibly increased anti-Türkiye statements since Israel’s attack on the Abu al-Duhur military air base.

Democrats party leader Yair Golan said Netanyahu made an “arrogant and dangerous” move with the attack.

“As Israel’s October elections approach, it is highly suspicious that Netanyahu would want an escalation of tensions with Türkiye and Syria, especially as the Trump administration encourages calm between the parties,” Lis said.
The election campaign built on anti-Türkiye rhetoric in Israel is not limited to statements by Netanyahu and figures close to him.

In addition, I24 television aired a documentary claiming Türkiye was trying to take control of East Jerusalem by focusing on the activities of Turkish institutions and associations in the city.
The documentary gave broad coverage to humanitarian aid provided by Turkish institutions and associations to Palestinians in the city and also included the activities of the Yunus Emre Cultural Center in East Jerusalem.

Texas seeks federal probe of airport washing facilities, Muslim group denounces move
Texas Governor Greg Abbott on Friday sought a federal probe into airport facilities for ritual washing before Islamic prayers, a move that a Muslim advocacy group called an "anti-Muslim political stunt."
In a letter to the Department of Justice, Abbott called on the department to immediately review the ablution facilities at Dallas-Fort Worth International Airport and George Bush Intercontinental Airport, casting them as discriminatory.
"Because the airports receive federal funds, they are subject to numerous conditions attached to that funding - including the requirement to comply with all applicable laws prohibiting discrimination," Abbott's office said in a statement.
Many Muslims wash their faces, arms and legs before daily prayers.
"These are not 'Muslim-only' spaces any more than a nursing room or an interfaith prayer room is 'Christian-only' or 'mothers-only,'" said the Texas chapter of the Council on American-Islamic Relations, an advocacy group.
"They are accommodations, open to any traveler, that happen to be used mostly by the Muslim community. That is not discrimination. That is what accessible public infrastructure looks like," CAIR-Texas said in a statement.
Last week, Abbott referred the airports to US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy for investigation and threatened to revoke state funding.
Following that referral, Abbott said, DFW abandoned its plans to install more ablution facilities. The airport said this week that officials had "determined the originally anticipated benefit may not be achieved" if the stations were built.
There are about 4.5 million Muslims in the US, including more than 300,000 in Texas, the World Population Review says.
US rights advocates say Islamophobia has risen since the September 11, 2001, attacks on New York and the Pentagon, and more recently because of anti-immigration policies, white supremacy and the fallout of Israel's war in Gaza.
Rights advocates have also documented a spike in anti-Muslim messaging and rhetoric in U.S. political campaigns as Muslim American politicians have risen to prominent offices and roles.
Republican governors in Florida and Texas have cast CAIR, which has opposed Republican President Donald Trump's crackdown on immigration and pro-Palestinian protests, as a terrorist group.
CAIR and other civil rights groups have denounced the claims and said Republicans have attempted to stoke fear against Muslims.

More than 16,000 doses of Ervebo vaccine arrive in Ebola-hit DR Congo
The doses are the first of 70,000 allocated for Kinshasa as experts warn of the virus’s exponential spread.
The Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) has received more than 16,000 doses of the Ervebo vaccine as the country faces its deadliest-ever Ebola outbreak.
The 16,250 doses arrived in the capital, Kinshasa, late on Friday evening, comprising the first of 70,000 that the World Health Organization (WHO) and partners pledged to provide on Thursday.

More doses are set to arrive next week.
Although the vaccine is approved against the Zaire strain of the virus, the Bundibugyo strain currently circulating in the country has no approved vaccine or treatment.
Early data from animal trials show it may offer some protection, according to the WHO.
Samuel Roger Kamba, the DRC’s health minister, told reporters Ervebo had been used several times in the past, including “on a very large scale” during the 2018 to 2020 outbreak.
Of the 70,000 doses intended for the DRC, 20,000 will be part of a late-stage clinical trial to test its effect on the Bundibugyo strain, the WHO said. The remainder is allocated to front-line and health workers.
The outbreak has killed more than 2,500 people out of nearly 5,300 confirmed cases, with the United Nations warning this week that infections continue to spread “exponentially”.
Although the outbreak was declared in mid-May, it is believed to have started weeks beforehand. Data from the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention, meanwhile, shows that transmission has not yet peaked and could reach three times its known rate.
Efforts to contain the virus have been stymied by ongoing armed conflict, delays in identifying cases and a lack of infrastructure in eastern DRC, experts say.

Hit by Trump tariffs, Quebec loses appetite for quick separation from Canada
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
10:13:18 UTC
19:13:18 KST

Hit by Trump tariffs, Quebec loses appetite for quick separation from Canada
MONTREAL, Aug 22 - When U.S. President Donald Trump levied 50% tariffs on Canadian steel in June last year, a steel factory in Canada's mostly French-speaking province of Quebec lost about a third of its orders for bolts and fasteners in less than a week.
The factory owner - The Heico Companies - froze hiring, closed a plant in the region and laid off several dozen people, said David Jeannotte, an operations director, whose own brother lost his job. The cuts were part of 140 layoffs by the company, mainly in Quebec.
The factory's troubles reflect broader anxiety over the fallout from Trump's trade war in Quebec, which is due to hold a provincial election by October 5. But while some previous economic slowdowns in the province prompted an increase in separatist sentiment, polls show that this time around, support for an independent Quebec is at its lowest level in decades, at about 30%.
“As long as Trump will be in his chair, I don’t feel that we even need to talk about that,” Jeannotte said.
Others in the region are echoing Jeannotte’s concerns, saying the threat Trump poses to Canada means the best way to preserve Quebec's unique French culture is to stay within Canada -- at least for now.
Trump's threats to make Canada the 51st state and the whiplash from his tariff policy have spurred an outpouring of Canadian patriotism in Quebec, a province that regularly threatens to break away and has had two previous referendums on the issue.
As the country's only majority French-speaking province, Quebec has a long-established separatist movement that argues independence from Canada is the best way to protect its distinct culture and language. Quebec has never formally signed the Canadian Constitution and separatists argue French Canadians are often overlooked by the English-dominated majority.
CAMPAIGN OF FEAR
The separatist Parti Quebecois currently holds a slim lead in provincial election polls and a win would mark the party’s return to power after a dozen years. But analysts say a vote for the party would be more about disappointment with the ruling party than an endorsement of the PQ’s independence platform.
While the PQ is committed to a third independence referendum if it wins, leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon vowed that won't happen while Trump is president, a tacit recognition of falling support for independence. Quebec narrowly voted to stay in Canada in a 1995 referendum, spurring a national reckoning that resulted in the federal government asking the Supreme Court to clarify the legal procedure for separation.
On Tuesday, Plamondon said in a post on X that deciding Quebec’s political fate “must not be hijacked by the upheaval of American politics, the outbursts of an unpredictable president or by a campaign of fear.”
The explicit acknowledgment of the risk Trump poses to Quebec's independence movement aligns with a broader pattern in which the U.S. president's policies and rhetoric, including his stance on Greenland, have undermined separatist causes elsewhere.
In both Scotland and Catalonia, efforts to break away from the United Kingdom and Spain have been complicated by uncertainty stemming from Trump's tariff threats and criticism of NATO.
A delayed Quebec sovereignty vote would be one less headache for Liberal Prime Minister Mark Carney, who himself upended polls favoring the Conservatives to win a national election last year after promising to be a tough negotiator with Trump.
Carney faces another separatist movement in oil-rich Alberta, which has its own referendum scheduled for mid-October. While conservative Alberta’s burgeoning independence movement aligns with Trump’s brand of conservatism, Quebecers have largely supported the rest of Canada in pressing back against the U.S. president’s tariffs and threats of annexation.
“Postponing a referendum is unfortunately a choice we have to accept,” said Stéphane Bédard, a former interim leader of the PQ. “Quebec is stronger than it’s ever been, but the external factor of Trump has created a lot of insecurity, so we have to be realistic.”
Trump is more disliked in Quebec, arguably the country's most progressive province, than anywhere else in Canada.
According to August data from the pollster Angus Reid, only 10% of Quebecers have a favourable view of the president, and even a deal to lower tariffs is unlikely to reverse public opinion.
“Trump represents everything that Quebec has fought against for the last 60 years in terms of creating a modern, progressive society,” said Jonathan Kalles, former Quebec adviser to ex-Prime Minister Justin Trudeau. Trump's conservative policies as well as his administration's comments that the province's French language requirements are a "trade irritant" are both unpopular.
The financial impact from his policies is also strongly felt in Quebec and economists note the province is among the worst hit by Trump's tariffs, given its concentration of industries like steel and aluminum.
A March report from the Bank of Montreal estimated Quebec's economy would grow about 1% this year, compared to more than 2% for Alberta and Saskatchewan.
Jeannotte, of factory near Montreal, said that before Trump levied tariffs on Canadian steel, about 90% of its products were destined for the U.S., with its bolts used in New York’s Empire State Building. Jeannotte said some staffers work without pay on some days and others have voluntarily reduced their hours.
AT THE NEGOTIATING TABLE
Still, some Quebec separatists say independence remains critical, even now.
Marie-Anne Alepin, president of the separatist Société Saint-Jean-Baptiste de Montréal, said Carney's decision to eliminate a tax that helps finance Canadian programming would cut funding for Quebec's French-language productions, highlighting that as an example of why the province should become independent. Ottawa has pledged to replace the tax with government funding.
“Canada is not capable of defending Quebec's interests,” Alepin said. “(Quebec) has to be at the negotiating table and to do that, we have to be a country.”
Vincent Rainville, a fourth-generation Quebec dairy farmer who owns more than 250 cows, disagreed, saying Trump's policies have complicated efforts to strengthen Quebec's economy and that a national response is required. Nearly half of Canada’s dairy farms are in Quebec.
"It's not just Quebec, it's all of Canada and all our industries that have been affected," he said. “If I supported an independent Quebec, I would not want to talk about that policy now." REUTERS

Former diplomats urge UK, France to defend Palestinian statehood

19:12:26 KST

Dozens of former senior French and UK diplomats on Saturday urged their governments to work together to uphold international law in the Palestinian territories, accusing Israel of seeking to "destroy" any prospect of a viable Palestinian state.
The 102 signatories of the letter published in Le Monde included former British ambassadors to the UN Jeremy Greenstock and Emyr Jones Parry as well the former directors for the Middle East at the French foreign ministry Yves Aubin de la Messuziere and Denis Bauchard.
They said the involvement of France and the UK was essential given the historic roles of the two powers in the Middle East and the fact that both permanent members of the UN Security Council, in 2025 recognised a Palestinian state.
"Our two nations believe that those responsible for war crimes and crimes against humanity must be held to account. Only then can our governments rebut the accusation of double standards. That is why they must act together to uphold international law in Palestine," said the letter.
It accused Israel of seeking "to destroy any prospect of an independent Palestinian state, showing contempt for the law, the rulings of the International Court of Justice and countless UN Security Council resolutions."
Israel launched a genocidal war in Gaza in 2023 that killed over 73,400 Palestinians followed by intensified illegal settlers’ violence in the occupied West Bank, sparking international concern over the conduct of Israeli troops and illegal settlers.
France and Britain this week joined other countries in releasing a statement condeming the Israeli government's release of new tenders for construction in the occupied West Bank.
The letter said house demolitions and "rampant settler violence -- with the connivance of the Israeli army and police" in annexed east Jerusalem and the West Bank amounted to "ethnic cleansing"
"The world no longer sees Israel as a genuine democracy -- there is nothing democratic about depriving others of their rights and land," said the letter.

IN MEMORIAM Siim Kallas
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
10:10:59 UTC
19:10:59 KST

One of the authors of the idea of Estonia’s economic independence
On 26 September 1987, an article by Siim Kallas, Tiit Made, Edgar Savisaar and Mikk Titma, titled “Proposal: The Entire Estonian SSR to Full Self-Management,” was published in the newspaper Edasi. The Isemajandav Eesti, or Self-Managing Estonia (IME), proposal called for Estonia to gain economic autonomy, transition to a market economy, and establish its own monetary and tax systems. The proposal brought into public debate Estonia’s right to make its own economic decisions and increasingly linked economic autonomy with political self-determination. IME also helped pave the way for the restoration of Eesti Pank and preparations for the introduction of Estonia’s own currency.
One of the leaders of the currency reform
Siim Kallas became President of Eesti Pank on 1 October 1991 and served in the position until 1995.
Kallas was a member of the Currency Reform Committee and was authorised to represent Estonia in negotiations with the Bank for International Settlements and with the countries where Eesti Pank’s gold had been deposited before the Second World War. As a result of these negotiations, approximately 11.3 tonnes of gold were returned to Eesti Pank, becoming an important part of the reserves backing the Estonian kroon.
On 20 June 1992, the kroon was reintroduced in Estonia, and the country left the rouble zone. The currency reform was a joint effort involving numerous politicians, economic experts, officials and employees of Eesti Pank. Siim Kallas was one of its key decision-makers and leading figures.
A Shaper of Estonia’s Economic and Political Landscape
In 1994, Siim Kallas was one of the founders of the Estonian Reform Party and became the party’s first chairman. He led the Reform Party for ten years. Kallas was elected to the 8th, 9th, 10th, 14th and 15th convocations of the Riigikogu.
From 1995 to 1996, Siim Kallas served as Minister of Foreign Affairs. During his tenure, Estonia submitted its application to join the European Union and began establishing the national coordination structures needed to prepare for accession.
From 1999 to 2002, Kallas served as Minister of Finance in Mart Laar’s government. During Kallas’s tenure, on 1 January 2000, a new corporate income tax system came into force under which corporate profits are not taxed when earned, but when distributed.
Prime Minister at the Threshold of NATO and European Union Membership
The government led by Siim Kallas took office on 28 January 2002 and remained in office until 10 April 2003. The 42nd Government of the Republic of Estonia was formed by the Reform Party and the Centre Party.
Kallas’s tenure as prime minister was marked by two decisions of major significance for Estonia’s foreign policy. In November 2002, at the NATO Prague Summit, Estonia was invited to begin accession talks with the Alliance. In December of the same year, Estonia concluded its negotiations on joining the European Union.
Estonia’s accession to NATO and the European Union was completed in 2004.
Ten Years as Vice-President of the European Commission
In May 2004, Siim Kallas became the first Estonian to serve as a member of the European Commission. Initially, he was responsible for economic and financial affairs. From November 2004 to 2014, he served as Vice-President of both European Commissions led by José Manuel Barroso. Siim Kallas was a committed European and a strong advocate of close cooperation among European countries and of the European Union.
During his first term, Kallas was responsible for administrative affairs, auditing and the fight against fraud. Under his leadership, greater transparency was brought to the use of European Union funds, decision-making processes and the representation of interests. The beneficiaries of EU funding were made public, and a register of interest representatives was established, along with a code of conduct.
From 2010 to 2014, Siim Kallas served as European Commissioner for Transport and Vice-President of the European Commission. During his tenure, a new framework for the Trans-European Transport Network (TEN-T) was developed, and the relevant legislation was adopted in 2013. Rail Baltica was also included in the Trans-European Transport Network. During Kallas’s tenure, the project’s importance as a railway linking the Baltic states with the rest of Europe was recognised, and decisions were taken that laid the groundwork for its future financing from the European Union budget.
After leaving the European Commission, Siim Kallas stood as a candidate for President of the Republic of Estonia in 2016. From 2017 to 2019, he served as Mayor of Viimsi Municipality, and in 2019 he returned to the Riigikogu. In September 2024, Kallas left the Riigikogu and retired from active politics.
Siim Kallas graduated from Tallinn Secondary School No. 22 with a gold medal in 1967 and from Tartu State University in 1972, graduating cum laude with a degree in finance and credit. During the Soviet era, he worked at the Ministry of Finance of the Estonian SSR, in the savings bank system, and as deputy editor-in-chief of the newspaper Rahva Hääl. From 1989 to 1991, he served as Chairman of the Estonian Trade Union Confederation and as a People’s Deputy of the Soviet Union.
Kallas wrote extensively on economics, politics, liberalism and the European Union. His books include Turumajandus ehk kodanike riik (The Market Economy: The Citizens’ State), Vabaduse ja kurjuse vahel. Euroopa Liidu lugu (Between Freedom and Evil: The Story of the European Union), Eduard Alver. Tema aeg ja inimesed (Eduard Alver: His Time and His People), Mina. Siim Kallas (I: Siim Kallas), Liberalism: ideed ja poliitika (Liberalism: Ideas and Politics), and Torupill ja nuga. Alverite saaga (Bagpipe and Knife: The Alver Saga).
From 1976 to 1989, he was editor and host of the Estonian Radio quiz programme Mnemoturniir.
Siim Kallas was awarded the Order of the National Coat of Arms, 2nd Class, in 2003 and the Order of the National Coat of Arms, 1st Class, in 2015.

Killing of a TCC employee in Lviv on August 21 — attacker notified of suspicion

Killing of a TCC employee in Lviv on August 21 — attacker notified of suspicion
Kyiv • UNN
The 25-year-old Lviv resident stabbed the TCC serviceman three times and threatened a police officer. The serviceman died, and the attacker was notified of suspicion.
In Lviv, a 25-year-old man was notified of suspicion of murdering a military serviceman from a Territorial Recruitment and Social Support Center during notification activities. He stabbed him three times, after which he threatened a police officer with a knife. The serviceman died from his injuries, and the attacker was notified of suspicion. This is reported by the Office of the Prosecutor General, according to UNN.
Details
According to the investigation, on August 21 at around 11:00 p.m. in Lviv, during notification activities, servicemen from the Lychakiv-Zaliznytsia District Territorial Recruitment and Social Support Center, together with police officers, stopped a 25-year-old local resident and asked him to present his military registration document. Instead, the man failed to comply with the request, began walking away, and then attempted to flee.
After running onto the grounds of a school on Stepan Bandera Street, he pulled out a knife and deliberately stabbed a 55-year-old junior sergeant of the Territorial Recruitment and Social Support Center three times: twice in the neck and once in the forearm. After that, the attacker began threatening a police officer with the knife. The law enforcement officer used his service firearm
According to law enforcement officers, the attacker, who sustained wounds to his leg and abdomen, was hospitalized and is currently in the hospital. Meanwhile, the serviceman died from his injuries despite resuscitation efforts.
The deceased had been mobilized at the end of June this year and was deemed fit for service in support units based on his health, in connection with which he was assigned to the notification group of the Territorial Recruitment and Social Support Center
At the scene, law enforcement officers seized a knife. Under the procedural guidance of the Halych District Prosecutor's Office of Lviv, the attacker was notified of suspicion of murdering a person in connection with the performance of that person's official duties and threatening to murder an employee of a law enforcement agency in connection with the performance of that employee's official duties (Clause 8, Part 2, Article 115; Part 1, Article 345 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine).
Investigative actions are currently ongoing, and all circumstances of the incident are being established.

On August 21 in Lviv, during a document check, a man pulled out a knife and fatally wounded a 55-year-old employee of a Territorial Recruitment and Social Support Center.

Swiss grape harvest begins earlier than usual
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
10:07:51 UTC
19:07:51 KST

Swiss grape harvest begins earlier than usual
In many regions, the grape harvest is set to begin as early as August this year. The yield is likely to be lower than in other years, but the quality of the 2026 vintage is "promising".
Several winegrowers, such as the Obrecht family in the Jenins wine-growing region of the Bündner Herrschaft, have already started harvesting grapes this week. This means that the “Läset” is taking place around three weeks earlier than usual in most of Switzerland’s wine-growing regions.
In the cantons of Schaffhausen and Thurgau, wine-growing commissioner Hansueli Pfenninger is expecting “a very early start to the harvest” – from the end of August. This situation has already occurred in 2003 and 2018. And just as in those two exceptional years, Pfenninger is also expecting an outstanding vintage in 2026.
Small grapes
In Graubünden, too, the drought will affect the grape harvest, predicts his colleague Walter Fromm. However, the lack of moisture does not affect all regions to the same extent. West of Maienfeld and east of Fläsch, the vineyards with light soils and low water-retention capacity are most at risk. It is also striking in many places that the grapes have turned out very small due to the lack of water.
+ Swiss winegrowers begin harvest in mid-August for first time
In some cantons of French-speaking Switzerland, there has never before been such an early grape harvest in August. Rémy Alain Reymond, head of the Neuchâtel Office for Viticulture and Agroecology, speaks of a “historically early ripening”. “We had expected a very early vintage, and yet many winegrowers are still surprised by it,” he added.
In Valais, the grape harvest is expected to begin in the week of August 24 for certain well-exposed vineyards and to extend to the entire region from August 31 onwards, which is particularly early. “According to ripeness checks, we are currently between six and twelve days ahead of 2022, which was a hot year,” the Valais Office for Viticulture and Wine told the Keystone-SDA news agency in response to an enquiry.
In the canton of Geneva, the harvest timing is classified as “rather normal for a year with a heatwave”, explained Dorian Pajic, head of the Viticulture and Oenology Programme at the Cantonal Office for Agriculture and Nature.
Heat determines quality
Finally, in the canton of Vaud, the grape harvest will begin in early September, around two days later than in 2003. It holds the record for the earliest harvest, as François Montet, president of the Vaud Winegrowers’ Association, emphasised. He noted, however, that the heatwave had no influence on the timing of the harvest.
This is determined by the timing of the vines’ flowering, which in turn is influenced by the spring warmth. The summer heatwave, on the other hand, determines the quality, he said, predicting that the 2026 vintage would be of very high quality.
Nevertheless, there are some concerns. According to oenologists, extreme heat and very strong sunlight can cause the grapes to scorch and suffer sunburn, which may lead to crop losses. Water shortages are also detrimental to the harvest yield. That is why many winegrowers are hoping for a few rain showers before they begin the harvest.

H1N1 alert: Health ministry lists symptoms to look for as Delhi crosses 1,700 cases
TOI News Desk / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Aug 22, 2026, 15:36 IST
Comments

H1N1 on rise in Delhi
NEW DELHI: The ministry of health and family welfare (MoHFW) on Saturday has urged people to recognise the H1N1 symptoms early and seek medical advice if they persist.In a post on X on Saturday, the ministry said swine flu can show up through symptoms including fever, cough, sore throat, headache, runny nose, body aches and fatigue. It advised people not to ignore persistent symptoms and to seek medical advice at the nearest healthcare centre.
The health ministry’s advisory also lists lethargy and loss of appetite, nausea and vomiting, joint and muscle pain, diarrhoea and headache among the common symptoms associated with swine flu.
Explaining the symptoms and transmission of H1N1, Dr (Major) Rajesh Bhardwaj, founder, ENT and Sleep Expert, MedFirst ENT Centre, said, “H1N1 infection, or swine flu, can be somewhat more dangerous and serious, which is why we are more concerned about it.”He said the infection spreads through respiratory droplets released when an infected person coughs or sneezes, and can also spread through close contact with an infected person.
“The symptoms include high fever, body aches, weakness, lethargy, cough, sore throat, difficulty breathing, and sometimes loss of the sense of smell. There can also be throat irritation and cough,” Bhardwaj said.
Staying home while sick reduces exposure to others. Covering coughs and sneezes, washing hands regularly and improving ventilation can also limit spread.
A mask can be particularly useful when someone has respiratory symptoms and must enter a crowded indoor setting.The Delhi government, in a post on X, shared precautionary steps. "Vigilance and timely treatment are extremely crucial for protection against H1N1," it wrote.It advised people to cover their nose and mouth while coughing or sneezing, wash their hands regularly, consult a doctor if symptoms appear and avoid taking medicines without medical advice.
On Friday, Union health minister JP Nadda reviewed Delhi’s preparedness for influenza and vector-borne diseases as Delhi has reported 2,392 influenza A cases this year, including 1,777 H1N1 infections.

Jafari: Bam Khatoon a worthy representative for Iran
TEHRAN – Marziyeh Jafari, head coach of Bam Khatoon, expressed pride in her players, insisting her side are a worthy representative of the country in the tournament.
Jafari spoke about her team's performance in the group stage of the AFC Women's Champions League, revealing the squad were severely hampered by injuries to three key players.
"Negin (Zandi) was unavailable, Mona (Hamoudi) was injured, and Fatemeh (Geraei) suffered a setback in the 20th minute of our opening match and unfortunately couldn't feature for the rest of the competition," she explained.
Jafari described the group as a "group of death. "CSKA Dushanbe not only had Tajikistan's full internationals but had also brought in four quality foreign signings from Africa. We didn't know much about them, but despite those circumstances, our players produced a good performance and thankfully we won the match.”
On the clash with Al Nassr, the coach was full of respect for the opposition. "Al Nassr are a very powerful side with quality players from various countries — French, Portuguese, Bahraini and Japanese. It's clear they've invested heavily in their squad."
"We knew it would be a tough game, and perhaps our players were somewhat overawed by the name of Al Nassr. We could have used our chances better. In the 85th minute the referee awarded Al Nassr a penalty which unfortunately was converted, but our players kept fighting and equalized in the 95th minute to keep our hopes alive,” she added.
She also pointed to Khatoon's long layoff from competitive action. "Our league ended in February, and about seven months have passed since then. It was natural that being away from match conditions would make things difficult for us. In contrast, teams like Al Nassr and Al Ittihad were competing in West Asian tournaments last month and had played good friendlies. They were also in a very strong position regarding the number of internationals and quality foreign players."
Despite the odds, Jafari stood firmly behind her squad: "Despite all these conditions, the players worked incredibly hard and got good results. As head coach, I'm proud of my players, and I believe Khatoon are worthy representatives of our beloved country in this tournament."
She stressed the importance of planning and clear goals. "I've always emphasized that we need to plan and have targets, and follow a clear path to achieve them. You can't just go game by game always chasing a result. I hope that in the final match, which we play on Sunday, we deliver a good performance and finish our campaign in the best possible way with a favorable result."

Poland Maintains Long‑Term Legal, Financial Protections for 1.7 Million Ukrainian Refugees
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
10:04:00 UTC
19:04:00 KST

Since the beginning of Russia’s full-scale invasion, Poland has provided legal and financial protection to 1.7 million Ukrainian citizens who were forced to leave their country due to the war, the Polish Ministry of Foreign Affairs reported.
The ministry noted that the assistance provided to Ukrainians represents one of the largest displays of public support in the country following the onset of Russian aggression.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
According to the Polish MFA, approximately 77% of Poles have actively participated in helping Ukrainian refugees in various ways. Furthermore, 7% of Polish citizens opened their own homes to host Ukrainians fleeing the conflict.
The total volume of funds spent by Polish society to support Ukrainians has exceeded 10 billion zlotys.
The Polish foreign policy department emphasized that these figures demonstrate the enormous scale of assistance Poland has provided to Ukrainians since the start of the full-scale war.
Changing public sentiment
The release of the refugee data follows recent polling indicating growing reservations among the Polish public regarding their country’s future role in supporting Ukraine.
An Opinia24 poll published in late July found that a majority of Poles oppose their country supporting Ukraine’s efforts to join the EU. The survey indicated that 52% of respondents opposed Poland supporting Ukraine’s EU membership efforts, compared with 33% who favored such support.
Ukraine Appoints 16 New Judges to High Anti-Corruption Court
Opposition was notably stronger regarding the potential deployment of Polish troops to Ukraine following the war. Sixty-five percent of respondents rejected the idea of sending Polish forces to supervise a ceasefire or peace agreement, while only 18% supported the proposal.
When asked whether their attitudes toward Ukrainians had changed since the beginning of Russia’s full-scale invasion, 54% of respondents said their views remained unchanged. However, 36% stated their attitudes had worsened, while only 3% reported an improvement.
Historical disputes and military aid
Views on continued military support remain closely divided, particularly when framed around historical disputes. When asked about assistance in the context of Ukraine’s commemoration of the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA), 44% of respondents said Poland should suspend military assistance, while 41% said Warsaw should continue supporting Ukraine.
A separate IBRiS poll published earlier in July found that 52.2% of respondents supported continued Polish military assistance overall, while 45.2% opposed it.
The Opinia24 survey also demonstrated approval for Polish President Karol Nawrocki’s recent decision to strip President Volodymyr Zelensky of the Order of the White Eagle, Poland’s highest state decoration. Fifty-five percent of respondents supported the decision, while 27% opposed it.
Poland has served as a major transit hub for international military and humanitarian assistance and has provided substantial weapons supplies to Ukraine since February 2022.
However, disputes connected to the UPA and the wartime massacres of Poles in Volhynia and Eastern Galicia have remained a persistent source of tension between Warsaw and Kyiv.

Unknown Publisher

Hong Kong police arrest 2 men allegedly linked to HK$500,000 phishing scam
Officers find 110 SIM cards and modem pool in hotel room allegedly used to send more than 2,000 scam texts about undelivered parcels and insurance fees
Hong Kong police have arrested two men suspected of using 110 SIM cards to send phishing messages from a base of operations in a hotel and conning victims out of more than HK$500,000 (US$63,766).
The force said on Saturday the men, aged 31 and 44, were arrested last Thursday on suspicion of conspiracy to defraud.
They were allegedly linked to recent phishing scams in which fraudsters posed as delivery company staff, claiming victims had undelivered parcels, or as employees of online payment platforms, saying victims had to pay a fee to cancel an insurance plan they had mistakenly subscribed to. Victims were then induced to call a fake customer service hotline.
After victims called the hotline, the fraudsters instructed them to transfer money to designated bank accounts using various pretexts, police said.
“Investigation revealed that the suspects had bought a bulk of SIM cards with real name registration from different people,” Inspector Kwan Yat-hei of the fraud division under the force’s commercial crime bureau said.
He added that the suspects had rented a hotel room as an operations centre, where officers found a modem pool – a device that allows users to control multiple SIM cards simultaneously – nine mobile phones and 110 SIM cards.

19:00:49 KST

'Aura farming' battles turn TikTok memes, poses and viral gestures into a contest where young people test their charisma, style and self-confidence.
Two teenagers stand face to face, surrounded by a crowd. They stare each other down and get ready to compete. But there are no punches here, no improvised rhymes and no typical dance-off. To win, you have to show who has more "aura".
The so-called "aura farming" battles, or "farmear aura", have taken to the streets a set of expressions born on social media. Teenagers and young adults, mostly between 14 and 20, compete using gestures, poses and recreations of some of the internet’s most recognisable memes and viral videos.
The phenomenon has already given rise to meet-ups in several Latin American countries, including Mexico, Argentina, Brazil, Peru and Bolivia, and has now reached Spain as well. And while for anyone unfamiliar with TikTok’s codes some of the performances can be hard to decipher, for the participants spotting the references is part of the game.
But what exactly does "farmear aura" mean, and why are teenagers competing to get it?
What does "farmear aura" mean?
The concept comes from combining two very different ideas.
On social platforms such as TikTok and Instagram, "aura" is used to describe the style, attitude or charisma a person projects. Saying someone has "100% aura", for instance, is a way of praising their ability to look attractive, confident or cool almost without trying.
"Farmear", on the other hand, comes from the world of video games. The English term "farming" refers to repeating certain actions to gain points or accumulate resources.
"Farmear aura" therefore means doing or showing something that symbolically earns you points for charisma, style or popularity. What began as an online expression has ended up turning into a real-world competition.
How do you win an aura battle?
At one of these contests held recently in front of the Palace of Fine Arts in Mexico City, participants drew on a whole catalogue of viral references in an effort to outdo their opponents.
Carlos Irving Quintana, a 14-year-old with purple hair, won applause from the crowd by recreating the famous "Siuuu" leap Cristiano Ronaldo uses to celebrate his goals. He then switched to "mewing", a trend popularised on TikTok that involves tensing the jaw and pointing at it with a finger to show off one’s profile.
His rival replied with the "6-7", a meme widespread among young people that does not have a specific meaning but has become a recognisable gesture on social media. Spectators crowd around the competitors and film their performances on their phones while music plays that sounds like a video game soundtrack.
The key is demonstrating that you have mastered the codes of the internet. The more memes and viral videos a contestant manages to weave into their routine, the better their chances of impressing the judges and the crowd.
But knowing the memes is not enough. Attitude is crucial. "Whoever looks better, shows off more, gets more laughs and has more confidence wins", explains 22-year-old Aldhir Gonzalez, organiser of the Mexico City competition, speaking to AFP.
From Cristiano Ronaldo to a giant shoe
Almost anything can become a prop for "aura farming". The winner of the Mexican contest was Kaled Rosales Salazar, who turned up wearing Rayo McQueen trousers – the lead character in the film "Cars" – and clogs.
In one of his duels, Rosales used an enormous white sandal as an accessory and mimed lassoing his rival and leading him away like a horse. The staging worked. The teenager walked away with the 3,000-peso prize, around 177 dollars.
In other competitions, however, the reward can be far more abstract. In Argentina, the prize is bragging rights: being able to claim you have "infinite aura".
The trend has grown to the point of reaching professional football. Argentine club Boca Juniors has jumped on the craze, posting on X an image of midfielder Santiago Ascacibar celebrating a goal and joking that his aura was unbeatable.
A trend that baffles adults
Not everyone gets the phenomenon. "Aura is a lifestyle" that "almost nobody understands", says the organiser of an upcoming battle in Buenos Aires.
And that lack of understanding is particularly visible between generations. While for many teenagers the poses and gestures are packed with instantly recognisable references, some adults see these competitions as a sign that popular culture is being dumbed down.
The backlash has even reached politics. A mayor in Honduras has banned the battles and said that if it were up to him there would be compulsory military service. Other experts, however, see positive aspects to the trend.
Venezuelan psychologist Maria Eugenia Tovar argues that this kind of contest can encourage face-to-face encounters between teenagers, something particularly significant for a generation used to interacting mainly through social media.
And that may be one of the keys to its success. A phenomenon born on TikTok and Instagram is managing to get young people to put down their individual screens for a few hours and meet up in person – even if everything ends up being filmed on a phone and posted online afterwards.
For Rosales, the winner of the Mexico City competition, the explanation is much simpler. He plans to take part in more battles, but not necessarily for the money. "More than for a prize, I do it to have fun and get out of the house", he tells AFP.

Global data shows a sharp rise in adult ADHD diagnoses and medication prescriptions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
10:00:45 UTC
19:00:45 KST

Diagnoses for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) have increased in many countries across all age groups, our latest review has found. We have also shown that prescriptions for ADHD treatments have seen similar increases across all age groups.
Our latest review, published in the Journal of Psychopharmacology, drew together the recently published research on ADHD diagnoses and prescriptions across the world.
We found that in the UK, increases in recorded ADHD diagnoses and treatment prescriptions occurred across all age groups between 2000 and 2018.
The greatest rise in ADHD diagnoses across this period was among children. However, there was also a distinct increase in adults. For example, among men aged 18-29 there was an approximately 20-fold increase in diagnoses and an almost 50-fold increase in prescriptions.
The sex ratio of ADHD diagnoses in childhood and adolescence was approximately 4:1 male to female. However, the ratio of diagnoses in adulthood is nearly 1:1. This shift may partly reflect increased recognition of how ADHD presents in girls and adults – groups that have historically been underdiagnosed.
Alongside these increases in ADHD diagnoses, there has also been an increase in prescriptions for ADHD treatments.
In England, prescriptions of central nervous system stimulants (the main prescription treatments for ADHD) increased by 32% in adults over 18 in 2021-22. In children under 17, prescriptions increased by 12% from 2022-23. This was also the first time that more adults were prescribed these drugs than children since records started in 2015.
A retrospective study of over 154 million people from 13 countries, including in North America, Europe and Asia, demonstrated that use of ADHD medication prescriptions had increased in these regions as well.
Why diagnoses and prescriptions are increasing
A few key factors can largely explain the increase in both ADHD diagnoses and prescriptions that we’ve seen. This includes increased public awareness of the condition, better understanding by doctors of the way symptoms present and the availability of new and improved medications.
Additionally, there is better awareness of how ADHD manifests in groups who may have previously been missed because their symptoms did not match with those typically exhibited in boys and adolescents. This includes women and girls and people with predominantly inattentive symptoms.
However, these factors may only tell part of the story. Our review also revealed other drivers may deserve careful consideration.
For instance, there has been much debate over whether there is an issue of overdiagnosis and over-prescribing. Legitimate questions about whether some attention difficulties might be over-medicalised have also been raised. On the other hand, some authors have argued that there is no evidence to suggest overdiagnosis is occurring in the UK.
Understanding the full picture requires looking beyond the obvious explanations to examine cultural, economic, social and technological pressures in a globally competitive environment that may be influencing both diagnosis rates and treatment choices.
Looking forward
The rising rates of ADHD diagnoses and treatment represent a complex picture. There have been genuine improvements in recognising a real disorder that was historically overlooked (particularly in adult men and women), better clinical awareness and perhaps also some degree of over-identification in certain environments.
What seems clear is that ADHD, long thought of as a children’s disorder, is now being treated as what it truly is: a lifelong neurodevelopmental disorder affecting millions of people across the globe.
As awareness continues to grow, the challenge ahead lies in preserving limited NHS resources, while ensuring those who genuinely need these resources have improved access.
The wait time for an ADHD diagnosis in England currently ranges from two to 15 years. With increasing rates of diagnoses and prescriptions to manage ADHD, there are concerns that demand will soon outstrip NHS capacity entirely.
What could be a solution is the discovery of ADHD biomarkers – an objectively measurable indicator of a biological state or condition that can be detected in signatures in the brain. Currently, ADHD is diagnosed by a doctor who often has to rely on self-reported symptoms. Having biomarkers could improve the accuracy of diagnoses, ensuring those who have the condition get the support they need earlier on.

Bildt says Baltic aggression would expose Kaliningrad
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
11:00:27 BST
19:00:27 KST

Carl Bildt has said that any Russian aggression in the Baltic would immediately affect the security of Kaliningrad, referencing the concentration of NATO aircraft that has operated around the exclave over the past week.
Writing on Friday, the former Swedish prime minister and foreign minister, now co-chair of the European Council on Foreign Relations, said: “I’m sure Russia has carefully noted the advanced NATO presence in the vicinity of Kaliningrad the last few days. It certainly sent a powerful signal. Any Russian aggression in the Baltic area will immediately impact the security of Kaliningrad.”
He posted alongside a flight tracking image showing two NATO E-3A Sentry airborne early warning aircraft from Geilenkirchen, registered LX-N90444 and LX-N90445, operating over Lithuania and Poland, together with a Multinational MRTT Fleet A330 tanker out of Eindhoven and a United States Air Force KC-135R from RAF Mildenhall.
As we reported this week, allied aircraft have been massing over the Baltic region in numbers and combinations rarely seen outside a declared exercise.
The activity on 18 August involved around 25 aircraft drawn from several member states, operating from Poland and the Baltic states, in a package overseen by the United States. Alongside American and Norwegian fighters and a NATO E-3A, flight trackers logged an EA-37B Compass Call electronic attack aircraft, an ARTEMIS II intelligence platform, Polish Gulfstream G550s, multiple MRTT tankers, a Lithuanian Let L-410 and American AH-64E Apache helicopters, with Polish ground forces participating.
Allied Air Command confirmed the activity but said it could not disclose further detail for operational security reasons. A United States Air Forces in Europe official subsequently confirmed the training was scheduled to run across several days, and further flights followed on 19 and 20 August.
What distinguishes the past week from routine patrolling is the mix of capabilities. Refuelling, airborne command and control, intelligence gathering and electronic attack were airborne simultaneously, which is the shape of a strike package rather than a surveillance sortie.
The presence of the EA-37B in particular has drawn attention. The aircraft is designed to disrupt communications, radar and navigation systems, and the type flew its first operational mission from Souda Bay on 19 August focused on the electromagnetic environment around Kaliningrad.
Kaliningrad is the reason the Baltic sits where it does in NATO planning. The exclave has no land connection to the rest of Russia, hosts the headquarters of the Baltic Fleet at Baltiysk, and carries air defence and missile systems whose reach extends well into allied airspace. It also sits alongside the Suwalki gap, the stretch of Polish and Lithuanian border separating it from Belarus and forming the only land route between the Baltic states and the rest of the alliance.
Bildt’s point cuts in the direction less often stated. The exclave’s geography, usually discussed as a threat to allied reinforcement, also leaves it surrounded by NATO members and dependent on sea and air corridors the alliance could close.
The build-up follows a period of steadily rising activity, recently a Royal Air Force RC-135W Rivet Joint flew a patrol around the exclave on 7 August, returning to RAF Waddington after routing through the North Sea into the Baltic. An Italian Eurofighter operating under NATO command shot down a drone over north-eastern Latvia on 14 August, in an incident Latvia’s armed forces attributed to Russian electromagnetic warfare pushing the aircraft off course. Baltic Air Policing detachments have continued to intercept Russian aircraft transiting between mainland Russia and Kaliningrad, typically flying without transponders or filed flight plans.
Running alongside all of it is Lion Protector 26, the Joint Expeditionary Force exercise which began on 3 August and runs to 12 October across Northern Europe, the North Atlantic and the Baltic, and which opened with the escorted movement of allied military equipment into Latvian ports.

Chinese man reunites with family after 25 years in total isolation to honour a promise
During his isolation, Li lived off the land by growing corn, raising livestock, and fishing, with the nearest grocery store 3km away
A Chinese man in his 60s has finally reunited with his family after spending 25 years in isolation to care for a house deep in the mountains, even after the owner had forgotten about it.
Li Guoyou, 63, recently received his renewed hukou booklet, China’s official household registration, at a police station in Pingtan, a town in southwestern Sichuan province. This marked his official identity registration in his hometown after nearly three decades away.
Li left home at the age of 24 in 1987, moving to Guangzhou in southern China in search of better work opportunities. Over time, he gradually lost contact with his two brothers, his only family after their parents died.
He returned home once in 1997, but did not meet his brothers, who were both working elsewhere. He left behind a landline number, which his family tried to dial repeatedly in the years that followed, but to no avail.
In 1998, Li migrated to Harbin, the capital of Heilongjiang province in northern China, where he met a highway restaurant owner named Lin. Lin took Li in as an employee, providing him with a means to make a living.

How to Increase Mental-Health Literacy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
10:00:04 UTC
19:00:04 KST

Imagine that someone you love starts turning down opportunities to attend social gatherings like going to the movies, picnics, and parties. Then this person stops responding consistently to your texts, avoids eye contact when you do get together, and seems to be losing their energy or spark. They have trouble keeping up with daily routines and talk a lot about physical struggles such as headaches and stomach aches. Something doesn’t feel right to you, but you’re not sure what is happening or what to do. Imagine now if the person all these things are happening to is you.
Nearly one in seven people worldwide have a mental-health disorder. With the prevalence of mental disorders so high, odds are we all know and love someone who is struggling. But most of us have limited understanding of mental health, and sometimes misguided or inaccurate knowledge. If we improve our understanding, this could help us better identify when we are in distress and get the help we need. It can also potentially assist us in helping friends, family members, neighbors, and co-workers. As a psychologist, I believe we could all benefit from increased mental-health literacy.
The concept of mental-health literacy was first coined in the mid-1990s by a group of Australian researchers who began a series of studies to understand the public’s knowledge about mental health. Since then, extensive research on mental-health literacy has taken place in the U.S., Australia, Canada, the U.K., India, Japan, and elsewhere.
Data from 16 studies indicate two major trends in public awareness about mental health. First, we’re making some headway in recognizing that mental disorders often have some biological underpinnings. Second, there seems to be more acceptance of professional help for such difficulties. But it’s not nearly enough.
Finding sound mental-health information can be challenging. The Internet has the potential to increase our access to evidence-informed knowledge and decrease unmet mental health needs, but there’s too much noise. And a lot of information online is of inadequate quality and lacks scientific evaluation. Rather than helping, random Internet searches on mental health could harm people most in need.
One way to further increase our mental health literacy is to take the free online Mental Health First Aid course. This could help us gain knowledge on how to recognize when a disorder is developing and provide information on help-seeking options and available treatments.
One of the best resources for evidence-based information is the National Institute of Mental Health. Established in 1949, this is one of the world’s largest research organizations funding brain and behavior research. It offers valuable online public resources including signs and symptoms of a broad range of disorders including anxiety, depression, eating disorders, and ADHD. It also provides information on the latest and best treatments and how to find a mental-health provider. Another accurate and up-to-date source is the National Alliance on Mental Illness, the largest grassroots mental-health organization in the U.S. They too offer research informed information online on how to find support including a helpline.
While mental-health literacy is everybody’s business, there are limits to the appropriate use of such information, particularly in our offers to help others. Let’s take the example of problematic drinking. It’s good to be able to recognize our own or a family member’s struggles with alcohol. But there are differences in providing someone with encouragement and assistance in getting help and respecting their boundaries if they refuse or are uninterested. Mental-health literacy can help us distinguish the best way to approach issues like these.
If you or someone you know may be experiencing a mental-health crisis or contemplating suicide, call or text 988. In emergencies, call 911, or seek care from a local hospital or mental health provider.

ICE agent jailed on allegations of breaking into ex-girlfriend’s apartment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
10:00:02 UTC
19:00:02 KST

A US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer was jailed on Friday on allegations of breaking into a woman’s apartment.
Thomas Bailey, 58, faces a charge of unauthorized entry of an inhabited dwelling after his arrest by the sheriff’s office of St Tammany parish, Louisiana, the agency said in a statement.
The sheriff’s office said Bailey entered his ex-girlfriend’s apartment near the community of Covington, a New Orleans suburb on the north shore of Lake Pontchartrain, without her permission. She was not in the apartment at the time, and the sheriff’s office said investigators booked him with a crime defined as the “intentional entry without authorization into any inhabited dwelling … used … as a home or place of abode by another person”.
Bailey is employed by an ICE office in the Louisiana community of Oakdale, which by car is about three hours to the west of Covington, the St Tammany sheriff’s office said. The agency’s statement noted that he was a resident of Lecompte, which is about a half-hour’s drive to the north-east of Oakdale.
The sheriff’s office referred to Bailey as a federal officer but did not provide specific details about his role within ICE, which has been at the forefront of the mass deportation campaign that the administration of Donald Trump has pursued during his second presidency. A page under Bailey’s name on the professional networking social media site LinkedIn refers to him as an “agent” of ICE.
An ICE spokesperson on Friday said in a statement that the agency could not comment on Bailey’s arrest “due to the sensitive nature of these charges and pending litigation”.
However, the statement said that ICE “stresses integrity and ethical behavior, and the vast majority of [agency] employees perform their duties with professionalism and honor”.
“ICE takes all allegations of employee misconduct seriously,” the statement continued. “Any allegations of misconduct are investigated by the appropriate agencies, and any employee who has committed provable misconduct will be held accountable. ICE takes swift and appropriate action to investigate and cooperate with outside law enforcement agencies when allegations of criminal conduct by an employee are suspected or alleged.”
Prior to Bailey’s case, ICE had been met with public scrutiny over its hiring practices after the Associated Press reported in February that a least two dozen of the agency’s employees and contractors had been charged with crimes since 2020. The wrongdoing in question involved physical and sexual abuse, misuses of authority, and corruption, according to the AP’s review.
The outlet later reported that rapid recruitment and expansion by ICE, particularly as the Trump administration prepared to implement its mass deportation agenda, had set the stage for an influx of employees with questionable qualifications.
Furthermore, in late July, the Trump administration’s border chief, Tom Homan, appeared on CNN and said he doubted that an ICE officer at the center of a recent fatal shooting “should have ever cleared vetting”.
Homan made that remark in the aftermath of the deadly shooting of Joan Sebastián Durán Guerrero on 13 July in Biddeford, Maine. The officer involved in that killing was later identified by news outlets as David Brouillette. Two of Brouillette’s ex-wives publicly described alleged abusive, violent and threatening behavior during their relationships with him.
Asked “should someone with those issues be an ICE agent”, Homan said: “No, if those … are facts … I don’t think he should ever have cleared vetting.”
A poll taken by PBS News, National Public Radio and Marist after immigration agents’ killings of US citizens Alex Pretti and Renee Good in Minneapolis in January determined Americans largely disapproved of ICE agents.
Nearly two-thirds of those surveyed – 65% – said they believed ICE had gone too far in enforcing the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown, the pollsters said.
A statement from the executive director of the Ohio Immigrant Alliance advocacy group, Lynn Tramonte, after Bailey’s arrest called on Congress to stop funding agencies like ICE until the screening of “every single agent for domestic violence and other dangerous behaviors”.
A bond amount for Bailey was not immediately set, St Tammany parish jail records showed on Friday. It was not immediately clear whether Bailey had an attorney.
“Regardless of where you work or what position you hold, the law applies equally to everyone,” a statement attributed to the St Tammany sheriff, Bret Ibert, said on Friday after Bailey’s arrest. “When someone enters another person’s residence without permission, we are going to investigate the circumstances and take the appropriate action based on the facts of the case.”
Bailey could receive up to six years in prison and a maximum fine of $1,000 if eventually convicted of unauthorized entry of an inhabited dwelling.

Lindsay Clancy trial: everything that happened this week in court
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
10:00:01 UTC
19:00:01 KST

The trial of Lindsay Clancy, the Massachusetts mother accused of killing her three children in January 2023, will likely head to the jury next week to decide if she is guilty of murder or was suffering from postpartum psychosis and should not be held criminally responsible.
The outcome may come down to expert witness testimony – and there have been many – but the trial will be remembered for the spotlight it put on maternal health care in the United States. Defense lawyer Kevin Reddington has said that, in addition to postpartum psychosis, Clancy also had bipolar disorder and was overmedicated.
‘Postpartum psychosis’
On Wednesday and Thursday, jurors were sent home early. Judge William Sullivan described the first as an “unforeseen circumstance” and directed the jury “not to speculate about what it is; you’re not to hold it against either side. It’s just something that we have to deal with”.
Thursday’s abbreviated session came after a hospital chaplain, Sheila Cavanaugh – who met with Clancy after the deaths of the children and her alleged suicide attempt – testified that Clancy recalled to her a voice that allegedly told her to kill her children. Clancy told her: “I am so glad my children are safe.’”
Cavanaugh said in the days after the murders, while Clancy was still receiving emergency care treatment at Brigham and Women’s Hospital, “her emotional state was very neutral, a flat affect.” She said that Clancy mentioned hearing a male voice multiple times.
“The voice, according to Lindsay, told her that if she did not follow the command, neither she nor her children would be safe,” Cavanaugh said. “She alluded to the fact that it was a male voice, and it was persistent.”
Cavanaugh said that she “replied theologically” to Clancy, saying, “Lindsay, your children are safe. They’re safe in heaven with God.”
Defense witness Paul Zeizel, a forensic psychologist who met with Clancy dozens of times and reviewed her medical records, offered powerful testimony this week and echoed Cavanaugh’s claims.
Ziezel recalled that Clancy had said during a telephone call with her former husband, Patrick Clancy, “that she heard a male voice ordering her, telling her that she didn’t have any choice, but she had to kill her children and then kill herself”.
Elsewhere in his testimony, Zeizel noted that Clancy had been “unable to conform her behavior to the rule of law. She had no appreciation for the wrongfulness of her act.” He said that psychological testing administered by a government doctor found no evidence she was manufacturing or exaggerating psychiatric symptoms.
The defense’s final witness was Dr Phillip Resnick, a forensic psychiatrist with expertise in postpartum disorders who had consulted on the case of Andrea Yates – a Texas mother who drowned her five children and was later found not guilty by reason of insanity – who said he believed Clancy was “frankly psychotic” on the day she killed her children.
He said Clancy was in a “postpartum psychosis” after her third child was born. On the day of the killings, he said, Clancy was hearing not only “command hallucinations” but felt what’s known as a “delusion of influence” and that an “external force” had taken over her body.
‘She needed help’
The defense rested their case after Resnick’s testimony on Friday and the trial moved into the rebuttal phase.
Prosecutors pushed back on defense claims that Clancy was suffering from a postpartum mental illness that caused her to break from reality. They contend Clancy acted deliberately and rationally when she took the lives of her children Cora, five, Dawson, three, and Callan, eight months, after sending her husband out on errands.
Prosecutors recalled psychiatrist Dr Avram Mack to the stand. Mack said that the medical standard for assessing if someone can be held criminally responsible for their actions under Massachusetts law, they would have to know their actions were wrong.
The burden of proof is on prosecutors to show that Clancy “did not suffer from a mental disease or defect at the time of the alleged offense” or that, even if she did, she “retained the substantial capacity to appreciate the wrongfulness or criminality of her conduct and to conform her conduct to the requirements of the law”.
Mack said Clancy suffered from a “major depressive episode” in 2022 and 2023, and that he had reached that conclusion based on Clancy’s descriptions of her feelings and the progression of her illness.
“Generally she was friendly and cooperative,” Mack said of his meetings with Clancy after the killings. “There were not many abnormalities in her presentation.” He said that “at some points she seemed distressed” and had told him she was “miserable”.
During cross-examination, Reddington’s line of questioning with Mack became contentious. Reddington criticized Mack for educating himself about Clancy’s background only through Clancy herself while she was medicated in a psychiatric hospital and notably without interviewing other people from her life.
Asked about Clancy’s condition in the aftermath of the birth of Callan, Mack testified that Clancy had been anxious about returning to work and having a nanny.
“There was some degree of wanting to be able to handle the children on her own,” Mack said. “She felt very positively about her ability to take care the children, but also some ambivalence about other people being able to take care of the children.”
Given the widespread interest in the trial online and beyond, the subject matter has ignited a movement for those invested in maternal and postpartum healthcare in the US. Earlier in the week, on Thursday, hundreds of women gathered outside the courthouse in support of Clancy, with many donning pink clothing with statements such as “She Needed Help.”
“Women are being dismissed, neglected and ignored when we speak up,” April Vincent, who was in attendance, said. “We’re scared because nobody takes us seriously.”
Possible outcomes
If jurors acquit Clancy of murder by reason of insanity, she will not go free but would be sent to a state psychiatric hospital and come up for periodic review for release. If jurors find for the prosecution, she will be sentenced to life without parole.
Closing arguments are slated to begin next week.
Still, Clancy’s legal battles will not end with the verdict for this trial. A civil case brought by Clancy and her former husband is pending against several mental healthcare providers, including two mental health workers who saw Clancy before the killings and testified at trial.

Young country diary: Camping in my garden, nose to nose with a fox | Ada
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
10:00:01 UTC
19:00:01 KST

Dad and I were boiling in the house because of the UK heatwave. So we decided to camp out and sleep in our garden instead. Before we went to bed, while playing catch, we could hear the swifts swoop around our house in the orange evening light.
Once it had cooled down, Dad said it was time for bed and tucked me up. At some point in the night, Dad heard something and he tried to wake me up. There was a vixen – a female fox – drinking from the pond, but I missed it. The next morning, Dad told me about the fox and I said, if it comes again, pull my toe.
There are about 150,000 urban foxes living in the towns and cities of the UK. They have amazing hearing – they can hear a watch ticking from 40m away, and a mouse moving around under the snow. That night, one did come to our garden again. Dad woke me up – I felt sleepy but it was exciting.
She was standing just 10cm away from the tent – we were nose to nose. She was looking through the mesh window with her sharp pointed teeth and her triangular ears pointing up into the night sky. The thing that stood out the most was her beautiful amber fur. I could see how soft it was, and her wonderful eyes that glistened in the moonlight.
You don’t need to live in the countryside to see amazing wildlife.
Ada, eight

NASA’s nuclear Dragonfly copter to search for signs of life on Titan: ‘A lot’s riding on it’

“There’s very little else coming down the pipeline,” Dreier said. “So a lot’s riding on it.”
The Trump administration cut NASA’s science mission budget in half in 2025, jeopardizing several planetary missions. The uncertainty in funding has put on hold future missions to Uranus, Venus and Enceladus, and a return of rock and soil samples from Mars, Dreier said.
Dragonfly is a survivor, just like its insect namesake. Turtle and other scientists who have spent decades working on the mission will be on edge when it makes its two-hour descent to Titan’s surface in 2034.
She often considers what it would be like to stand on Titan’s surface. Despite the cold, there’s no radiation to worry about and only gentle 10 mph winds to disturb those dunes.
“It’s a pretty benign environment and well-protected,” Turtle said. “It would be fascinating to explore and to consider, hang-gliding over the surface. It would be just wild.”
