Persuasion, denial and bluster: Trump ‘stuck’ on Iran war ahead of elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
09:00:05 UTC
18:00:05 KST

In the aftermath of his devastating election defeat, the US president remained haunted by regrets over Iran.
Months before Jimmy Carter lost the 1980 presidential election to Ronald Reagan, eight US servicemen died in a botched high-risk rescue mission that failed to secure the freedom of dozens of US hostages seized in Tehran.
As he addressed students and academics, keen for reflections on his single-term presidency, one of the students asked Carter: what do you most regret?
“Not sending more helicopters for the hostage rescue,” he immediately replied, according to Larry Sabato, director of the Center for Politics at the University of Virginia, who hosted the former president. “It was very much on his mind,” said Sabato.
Carter’s fate nearly half a century ago may also be on the mind of Donald Trump as he prepares to embark upon a midterm election campaign over the coming months, while embroiled in a military struggle with Tehran. The Iranian regime is proving equally intractable to that faced by his Democratic predecessor.
Trump’s efforts to finish the war he started along with Israel almost six months ago, on 28 February, have foundered after a ceasefire agreement signed in June collapsed – leaving Iran in control of the strait of Hormuz, a waterway that was the conduit for one-fifth of the world’s oil supplies before the conflict.
The Iranian stranglehold has pushed up oil prices, stoked inflation and raised living costs in the US, all as Trump’s Republican party already faced an uphill struggle to retain control of US Congress in November’s midterm elections.
With public support for the war running low, polls show a majority of American voters believe they are worse off since Trump returned to office in January 2025. That indicator alone has echoes of Reagan’s famous question to voters during his 1980 presidential debate with Carter: “Are you better off than you were four years ago?”
‘Trump can’t change course’
While the circumstances are different, Trump’s troubles have a broader resemblance to Carter’s dilemma, which began when revolutionaries stormed the US embassy in November 1979 and held 52 diplomats and military personnel hostage.
That was compounded after a daring rescue attempt the following April had to be aborted when three out of eight helicopters deployed on the mission developed mechanical faults. One of the remaining craft collided with a transport plane, killing eight US servicemen and intensifying the ignominy.
Later efforts to negotiate the hostages’ release before the presidential election failed, most notably on the weekend before polling day, when a putative deal collapsed, making Carter’s electoral defeat almost certain.
They were eventually released after 444 days in captivity, minutes after Reagan was sworn into office on 20 January 1981.
The historic parallels are imprecise, but sufficient to be perceived by both Trump and Iran’s current leaders, analysts say.
“Carter couldn’t change course, and maybe that’s what’s most applicable, because Trump can’t change course either,” said Sabato. “Carter was stuck because, after the failed rescue, the hostages were dispersed throughout Iran and there was no way to recover them.
“Trump is stuck because he never had a good rationale [for the war]. He just wanted another victory. All they had to say to Trump to get him to go in was ‘Mr President, this is just going to be another Venezuela, and then we can go in and do Cuba.’”
With a 60-day ceasefire since June’s memorandum of understanding (MOU) signed in June lapsing this week without any formal resolution, Trump now faces entering an election campaign on the back of an unpopular war that he appears to be losing.
Payback time?
So far, Trump has responded with a mixture of half-hearted persuasion, denial and threatening bluster.
Appearing at the Nassau county police academy in Garden City, New York, on 14 August, he downplayed the war’s impact on fuel prices as necessary to prevent “an evil country” obtaining a nuclear weapon. “Remember that, when you have to pay a little bit more, you’re at $4, it’s OK,” he said.
In an interview with Fox News, he then threatened to “bomb the shit out of” Oman if it “gets in the way” of efforts to end the conflict with Iran. In a futile gesture that drew Iranian mockery, he also declared the strait of Hormuz a “new US territory” on social media.
And in recent days, the president has threatened to unleash “Economic Warfare and Isolation on an unprecedented scale” against Iran – omitting details of what precisely this might mean, but vaguely warning countries that provide “any type of lifeline” to Tehran that they, too, will suffer.
The fluctuations seem to betray frustration over a paucity of viable options – a predicament that analysts expect Iran’s leaders to exploit by seeking to deepen Trump’s unpopularity as the midterms approach.
“They are determined to make him pay the consequences of starting this war at the midterm elections,” said Vali Nasr, an Iran expert and international relations professor at Johns Hopkins University.
The approach involves depriving Trump of the option of putting the war on the back burner, or simply declaring victory.
“The whole point Iran is making is that ‘We’re not going to let him decide the sort of ebb and flow of this war,’” said Nasr. “Their position is ‘We have a vote here, and we’re not just going to make it convenient for him’ …
“They have intimated that they are giving him four weeks to go back to the MOU and fully implement it, otherwise they are going to escalate. That means a broader scale of attacks on Gulf targets, more attacks on US bases and US military assets. It’s exactly the opposite of this going low-key, and off the front pages of newspapers.”
The more aggressive Iranian stance has been signaled by a recent shake-up in the regime’s leadership that has included the promotion of Mohsen Rezaei, a former commander-in-chief of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) for most of the 1980-88 war with Iraq, as secretary of the powerful supreme national security council.
The reshuffle also includes the appointment of Hossein Taeb, a hardline cleric and former intelligence chief, as head of the Basij, a volunteer militia, with a brief to turn it into a neighborhood surveillance unit that will root out domestic opposition and perceived Israeli penetration of Iranian society.
‘Really not in a hurry’
“It’s fair to say that the Iranians have decided that they are going to make life more miserable for Trump in a variety of ways,” said Mehrzad Boroujerdi, a political scientist and vice-provost at Missouri Science and Technology University. “They are certainly going to do whatever they can to hurt him in the midterms.
“Every US public opinion poll I have seen makes a direct correlation with the Iran war and that’s in the minds of the White House in terms of what to do, and the reason we are seeing this switch from Trump threatening military action to basically resigning himself to this idea of the economy being the achilles heel of the Iranian regime, and trying to pressure them to come to the negotiating table.
“But they are really not in a hurry. They do not see the economic condition as that dire for them.”
What may become increasingly dire in the run-up to the midterms is the outlook for the US and global economy, according to Alan Eyre, a former state department Iran specialist, who argued that a race between “two ticking economic clocks” would favor Iran.
“It’s going to get ugly as we head into the midterms,” he said. “We have buffered it to an extent by releasing oil from the strategic petroleum reserve, jawboning the market, and by the Chinese decreasing oil imports, but the resiliency of the system is decreasing significantly and an inflation spike is on the way.”
The driver of a coming economic crunch, argued Eyre, is the rising price of diesel, central to the modern economy because it is the essential fuel in supply chains. “Diesel price is currently $5.44 a gallon. A week ago, $5.30 a gallon. A month ago, $5.06 a gallon. A year ago, $3.70 a gallon,” he said.
Facing an array of bad options, Trump’s only recourse is to choose the least worse – which may also be tantamount to admitting defeat.
“The least bad option is trying to reopen the strait of Hormuz as quickly as possible, as much as possible, under Iranian control, because they are not going to give up control of the strait in the short to mid-term,” said Eyre, who was the state department’s first Farsi-speaking spokesperson under the Obama administration at a time when it was trying to forge stronger ties with Iranian communities across the world.
But Iran is not proffering Trump an olive branch in his hour of need.
‘An electoral wood chipper’?
Even reopening the strait is unlikely to trigger an immediate economic revival as maritime insurance companies take time to assess whether the waterway is safe for ships to use again.
Trump may be oblivious to the electoral fate of members of his own party in US Congress, whom he has treated with scant regard. “He sees his brand as separate and better than the Republican brand,” said Eyre. “And the fact that the Republican party might be walking into an electoral wood chipper in November doesn’t really seem to be motivating him.”
Trump, indeed, may already be preparing for life under a Democratic-controlled Congress. This month he announced the appointment of Will Scharf, a rightwing lawyer, as the new White House legal counsel, with the apparent brief of fighting off an anticipated wave of Democratic demands for subpoenas, documents and congressional investigations.
The president, who publicly refused to accept his defeat to Joe Biden in the 2020 presidential election, has also been laying the groundwork to challenge the integrity of November’s poll results, too.
Engineering a electoral drubbing for Trump remains a prize worth pursuing for Iran’s leaders. Such an outcome would set the stage for congressional Democrats to ramp up scrutiny of US conduct in the war.
The outcome of the elections, now less than three months away, “could make the last two years of Trump’s presidency much more difficult for him, and make him much less effective”, said Nasr, of John Hopkins University. “It’s not just the midterms. The day after the elections, all focus will shift to 2028.
“If Trump doesn’t have a way to finish this war, or it becomes nastier with a greater impact on the global economy, then it will begin to become an issue for the presidential election.”
Even that might pale in comparison with the visceral satisfaction a now ageing revolutionary leadership generation would take in delivering a coup de grace reminiscent of that dealt to Carter 46 years ago.
“Why wouldn’t they do the same thing?” asked Sabato, who recalled how Carter reacted with grim resignation when he learned that the last chance of an 11th-hour pre-election deal to free the hostages had collapsed. “They remember the history, and they won then.
“They want to win again against a foe that I’m sure they despise much more than Jimmy Carter. For them, this guy is worse in every way that a human being can be worse.”

Former British and French diplomats urge action over Israel’s ‘erasure’ of Palestine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
09:00:04 UTC
18:00:04 KST

More than 100 French and British former diplomats have said Palestine is being erased in front of the world’s eyes and called for urgent action including trade and arms sales bans to press Israel to accept a Palestinian state.
An unprecedented joint letter dispenses with diplomatic language by accusing Israel of ethnic cleansing and warning that the world no longer sees Israel as a genuine democracy.
Arguing that Britain and France played a key role in the formation of the modern-day Middle East and noting that both countries took the step of recognising Palestine as a state in 2025, the diplomats contend that their countries now have a responsibility “to make common cause on the region’s fundamental fault line – equal rights for Israeli and Palestinians”.
The letter, addressed to the French president, Emmanuel Macron, and the British prime minister, Andy Burnham, has been signed by 52 French former diplomats and 50 British former ambassadors, many of whom served in the Middle East, in senior posts in Egypt, Iran, Bahrain, Israel, Syria, Turkey, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia and Qatar.
The list of British diplomats include two former envoys to the UN, Jeremy Greenstock and Emyr Jones Parry, and a former Foreign Office director of the Middle East, Edward Chaplin. The French signatories include Patrice Paoli, a former Middle East director at the French foreign ministry, and Stanislas de Laboulaye, a former consul general in Jerusalem.
The letter, given to the Guardian and Le Monde, is published two days after the UK and France along with nine other countries condemned the Israeli government’s publication of construction tenders for the E1 settlement project, saying the proposed housing “will take Israel further from peace and undermine its international standing”.
That statement contained no clear threat of consequences apart from a warning to businesses in their jurisdictions not to become involved in bidding since there could be legal and reputational consequences arising from investing in the construction of an unlawful settlement.
The UK foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, described the tenders for 1,200 homes bisecting the West Bank as a destructive threat to the viability of a two-state solution and summoned the most senior Israeli diplomat currently in the UK, the chargée d’affaires, Daniela Grudsky Ekstein.
In response, Israel’s foreign minister, Gideon Sa’ar, vowed Israel would not remain passive, saying the “Jewish people have a right to live throughout Israel just as British people have a right to live throughout the UK”.
The diplomats hope their letter will put pressure on Macron and Burnham to impose specific penalties on Israel in an effort to keep the two-state solution alive.
Diplomacy surrounding the terms for Israel’s withdrawal from Gaza has largely been subcontracted to the negotiations between Israel and Jared Kushner, Donald Trump’s son-in-law and envoy, but Israel has rejected the latest 15-point US-led peace plan for Gaza, leading to criticism from eight Muslim countries including the United Arab Emirates, Israel’s closest Muslim ally. They said Israel’s actions “fundamentally undermine the collective efforts undertaken to achieve a just and lasting peace”.
An internal debate has swirled among diplomats over whether the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, through military and political provocations, is seeking to goad countries into reprisals that will help his chances in elections, due on 27 October.
The former diplomats argue the overdue step of recognising Palestine “needs to be made real by urgent action to safeguard the Palestinian right to self-determination, as the Israeli government seeks to destroy any prospect of an independent Palestinian state, showing contempt for the law, the rulings of the international court of justice and countless UN security council resolutions”.
They write: “Our governments care about the security of the Israeli people, just as they are appalled by the suffering of the Palestinian people under occupation. Hamas committed heinous crimes on 7 October 2023, but nothing justifies Israel’s systematic policy of destruction of Gaza and its population. Mr Netanyahu’s assertion that Israel must live by the sword is morally wrong and counterproductive. It imperils Israel’s security and leaves no room for negotiation. As a result, the world no longer sees Israel as a genuine democracy – there is nothing democratic about depriving others of their rights and land.
“In Gaza, 2 million Palestinians are kettled into 30% of their devastated land, hungry, lacking medicine and housing. Over 1,200 Palestinians have been killed since the so-called ‘ceasefire’. In East Jerusalem and the rest of the West Bank, Palestinian house demolitions and rampant settler violence – with the connivance of the Israeli army and police – amount to ethnic cleansing. Palestine is being erased before our eyes. This policy of occupation and destruction extends to Lebanon – where many villages have been razed – and Syria. It is a stain on the conscience of humanity, requiring the UK and France to act.”
They urge the two states to take seven policy steps:
- 
  Uphold the decisions of the international court of justice and the international criminal court.
- 
  Suspend the EU-Israel association agreement and the UK-Israel trade and partnership agreement for breach of human rights provisions.
- 
  Suspend arms transfers to and from Israel and all bilateral military cooperation.
- 
  Insist on unrestricted aid access to Gaza, led by the UN Relief and Works Agency, other UN agencies and international NGOs, with consequences for non-compliance, and access too for journalists, diplomats and parliamentarians.
- 
  Ban all trade with settlements, including goods, investment, insurance and other financial services.
- 
  Warn potential bidders for the “red line” E1 settlement or other settlement financing/construction that their interests in and with the UK and France will suffer.
- 
  Make it an offence for British and French citizens to buy property on stolen Palestinian land and remove charitable status from “charities” funding settlements.
The diplomats balance their criticism of Israel by saying Palestinians “have to ensure that the state recognised by over two-thirds of the world is democratic and law-abiding, despite the occupation. Gaza and the West Bank need to be reunited politically, administratively and economically. Palestine’s political leadership is unrepresentative and dysfunctional. The elections in November [in Palestine] must lead to democratic renewal.”
But they argue: “While our two governments can do much to help Palestine to be a fully functioning democratic nation, the focus needs to be on Israel’s determination to prevent that outcome.”
The Israeli embassy in London was contacted for comment.

Living in fear, and not being paid: the health workers on the frontline of DRC’s Ebola outbreak
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
09:00:04 UTC
18:00:04 KST

Every day, Sophie Mwadawa Kabundo goes to her job as a nurse at an Ebola treatment centre in the north-east of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, afraid she will contract the virus and pass it to her family and friends.
“More and more confirmed cases are being admitted here … Some of our colleagues have died,” said Kabundo. “We fear that, despite our vigilance, workplace accidents may occur and put us in ever greater danger … We go to sleep already worrying about the days ahead, as patients continue to pour in.”
Martin Bolombi, her colleague at the Elikya treatment centre in Bunia, the capital of the hardest-hit province, Ituri, holds similar fears. “Personally, this outbreak is causing me a lot of stress,” he said. “But I have no choice but to pluck up my courage and ensure that the situation is brought under control first, before it can stabilise.”
That courage is all the more remarkable given that both workers on the frontline of the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak on record said they were not being paid.
“I have been working since May and have only been paid for June,” said Bolombi, a hygiene worker who was among about 100 people who protested outside the Elikya treatment centre during a strike last month over unpaid bonuses.
Kabundo said she was also missing wages. “We are not being paid and we want the government to provide solutions as soon as possible,” she said. “We are under immense pressure … We are exposed to the risk of infection, and our families and other loved ones may contract the disease because of us.”
Unpaid wages are just one of the factors – alongside misinformation, community mistrust and infrastructure deficits – hampering efforts to tackle the outbreak in the DRC, one of the world’s poorest countries.
More than 2,500 people have now died in the outbreak, which is spreading exponentially in an area larger than France, the senior UN Ebola coordinator, Julien Harneis, said on Friday. Speaking on a video call from Bunia, Harneis called for more aid, saying the existing pool of funds would run out within weeks. He said 160 healthcare workers had fallen ill with Ebola, and 43 of them had died.
“The outbreak is growing faster and wider than the Ebola response,” he added. “And all of this is happening in an area that has had three decades of conflict and is generating huge humanitarian needs.”
The World Health Organization estimates that the outbreak is on course to exceed west Africa’s 2014-16 Ebola outbreak as the biggest ever globally. In the previous outbreak, more than 28,600 cases and 11,325 deaths were recorded across Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone, according to WHO data.
The infections in DRC are of the rare Bundibugyo species of the virus. There are no approved treatments or vaccines for the strain, but trials for both are under way.
Bolombi said he was working seven days a week, with barely any time to see his family, as the outbreak was getting worse. “Logistics have improved compared to the early days of the response, but this is still not enough, as needs are growing as the disease progresses,” he said.
Despite the enormous challenges and lack of renumeration, Kabundo expressed pride that there had been “a large number of recoveries” at the Elikya treatment centre. “This progress must be highlighted, but it is no excuse to rest on our laurels,” she said.
The Congolese health ministry did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Ebola is transmitted to people from wild animals and then spreads between humans via direct contact with the organs, blood or other body fluids of infected people, including dead bodies. It can also be spread through contact with contaminated surfaces and materials, such as bedding or clothing.
Initial symptoms can include fever, fatigue, muscle pain, headaches and a sore throat. These progress to vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal pain, rash and symptoms of impaired kidney and liver functions.
Widespread mistrust and misinformation have resulted in people with the virus not attending health centres for treatment until it is too late, as well as attacks on health facilities and ambulances.
Dr Eddy Kambale Kahandukya, a deputy medical coordinator for the charity Médicins Sans Frontières in the DRC, said: “The lack of community engagement remains a major challenge in breaking this chain of transmission … For example, patients who suspect they have symptoms and are awaiting laboratory results seek refuge within the community and end up creating new clusters that further fuel the spread of the epidemic.”
Fear was a big driver of the lack of trust in the authorities’ response to Ebola, said Manon Dumortier, an emergency coordinator in Bunia for the aid group Mercy Corps.
“It’s scary, right? … Suddenly there are so many people dying and you don’t know what it is about,” she said. “People are just disappearing, going to health centres and you cannot even see them before they are being buried. This is just raising a lot of speculation and rumours.”
The WHO declared the outbreak a public health emergency of international concern in May, but later said sequencing showed the outbreak had started months earlier in February.
The virus has spread to six of the DRC’s 26 provinces, concentrated in the country’s north-east. More than 4,200 of the confirmed cases are in Ituri, which borders Uganda and South Sudan.
Uganda reported 20 cases and two deaths, all in the capital, Kampala. The government declared the country Ebola-free on 28 July after the last Ebola patient, a Congolese national, was discharged on 16 July.

====================================================================================================

Plug-in solar: could a low-cost panel cut your bills?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
09:00:03 UTC
18:00:03 KST

Despite this summer bringing hours of sunshine, many Britons have been unable to cash in on free electricity generated by the sun. Rooftop solar panels are usually out of the question if you live in a flat or rent your home, and the cost has made them prohibitive to many more households.
However, this could be about to change because next week the first wave of low-cost “plug-in” solar panels will go on sale in Great Britain.
Also known as “plug‑and‑play” or “balcony” solar, the clue to what makes them different is in the name: you can fix them to a balcony or garden wall, then plug them in like a toaster.
The mini solar systems are a familiar sight on balconies in Spain and in Germany, where they are known as a Balkonkraftwerk (balcony power plant), but until a recent change in the law, they were not permitted in Britain.
Matt Parry from the Renewable Energy Association, a trade body for renewable energy, says the kits are a gamechanger. “It democratises solar and gives everyone the chance to get it,” he says.
How the kits work
Unlike traditional rooftop solar panels, which require a professional to install, balcony solar kits – which commonly include one or two panels – can be plugged in to a three-prong wall socket.
You can fix them on a balcony railing, shed roof or garden wall – anywhere with good sun exposure and safe access.
When sunlight hits the solar panels, they generate a direct current. The microinverter then converts this to an alternating current, which flows into your home’s electrical system, reducing the amount you draw from the grid.
Previously, rules around the installation of solar were what was holding people back. But last year the government announced it would make it possible for plug-in solar to be used in this country.
To make this a reality, it has updated wiring regulations to allow households in Great Britain to connect plug-in solar panels capable of generating up to 800 watts of power into the mains without the need for an electrician. (The rules are different in Northern Ireland.)
Buying panels
Big names including B&Q, Currys, Lidl, Wickes and Amazon are lining up to sell plug-in solar.
Given the size (and weight) of these devices, it is expected that many will be bought online.
Although you may have already come across plug-in solar panels for sale, industry experts suggest waiting until the regulations take effect on 27 August before making a purchase.
Electrical Safety First, the consumer safety charity, is urging shoppers to stick to reputable high street retailers and their websites to ensure the device complies with the rules.
Luke Osborne, the charity’s technical director, advises people to “avoid buying these devices from third-party sellers on online marketplaces. These platforms are now not legally responsible for the safety of goods sold via their sites, exposing people to substandard versions that may put you and your home at risk.”
Andrew Moore, the founder of the British solar panel brand UKSOL, says: “We are working towards making the initial products available from 27 August.”
His company will initially sell 460W and 890W kits, starting at £599 and £999 respectively, and it plans to launch another four models in late September, with prices starting from £499.
Sizewise, plug-in solar setups are usually smaller than rooftop options, but sizes vary. The UKSOL 460W single panel kit measures 1,762mm x 1,134mm x 30mm and weighs 25.5kg. The 890W kit comprises two panels.
Setting up
The official guidance suggests that it will take about an hour to set up your system. It estimates 15-25% of people will need professional support mounting the panels, and about 15% will need minor electrical works. UKSOL suggests it takes two people to handle and position the panels, as each one weighs 25kg.
Osborne says plug-in solar systems should not be connected via extension leads, cable reels, multiway adaptors, travel adaptors or plug-in RCD adaptors. “These accessories can overheat, become overloaded and create additional safety risks,” he says.
There is also some other housekeeping. The owner has to tell their distribution network operator that they are using them (there should be a form in the box). You can find out who it is by inputting your postcode on the Energy Networks Association website. You will also be able to consult the ENA’s Connect Direct site for a list of approved devices, which is a good place to start before you buy.
Savings
Plug-in systems are about a fifth of the size of a typical residential rooftop solar system, which means they will not provide enough energy to power a home on their own – but they could cut your bill.
One drawback is that you need to be home to use the power generated because without a battery it is not being stored for later, so flows back to the grid.
However, the adoption of balcony solar could, in time, pave the way for plug-in batteries in British homes, too. If paired with a plug-in solar system, households could store their own renewable electricity during the day and use it to run their appliances in the evenings. The government is reportedly considering plans to bulk-buy the devices and distribute them to low-income homes.
A basic plug-in solar system costs about £400. Parry says it will “give you back, at worst, £40 a year, and at the best about £110. If it’s the worst-case scenario, it’s going to pay for itself in 10 years, but at the best-case scenario, it’s four.
“If you’ve just got 800W, it’s only at its very peak that it will give you that.”
He adds: “The slight downside is that plug-in solar is hitting the markets as the summer’s coming to an end. It’s going to be more use in May next year.”
Moore says that the level of saving is affected by a number of things, including the system size, location, orientation and actually being home to use the power.
He expects the 460W system his company will be selling to save a typical household about £80-£120 a year, “while the 890W system could save more”.
He adds: “The greatest savings are achieved when households use appliances during daylight hours, as this increases the proportion of generated electricity used within the home.”
You can buy a more expensive 2,000W kit (the inverter will only allow 800W through) to maximise your power-generating capacity, but these are more expensive.
Staying safe
Although there is no obligation to do this, before buying a kit, some experts think you should get your home electrics checked by a professional. That is because this is the first time that British residential wiring circuits will take power in via a three-point socket rather than simply being used to distribute electricity.
Electrical Safety First is concerned about the impact on residual current devices, or RCDs, which sit in a household electricity box and cut off the power if someone drills through a wire or runs their lawnmower over a power cord. Electricians are concerned they may burn out when plug-in solar panels start adding electricity to the circuit.
A Department for Energy Security and Net Zero spokesperson says: “Plug-in solar panels will be available to buy this summer, and stringent verification and registration checks are already in place. They are a transformative technology that can save people hundreds of pounds on their bills.”
Box] Renters
Plug-in solar should make it easier for tenants to take advantage of renewable energy, as any kit they buy can be moved from place to place.
But if you are renting, you should ask permission from your landlord before you invest in any panels.
The rules on what you can do with regard to fixing brackets to hold them, for example, may vary depending on what your tenancy agreement says.
There’s “no reason” why your landlord should be against the idea, Parry says. “He or she can look at the information and know it’s super, super safe.”
Meera Chindooroy, the deputy director of campaigns, public affairs and policy at the National Residential Landlords Association, says that while the organisation supports the “principle of tenants benefiting from plug-in solar panels … landlords would first need to be satisfied that the panels meet all required safety standards”.
She adds: “It would not be right for landlords to be held responsible for the safety of equipment they were not asked about in the first place.”

NASA Cancels Its Rescue Mission for the Aging Swift Telescope
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
09:00:00 UTC
18:00:00 KST

The Swift space observatory has been in operation since 2004. It specializes in gamma-ray bursts (GRBs), the most energetic electromagnetic explosions known in the universe. Its original mission was supposed to last just two years. More than two decades later, it continues to explore some of the most violent phenomena in the cosmos. Now it is nearing the end of its life.
Swift doesn’t have a propulsion system capable of significantly raising its orbit. Although it is hundreds of kilometers above the Earth’s surface, there are still atmospheric particles at that altitude that exert a small but constant drag on the satellite. With each orbit around Earth, it loses a tiny amount of energy and, little by little, altitude as well. If this process continues without intervention it will eventually reenter the atmosphere.
NASA knew that Swift had limited time left. Some models had indicated that the observatory could remain in orbit until the 2030s, but increased solar activity during 2024 changed those projections. Energy from the sun heated and expanded the upper layers of Earth’s atmosphere, increasing the drag on the satellite and accelerating its descent. Estimates eventually placed its likely reentry before the end of 2026.
Faced with the rapid deterioration of Swift’s orbit, NASA decided to attempt a rescue maneuver straight out of a movie. The plan was simple in concept but astonishingly complex to execute. A robotic mission would catch up to Swift, capture it with mechanical arms, and use its own thrusters to raise the observatory to a safer orbit, where it could continue operating. To do this, NASA turned to the company Katalyst Space Technologies and its LINK spacecraft.
LINK was launched into space on July 3, 2026. However, problems arose soon after. The spacecraft suffered failures in its attitude control system, which is responsible for keeping it properly oriented and stable in space. For weeks, engineers worked to regain control.
On Wednesday, NASA canceled the rescue mission. In a statement, agency administrator Jared Isaacman explained that the decision was due to problems with the spacecraft’s control system. LINK will no longer capture Swift or raise its orbit. The spacecraft will continue to approach the observatory to conduct demonstrations of rendezvous, navigation, and close-proximity operations. The agency hopes to use this attempt to gather information that can be applied to future missions aimed at repairing, relocating, or extending the lifespan of satellites in orbit.
“This is not the outcome we were working toward, but it does not change why this mission was worth attempting. The team moved with extraordinary speed to give Swift a chance to carry out more science while advancing capabilities America will need for satellite servicing in the future. We are going to learn everything we can from LINK’s rendezvous attempt and put those lessons to work on the missions that follow,” Isaacman said in a press release.
The agency had warned from the outset that this was a high-risk mission. Swift was not built to be captured or repaired in orbit, while LINK was developed and launched against the clock in response to the observatory’s rapid descent.
“NASA should be willing to move quickly and take smart risks when the potential return is worth it, and that is exactly what we did with this mission,” Isaacman noted.
Without an intervention to raise its orbit, Swift will continue to lose altitude until it reaches the denser layers of the atmosphere. During reentry, much of the observatory will be destroyed by intense heating and aerodynamic forces. It is still too early to determine exactly when and where this will occur.
For now, NASA estimates that Swift will likely reenter the atmosphere before the end of the year.

Moped mania: chasing teenage kicks at 30km/h
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
09:00:00 UTC
18:00:00 KST

Moped mania: chasing teenage kicks at 30km/h
In Switzerland, many people’s first taste of independence and freedom was a moped. Following a period of decline, they have been enjoying a revival for some years, particularly on the roads of German-speaking Switzerland. A report on a gathering of ‘Töfflibuebe’ (moped boys) amid clouds of nostalgia and bluish smoke.
For his ride, Claudio Lang has chosen the Condor-Puch X30 NS. At first glance, there’s nothing special about it: a red frame, a chrome fuel tank and mudguards, spoked wheels and high handlebars. It’s a classic from the 1970s. But if you look a bit more closely, you’ll spot something unusual: it has a four-speed gearbox. “I modified it with a friend. I certainly don’t want to have to pedal uphill,” he says with a smile in front of his garage, a few kilometres from Olten, northern Switzerland.
Lang is a proud Töfflibueb, or moped boy, as people who are passionate about vintage mopeds describe themselves. You sometimes come across them on the country roads of the Swiss Plateau during their group rides.
Lang’s garage is a sort of land of plenty for lovers of Mofa or Töffli, as mopeds are called in German-speaking Switzerland. There are models from various makes, some of which I didn’t even know existed. My knowledge extends no further than the classic Sachs from my teenage years: unreliable, noisy and a real money-pit, guzzling up every last penny I had.
Addiction to two-strokes
“My passion for mopeds was rekindled 12 years ago and, over time, has really taken hold,” says the almost 60-year-old, who works as a lorry driver. “Today, rather than a passion, I’d describe it almost as an illness, an addiction.”
Lang owns 32 mopeds: Ciao Piaggio, Boxer, Sachs, Hercules, DKW, Alpha Chopper, Puch Maxi, Puch Velux, Maxi N, Maxi S. “The best bit is restoring them to their former glory,” he says. “Sometimes the hunt for spare parts can be nerve-wracking. But that’s also what makes this hobby so interesting.”
More
Penalties and peculiarities of the Swiss Highway Code
The 1980s, when Lang was a teenager, was the golden age of mopeds. He owned one too, which ended up in a corner and was eventually sold because his dream was a Harley-Davidson.
He still has that one, but it almost met the same fate as his first moped. “I don’t enjoy the Harley any more. It’s different with the moped,” he says. “You can’t just buy one ready-made. You have to fix it up yourself. And if you can’t find the parts, you have to ask your mates to give you a hand, milling and adapting parts that are now impossible to find. And that strengthens friendships even more.”
The spirit of the ‘Töfflibuebe’
In early June, the Töfflibuebe community gathered in Trimbach, canton Solothurn, for the Isebähnli-Töffli-GP, a rally which, for the past ten years, has brought back to the roads of the Jura and the Swiss Plateau the crackling sound and clouds of bluish smoke from two-stroke engines.
More than 300 enthusiasts tackled a route of around 90 kilometres, many with a jerrycan of petrol-mixture on their luggage rack.
“I haven’t missed a single edition,” Lang says. For the occasion he wore his sleeveless denim jacket covered in patches and badges, a memento of many rallies across Switzerland and abroad. He brought with him throttle and brake cables, chains and tyre sealant spray. “If anyone has a problem,” he explains, “I stop and lend a hand. That’s also the spirit that unites us.”
For Martin Sulzer, chairman of the organising committee, the success of the event lies precisely in this spirit. Launched in 2017 with around 140 participants, the GP has grown to attract people from all over the country: from Central Switzerland, Graubünden in the east, Ticino in the south and the French-speaking region in the west.
“The moped is a sort of social leveller, making us all equal: the bank manager and the domestic worker, the pensioner and the teenager,” Sulzer says. “Today, for me, the moped is above all a sort of time machine that takes me back to when I was 14.”
The revival of the ‘tin horse’
Particularly between the 1960s and the 1980s, the roar of the two-stroke engine was the soundtrack of youth culture. In some parts of Switzerland, the Töffli craze continued even beyond that. The moped meant wind in your hair, espadrilles on your feet, an unbuttoned denim jacket and music blaring in your ears from a Walkman. The moped was the key to an unexplored, fascinating and surprising world.
At 14, young people could finally leave behind the monotony of village life and head for the nearest big city, the nightclub, the world of grown-ups.
“With the Mofa, we could finally go to Lucerne, where there was a McDonald’s,” Sulzer recalls. “We then started ‘tuning’ it so we wouldn’t starve on the road. From then on, another thrilling element was added: the fear of getting caught by the police.”
In fact, moped owners often made unauthorised modifications to the engine to exceed the permitted speed limit of 30km/h.
Those days are now long gone. The catalytic converter, which made the moped much slower, the compulsory wearing of helmets – which killed the Easy Rider feeling – and growing environmental awareness sealed its slow and inexorable decline.
But not its end! According to data from the Federal Statistical Office, the moped is enjoying a revival, at least in some German-speaking cantons. In Zurich, there were around 12,100 mopeds registered in 2015; by 2025, this figure had risen to 17,350 – an increase of over 43% in just ten years. In Graubünden, Lucerne and Solothurn, the increase stands at around 30%.
At the Isebähnli-Töffli-GP gathering, you can’t help but notice, at a glance, plenty of Töfflibuebe in their sixties. Riding their mopeds, they may well be hoping to turn back the clock, to return to their teenage years and relive that sense of freedom and the wind in their hair – back when they had some. However, those carrying a few extra kilos are forced to dismount on the steeper stretches of road to reach the top of the climb.
During the breaks, over a coffee and a bratwurst, memories of a past both distant and recent intertwine: the first kiss on their two-wheeled steed, the engine secretly souped up, the successful hunt for a spare part that’s now impossible to find.
Lang listens, laughs and tells stories. Back home, there are still a few mopeds waiting to be fixed. He’s almost out of space in the shed, though, and parting with those pieces of his life won’t be easy. One, in any case, will stay where it is: the moped his son and his circle of friends gave him for his 50th birthday. “Naturally, I have a special bond with that one,” he says.
Then his thoughts turn straight to the next trip. Every year, with his friends, he travels through a different region of Switzerland. Someone organises the route, the hotels and the van for the luggage. Then they set off together, slowly, with the engine sputtering and leaving a bluish cloud in their wake.
In Switzerland, new mopeds are now a niche product. The last remaining Swiss manufacturer is Amsler & Co. of Feuerthalen, canton Zurich, which has been producing the Pony since 1995, having launched the brand in 1961.
The current models, the GTX and Cross, remain true to the classic formula: a 49cm³ Beta two-stroke engine, a two-speed automatic gearbox, a top speed of 30km/h and a catalytic converter. An electric starter, indicators, a brake light and a horn are available as optional extras.
Edited by Zeno Zoccatelli. Translated from Italian, sub-edited by Thomas Stephens

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The leader of Thailand’s largest opposition party has publicly acknowledged meeting Taiwan’s representative to Thailand.
Natthaphong Ruengpanyawut, head of the People’s Party, said in a Facebook post Thursday that he had dinner the previous night with Lan Hsia-li (藍夏禮), Taiwan’s representative to Thailand, and staff from the Taipei Economic and Cultural Office (TECO), according to CNA.
In the same post, Natthaphong noted he was heading to Chiang Mai to look into cross-border drug issues and outlined the party’s recent flood relief and recovery work. He framed the Taiwan dinner as part of a broader schedule.
TECO confirmed the meeting, saying the two sides exchanged views on Taiwan-related topics of interest and welcomed further dialogue, CNA said.
The People’s Party won 120 seats in February’s general election, making it the second-largest party in parliament and the main opposition force behind the 192-seat Bhumjaithai Party.
Hung Ming-chien (洪銘謙), a Taiwan–Thailand exchange association board member, called the public disclosure unusual. CNA quoted Hung as saying past interactions between the People’s Party and Taiwan mostly occurred at public events, with little direct bilateral engagement and even less public acknowledgment.
Hung said the post suggests the party is prepared to face possible Chinese displeasure while showing “a continued rise in friendliness toward Taiwan.” He described this as positive for democratic-leaning interactions between the two sides.
He added that as Thailand’s ruling party pursues a relatively China-friendly line, the opposition could differentiate itself by emphasizing oversight of Chinese “gray industry” activities while also adopting more pro-Taiwan and pro-US positions. This would give voters clearer policy choices.

Israeli army warplanes had attacked the abandoned Abu al-Duhur Military Air Base in eastern Idlib province in northern Syria.
No information was shared on whether there were casualties or injuries in the attack.
A Syrian official said Israeli warplanes carried out eight attacks on the air base, targeting the runway and an inactive structure in a hangar.

Supacat opens new UK production facility in Devon
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
08:54:03 UTC
17:54:03 KST

- Supacat opened a new production facility, the Jones II Building, at its Devon headquarters, named for company co-founder Nick Jones.
- The company said the facility will expand production capacity but did not disclose its size, cost, or which vehicle programs will be built there.
Supacat has opened a new production facility at its headquarters in Devon, England, naming the building after company co-founder Nick Jones.
The British vehicle manufacturer said Maj. Gen. Chris King cut the ribbon at the opening, which the company described as marking the launch of a facility expansion. Supacat did not disclose the size of the new building, its construction cost, or a timeline for when full production would begin there.
Supacat said the facility, called the Jones II Building, will expand its production capacity. The company said this is intended to speed up delivery of tactical vehicles to the British Army and other military customers, though it did not specify which vehicle programs would be built at the new site or provide production figures.
Supacat was founded in 1981 by Nick Jones and David Clayton at Dunkeswell Aerodrome in Devon, initially developing high-mobility all-terrain vehicles. The company’s first major program came during the 1982 Falklands War, when the Ministry of Defence issued an urgent requirement for lightweight transport vehicles capable of operating in rugged terrain. Supacat has since built vehicles including the Jackal, a wheeled reconnaissance and fire support platform used by the British Army and RAF Regiment, and the All Terrain Mobility Platform, in service with British airborne forces since 1988. Supacat has operated as part of SC Group since 2015, alongside sister companies SC Innovation, Proteum, and Blackhill Engineering.
Supacat and Babcock International Group opened a separate new production facility, the Raglan Building at Babcock’s Devonport site in Plymouth, in 2024 to build 70 Jackal 3 vehicles for the British Army under a single-source contract. That contract could expand to as many as 240 vehicles if the British Army exercises an option, according to Babcock. Under that arrangement, Babcock builds 62 of the vehicles at Devonport, while Supacat builds the remaining eight at its own facilities. The Jones II Building announced this week is located at Supacat’s headquarters, separate from the Devonport site.
Supacat has faced financial pressure on other parts of its business over the past year and a half. SC Group Chief Executive Nick Ames said in April 2025 that several major banks had declined to provide the company with commercial accounts or loans due to internal policies restricting defense-related lending, which he said made it “almost impossible” to fund investment in British manufacturing. Separately, the company’s existing Jackal support contract with the Ministry of Defence was projected, as of August 2025, to expire in early 2026 without renewal, a lapse that could have put up to 150 jobs at Supacat’s Derbyshire facility at risk. It is not known whether that contract has since been renewed.
Lizzie Jones, Supacat’s Operations Director, said earlier this year that the company had several ongoing projects planned for 2026, including customer-specific vehicle programs and continued development of new vehicle designs, in addition to the new production facility.

Four times more pixels: Ukrainian company develops Oko HD thermal imaging camera – photo
Ukrainian company Oko Camera is developing a new Oko HD thermal imaging camera, featuring a 1280×1024 resolution sensor.
Source: Oko Camera in a comment to Ukrainska Pravda about the development at DALO Industry Days 2026 in Herning
Details: The distinguishing feature of the Oko HD lies in its sensor, which will contain four times more pixels than the company's previous product lines. This will allow the range at which targets can be identified to be increased.
One of the camera's main purposes is observing objects at long distances: this sensor should allow targets to be detected and identified from afar. The company has not yet disclosed the exact distance.
"LWIR cameras – that is, long-wave infrared cameras – with HD resolution are not common on the global market. In Ukraine, they essentially don't exist at all right now. This camera will have a significantly greater detection range, which directly affects the ability of the unmanned or robotic system it's integrated into to see targets at long distances," Oko Camera's partnerships manager told Ukrainska Pravda.
The Oko HD is currently at the prototyping stage. The company plans to produce the first working samples by the end of 2026 and hand them over to clients who have already made inquiries about the cameras. The company expects it to become one of the most affordable thermal imaging HD cameras on the global market.
Once testing confirms the specified characteristics, the company plans to launch the Oko HD into production in 2027.
Background: In July, Oko Camera revealed a prototype of a new thermal imaging camera for reconnaissance drones.

Somali pirates hijack oil tanker off Yemen in latest attack

Unknown Publisher

17:53:02 KST

Somali pirates hijack oil tanker off Yemen in latest attack
MOGADISHU, Somalia (AP) — Somali pirates hijacked an oil products tanker off Yemen, a Somali maritime security official said, the latest in a resurgence of piracy that has seen six commercial vessels seized since April across the Gulf of Aden and western Indian Ocean.
Six armed pirates hijacked the Eritrean-flagged M.T. Sibu 1 on Thursday about 136 nautical miles (252 kilometers) east of al-Mukalla, Yemen, and took it toward Somalia’s Puntland coast, the official, who has knowledge of the incident, told The Associated Press on Friday. He spoke on condition of anonymity as he was not allowed to discuss the matter publicly.
The Sibu 1, managed by the UAE-based Qatrat Alnada Almasi Ship Management, was sanctioned by the U.S. Treasury Department last year for allegedly belonging to an Iranian “shadow fleet” used to transport petroleum products seeking to evade U.S. sanctions.
The tanker had 20 crew members aboard: 16 Indians, one Syrian, one Sudanese, and one Iraqi. The nationality of one crew member was not immediately known. The vessel’s previous port of departure and intended destination remained unclear.
The hijacking came three days after pirates seized the Lutuf, a Cameroon-flagged general cargo vessel, off Somalia’s coast. The vessel had 10 crew aboard, including six Indians, a Turkish national, a Georgian national and two Serbian security guards, according to maritime tracking reports.
The Sibu 1 is the sixth commercial vessel hijacked by Somali pirates since April 21, when the Palau-flagged tanker Honor 25 was seized off Somalia. Pirates later seized the Sward on April 26, the Eureka on May 2, the Asana on July 17 and the Lutuf on Aug. 17.
The attacks have occurred increasingly far from Somalia’s coastline, including the hijacking of the Eureka while anchored off Yemen and the Asana about 65 nautical miles (120 kilometers) southwest of al-Mukalla. The International Maritime Bureau recorded 38 piracy and armed robbery incidents worldwide during the first half of 2026, including five hijackings. Somali pirates accounted for 94% of crew members taken hostage during that period, the bureau said.
Puntland’s Security Ministry said Friday that its investigations indicated that forces beyond Puntland’s control were behind the renewed piracy, but did not identify any group or country. The claim could not be independently verified.
Puntland said it had deployed security forces along its coast and condemned airstrikes that it said struck fishing vessels and property near coastal communities where hijacked ships were being held. It called on the countries involved to explain strikes near Garacad on Aug. 18 and Aug. 20.
The ministry did not identify who carried out the strikes, and the allegations could not be independently confirmed.

Brazil’s Lula seeks end to ‘baseless tariffs’ in call with Trump

Brazil’s Lula seeks end to ‘baseless tariffs’ in call with Trump
Washington imposed two new sets of tariffs on Brazil in July, a key campaign issue ahead for the left-wing president ahead of the presidential election in October
Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva urged US counterpart Donald Trump in a phone call on Friday to resolve their countries’ trade dispute, saying US tariffs were imposed on “baseless” grounds.
Washington imposed two new sets of tariffs on the Latin American giant in July, a move that has become a key campaign issue ahead of Brazil’s presidential election in October.
Lula – who is seeking a fourth and final term in office – told Trump that the tariffs “negatively affect both Brazil and the United States,” according to a statement from his office.

Why this is end of the line for Trump in Iran war?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
08:49:10 UTC
17:49:10 KST

Donald Trump's declaration of an unprecedented economic war against Iran cannot be seen merely as a sign of the start of new economic pressure. This decision shows, more than anything else, that Washington, after months of military and sanctions pressure, is facing the narrowing of its effective options. Instead of finding new and decisive targets inside Iran, the United States has now shifted the scope of pressure beyond Iran's borders and is targeting countries, banks, and companies that still allow Tehran to trade and maintain financial access. In fact, Trump's new policy can be seen as an attempt to compensate for the failure of previous pressure; a shift from direct pressure on Iran to pressure on the network that allows Iran to circumvent sanctions.
Over the past years, the United States has placed almost all major sectors of Iran's economy on the sanctions list; from oil and petrochemicals to shipping, metals, the automotive industry, the Central Bank, financial networks, and various economic institutions. The Atlantic Council has also emphasized, in its review of sanctions on Iran, that almost all sectors of Iran's economy have been targeted by US sanctions.
Therefore, Washington's problem is no longer finding a sector of Iran's economy that has not been sanctioned; the problem is that each new sanction, compared with previous sanctions, does not necessarily create new and decisive pressure.
This is why Trump now speaks of an unprecedented economic war, but the main arena of this war is no longer only Iran. The United States wants to pressure foreign banks, shipping companies, oil buyers, trade intermediaries, and even governments that cooperate with Tehran.
This policy shift must also be seen in the context of recent military developments. Washington has turned to intensified economic pressure at a time when military pressure has failed to achieve the political goals the United States expected. If military power alone could have forced Tehran to accept Washington's demands, there would have been no need to declare a new "economic war."
It can therefore be said that Trump's new policy is a kind of change of playing field; the United States has not retreated from the military field to the economic field, but it is trying to complement insufficient military pressure with economic pressure.
In the view of Western experts, the problem is that Iran's economy, over several decades of sanctions, has gradually developed mechanisms to cope with these pressures. Informal trade networks, oil sales, financial intermediaries, the use of local currencies, and cooperation with non-Western partners are part of these mechanisms.
The biggest challenge to the new US policy is China. According to data from the company Kpler, cited in a recent Al Jazeera report, more than 80 percent of Iran's oil exports in 2025 have gone to China. A significant portion of this oil also goes to small Chinese refineries, and payments are made through small banks, trading companies in Hong Kong, and settlement in yuan.
This creates a serious problem for Washington. Sanctioning an Iranian company is fundamentally different from sanctioning a major Chinese bank. In the first case, the main cost falls on Iran; but in the second case, the United States enters into direct confrontation with one of the world's largest economies.
For this reason, as Bloomberg has reported, the United States has previously warned two major Chinese banks about the risk of secondary sanctions related to Iran, but has not yet sanctioned them directly.
Here one of the most important contradictions of Washington's sanctions policy becomes apparent. The power of US sanctions stems largely from the dominance of the dollar and broad access to the US financial system. But the extensive use of this very tool has encouraged target countries to find alternative paths.
Chatham House analyses show that the expansion of sanctions has contributed to deepening cooperation among countries such as Iran, China, and Russia and has pushed them toward creating payment and settlement routes that are less dependent on the dollar.
This means sanctions may create pressure in the short term, but in the long term they increase the incentive of target countries to reduce their dependence on the US financial system.
As a result, the tool Washington uses to preserve its economic power can gradually increase the incentive to create rival tools.
The main problem with Trump's new policy lies precisely here. The more the United States expands the scope of secondary sanctions, the greater the likelihood of colliding with the economic interests of major powers. Sanctioning buyers of Iranian oil can affect global oil supply and raise energy prices. Pressure on China can lead to a reaction from Beijing. Targeting foreign companies can also deepen the rift between the United States and its trading partners.
Washington therefore faces a difficult equation: to increase pressure on Iran, it must shift pressure onto other countries; but the larger this circle becomes, the higher the cost of implementing the policy for the United States itself.
The ultimate goal of US sanctions is not merely to reduce Iran's income; the main goal is to change Tehran's political behavior. But the experience of past years has shown that economic pressure does not necessarily lead to a change in political behavior. Iran can pay higher costs, change its trade routes, and expand economic cooperation with countries such as China and Russia. Even Chatham House has warned, in its examination of the consequences of sanctions, that broad pressure can help form parallel financial and trade networks; networks that ultimately reduce the effectiveness of the US sanctions tool. For this reason, the main question for Washington is no longer "what can be sanctioned against Iran?" but rather "how many other countries is the United States willing to enter into conflict with in order to close each of Iran's economic routes?"
If we place Trump's new policy alongside the military developments of recent months, a clearer picture emerges. After the experience of military pressure, the United States has now returned to sanctions; but this time almost all of Iran's economy has already been sanctioned, and to find new targets, Washington is forced to go after Iran's external network. This is the very point at which "maximum pressure" can turn into "costly pressure." The United States can increase economic pressure, but it cannot expand it indefinitely without cost. China stands in the way of this policy, Russia has greater incentive to cooperate with Tehran, and Iran itself has gained considerable experience over the years of sanctions in creating alternative routes.
Ultimately, Trump's new policy is less a sign of the discovery of a new economic weapon against Iran than a sign of the narrowing of Washington's previous options. After military pressure failed to produce the expected result, the United States is now trying to continue the same pressure in the economic arena.
But this time there is one fundamental difference: the target is not only Iran. To isolate Tehran, the United States must also pressure China, financial networks outside the West, oil buyers, and international companies.
And this is precisely where the tables may turn; the sanctions that were supposed to isolate Iran can deepen Iran's cooperation with the East, increase the use of non-dollar currencies, and reduce the dependence of some countries on the US financial system.
Under such conditions, Trump's unprecedented economic war may be less the beginning of a new phase of pressure on Iran than a sign that US sanctions policy has reached the limits of its own power.

Turkish and Japanese officials and experts met in Tokyo to examine how artificial intelligence and geopolitical competition are reshaping strategic communication, economic security and global supply chains.
The STRATCOM Roundtable and STRATCOM Public Forum, organized by Türkiye’s Presidential Communications Directorate and its embassy in Tokyo, brought together representatives of public institutions, international organizations, technology companies, think tanks and universities.
The roundtable focused on the effects of emerging technologies on global governance, digital sovereignty, information security and international cooperation. Participants also discussed disinformation, the changing role of public diplomacy and the use of technology in crisis management.
A separate public forum on managing economic security examined critical technologies, reliable supply chains, data security and the transformation of the digital economy.
In a video message, Presidential Communications Director Burhanettin Duran said digital technologies had widened access to information but also created new vulnerabilities through manipulation, polarization and uncertainty.
“Today, we are facing what can be described as a crisis of truth and a crisis of communication,” Duran said.
He called for greater international cooperation, exchanges of experience and the development of common principles, saying no country or institution could address such challenges alone.
Türkiye’s ambassador to Japan, Oğuzhan Ertuğrul, said multiple crises and growing uncertainty were placing further pressure on the international order. He called for stronger cooperation based on diplomacy and multilateralism, alongside reforms to global institutions.
Ertuğrul said Türkiye and Japan possessed complementary strategic capabilities and could work together to support international peace, stability and prosperity.
Deputy Communications Director Ferhat Pirinççi said information security and a reliable information environment were central to economic resilience. Disinformation could directly affect economic stability, the investment climate and public confidence, he said.
Pirinççi added that the two countries could deepen cooperation in technology, innovation, strategic communication and crisis management.
AK Party Deputy Chair Ömer İleri said protectionism, the growing emphasis on domestic production and the increasing importance of AI and data were transforming both geopolitical and technological competition.
Akira Igata of the University of Tokyo’s Research Center for Advanced Science and Technology drew attention to disinformation and influence operations targeting companies involved in critical-mineral supply chains and data-center infrastructure.
He called for closer cooperation between governments and businesses, as well as greater information sharing and education.
Kazuto Suzuki, a professor at the University of Tokyo’s Graduate School of Public Policy, said interdependence among major powers, particularly the United States and China, continued to shape economic security policies.
Diversifying critical supply chains and reducing strategic vulnerabilities were becoming increasingly important, he said.
Kunihiko Miyake of the Canon Institute for Global Studies said technological tools alone could not ensure effective communication, which also required a clear strategy and messages tailored to their intended audiences.

Who Is Lev Shlosberg, the Russian Politician Jailed for Opposing Russia’s War?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
08:43:00 UTC
17:43:00 KST

Russia has sentenced Lev Shlosberg, the 63-year-old deputy chairman of the liberal Yabloko party – and one of the few prominent opponents of Russia’s war against Ukraine who chose to remain in the country – to 11 years and one month in a penal colony for participating in a debate and reposting a newspaper cover.
On Aug. 17, a court in the northwestern city of Pskov found him guilty of repeatedly “discrediting” the Russian military and spreading “false information” about it. The court also prohibited him from administering websites for six years,Reuters reported.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
On the same day, Russia’s Supreme Court rejected Yabloko’s appeal against its exclusion from the Sept. 18-20 parliamentary election. Yabloko was the only registered Russian party openly campaigning for an end to the war.
The two rulings removed both an anti-war party from the ballot and one of its best-known politicians from public life. Dozens of people who gathered near the Supreme Court were detained.
Eleven years for a debate and a repost
One part of the case concerned Shlosberg’s January 2025 online debate with historian Yuri Pivovarov.
Shlosberg argued that Russia and Ukraine should agree to an immediate ceasefire. Pivovarov warned that a premature settlement could produce another war and supported Ukraine fighting until victory.
Investigators claimed that a recording of the debate posted on the Russian social network Odnoklassniki “discredited” the military. Shlosberg said he did not control the account and had not uploaded the recording.
Russian Emigration Interest Doubles Amid Fears of Mobilization This Fall
The second charge concerned a repost from Feb. 25, 2022 – the day after Russia launched its full-scale invasion. It showed a Daily Mirror front page featuring an injured Ukrainian woman alongside Russian leader Vladimir Putin.
The law criminalizing “false information” about the Russian military was signed on March 4, after the repost had already appeared. The court nevertheless used the publication to help impose a sentence of more than 11 years.
The proceedings were troubling even by the standards of a Russian political trial. According to Deutsche Welle, closing arguments began without any of Shlosberg’s three lawyers present. The court refused to postpone the hearing and imposed a state-appointed lawyer whom he had rejected.
The sentence incorporated an earlier punishment of 420 hours of compulsory labor for allegedly failing to comply with the requirements imposed on a so-called “foreign agent.”
Amnesty International called the prosecution retaliation for exercising freedom of expression. Human Rights Watch demanded his release and noted that the offending “false information” included the image of a wounded Ukrainian civilian.
Pskov politician who investigated Russia’s secret war
Shlosberg was born in Pskov in 1963 into a family of teachers. He studied history at the Pskov Pedagogical Institute, later worked as a teacher and social worker, and helped establish the non-state Pskov Free Institute in the early 1990s, according to a biographical account published while he was in pretrial detention.
He joined Yabloko in 1994 and led its Pskov branch from 1996 until 2023, when he became one of the party’s deputy chairs.
Unlike opposition figures whose careers were made in Moscow, Shlosberg built his reputation through local politics, journalism and civic work. He was twice elected to the Pskov Regional Assembly, first serving from 2011 to 2015 and then from 2016 to 2021.
He was also the publisher and editor of Pskovskaya Guberniya, a regional newspaper whose reporting brought him national attention, and nearly cost him his life.
In August 2014, while the Kremlin denied that regular Russian troops were fighting in eastern Ukraine, the newspaper investigated the funerals of service members from Pskov’s 76th Guards Air Assault Division.
The soldiers had officially died in unclear circumstances. The evidence indicated that they had been killed during Russia’s undeclared intervention in the Donbas.
The issue was particularly sensitive in Pskov. The division was one of the region’s most important military institutions, and reporting on its losses punctured Moscow’s claim that the war was a purely Ukrainian conflict involving local “separatists” and Russian volunteers.
On Aug. 29, 2014, unknown assailants attacked Shlosberg near his home. He was hospitalized with a concussion, facial injuries and temporary memory loss. The assault followed a wider series of threats and attacks on journalists trying to establish how Russian soldiers had died in Ukraine, according to the Committee to Protect Journalists.
No one was held accountable for the attack.
In 2015, fellow regional deputies stripped Shlosberg of his mandate after he represented a civic organization contesting its designation as a “foreign agent.” He considered the decision political retaliation. The following year, he received the inaugural Boris Nemtsov Prize for his defense of democratic values and returned to the regional assembly in an election.
Opposition to Crimea seizure
Shlosberg opposed Russia’s seizure of Crimea from the beginning. In a 2016 essay titled “The Crimean Dead End,” he described how Russian troops blockaded Ukrainian military facilities before a referendum held under occupation.
Yabloko’s subsequent election platform stated that Crimea belonged to Ukraine, that its annexation was illegal and that it should be reversed. This was an unusually direct position for a party still permitted to operate legally in Russia.
After the full-scale invasion began, Shlosberg continued to oppose the war publicly. He described the war as a game of “bloody chess” and argued that peace had to precede political change.
“We must first stop killing people,” he said in the debate that later became part of his criminal case. “If we achieve peace, we will regain freedom.”
The repression accumulated gradually.
Russian courts repeatedly fined Shlosberg and his wife, Zhanna, for allegedly “discrediting” the military. In June 2023, the Justice Ministry designated him a “foreign agent,” a label used to stigmatize critics and exclude them from political life.
In 2024, he was fined for reposting Arnold Schwarzenegger’s March 2022 appeal to Russians about the war. Authorities searched his home and the home of his elderly father.
In June 2025, he was detained over the debate with Pivovarov and placed under house arrest. When investigators opened the separate “false information” case in December, he was transferred to pretrial detention, where he remained until his conviction.
Despite other prominent anti-Putin figures like Maxim Katz, Shlosberg refused to leave Russia and compared himself to Antaeus, the figure from Greek mythology who lost his strength when separated from the earth.
Anti-war position that Ukrainians strongly disputed
Despite Shlosberg’s opposition to some of the Kremlin’s actions, his stance toward Russia’s war on Ukraine still raises an eyebrow.
His position after the full-scale invasion centered on a form of radical pacifism and an immediate, unconditional ceasefire. In a December 2024 Yabloko essay, he argued that shooting should stop first and questions of territory, borders, sanctions and European security should be negotiated afterward.
For Ukrainians, the problem is obvious. A ceasefire that does not require Russian withdrawal may freeze an occupation achieved through aggression, give Moscow time to rearm and leave millions of Ukrainians under Russian rule.
That year he also made another controversial statement. He argued that Ukraine ceased to be a victim when it began resisting, saying that the “myth that Ukraine remains a victim” did not correspond to history.
After Ukraine’s operation in Russia’s Kursk region, he attacked exiled Russian opposition figures who supported Kyiv and called them the “party of other people’s blood.” Critics accused him of focusing on Ukrainian military action while failing to recognize Ukraine’s right to strike the forces and infrastructure used to attack it.
Why the Kremlin chose this moment
Four and a half year into the full-scale war, the Kremlin has tightened its grip on all opposition. Even parties without wide support like Yabloko.
Shlosberg’s Fellow Yabloko deputy chair Maxim Kruglov was also sentenced to seven years in June for allegedly spreading “false information” about the military. Other party members have been imprisoned, declared “foreign agents” or excluded from elections.
On Aug. 10, the Supreme Court removed Yabloko from the ballot following a complaint by the ultranationalist Rodina party. A week later, the court rejected Yabloko’s appeal while Shlosberg was being sentenced in Pskov.
In his final statement, Shlosberg called the war a catastrophe and warned that Russia would eventually have to confront the full list of its dead. He said military cemeteries were expanding faster than maternity wards, kindergartens and schools.
The judge repeatedly interrupted him, and in the end granted the 11 year sentence that epitomizes modern Russia’s zeitgeist: that of a state edging on totalitarianism as the Russian authorities continue to ban social media, interfere with the private lives of its citizens, and silence all criticism.

Is India falling short on sugar supplies ahead of festive season?
While the mammoth Indian festivals of Dussehra and Diwali are still weeks away, a sharp rise in sugar prices is setting off alarm bells. That's despite the government’s assurances that it is taking measures to assuage concerns.
The all-India modal retail price of sugar rose to Rs 65 per kilogram on Friday from Rs 45 on July 21 and Rs 50 on July 31, according to the Department of Consumer Affairs. The rise has been attributed to lower-than-expected sugar production and stocks at a nine-year low.
Indian Sugar & Bio-energy Manufacturers Association had initially estimated gross domestic sugar production for the 2025-26 season at 343.5 lakh tons, the Indian Express reported. After diversion of 34 lakh tons for ethanol production, net output was projected at 309.5 lakh tons.
Opposition Congress President Mallikarjun Kharge questioned Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government over rising prices and declining stocks, highlighting the decision to divert sugarcane toward ethanol production.
India is one of the world's largest sugar producers and exporters. However, current exports have been halted, and the government has allowed the duty-free import of 1 million tons of sugar.

Gandhi's personal notes sell for $1.7 million, setting auction record
A collection of handwritten notes by Mahatma Gandhi has sold for $1.7 million in Mumbai, the highest price ever paid for an Indian historical document at auction, auction house Saffronart said.
The 688 notes were written by Gandhi to his close associate Anand Hingorani between 1944 and 1946, following the death of Hingorani's wife, Vidya. Later compiled into a book titled "A Thought for the Day," the writing touched upon a number of themes including truth, God and non-violence, offering personal insights on principles that Gandhi was closely associated to publicly.
The collection, preserved by Hingorani's family, was sold under the title "Gandhi: From the Collection of Anand T Hingorani." Gandhi's portable spinning wheel, notes on the discipline of spinning, manuscripts, letters, photographs and other personal items were also part of the auction.
Hingorani first met Gandhi in 1930 and later joined him on the Salt March, a campaign of peaceful resistance against Britain's salt monopoly.
"What makes this collection particularly compelling is the opportunity to see one of the most significant figures in India's history through the lens of a close, personal relationship," Saffronart co-founder Dinesh Vazirani said.
Gandhi led India's non-violent struggle for independence from British rule and influenced similar movements worldwide. He was assassinated in January 1948.
