How a tiny bloodstain exposed ISIS terrorist in Jerusalem couple’s murder after 3 years of dead ends
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
08:10:03 UTC
17:10:03 KST

The January 2019 murder of Yehuda and Tamar Kaduri in Jerusalem was not solved in a straight line. Two investigative teams worked in parallel, different theories were pursued and discarded, and detectives even tried to trace the origin of a bag and a shoe seen in surveillance footage. Suspects were arrested, including members of the family, and later released. Only three years later, after an entirely different murder, did investigators make the connection that brought them back to the old crime scene.
They then realized the killer had effectively been under their noses all along: Wassim Assaid, who was arrested by the Shin Bet two days after the Kaduri murders, not in connection with the killings but over his affiliation with ISIS. Assaid remained in administrative detention for about three years. Just one week after his release, he committed another murder. Even after that breakthrough, investigators still needed what prosecutors would later describe as the “golden evidence.”
The home of Assaid’s mother had been searched repeatedly, but only later did she tell investigators about a storage room behind the building that he used. There, according to Jerusalem District Prosecutor Amir Cassantini and Deputy District Prosecutor Shira Kani Tal, investigators found a black-and-green bag and a pair of shoes, among other items. A tiny stain was visible on one of the shoes. Initial testing showed it was human blood, and the shoe was sent to the National Center of Forensic Medicine.
“We really remember the phone call from Nurit Bublil,” Cassantini said, referring to the head of the forensic institute’s laboratory division. Then came the news: the blood belonged to Yehuda Kaduri. “Put yourself three and a half years after the murder,” Cassantini said. “We suddenly had what you call golden evidence. We understood that this was an incredible closing of the circle.” For prosecutors, it was exactly what they had been searching for. They already had a highly detailed confession from Assaid, but they had insisted that the confession alone was not enough.
A murder that left investigators with almost nothing
To understand why a few drops of blood mattered so much, it is necessary to return to the Kaduris’ home on Mordechai Elkahi Street in Jerusalem and to a murder that for years left more questions than answers. According to findings by the Jerusalem District Court, Assaid entered Israel intending to murder Jews for nationalist and ideological reasons. He reached the Armon Hanatziv area after previously hiding a switchblade and stun gun in a bomb shelter.
He saw Yehuda Kaduri arrive by car wearing a kippah, unload shopping bags and enter his home. Assaid followed him. When Yehuda later returned to the car, Assaid approached the apartment, found the door unlocked and entered. Inside, he found Tamar Kaduri in the bedroom and murdered her. He then remained in the apartment and waited for Yehuda to return. When Yehuda came home, put away the groceries and sat down to eat, Assaid killed him as well.
The court found that Assaid remained inside the apartment for several more hours. He washed his hands and the knife in the kitchen sink and left in the morning after taking rings and cash. Before leaving, he removed the key from the inside of the door and locked the apartment behind him. At the time, however, investigators had no idea who the killer was.
“When the Jerusalem Central Unit realized the investigation wasn’t progressing, they opened two investigative teams, two separate task forces,” said Cassantini, who prosecuted the case alongside attorney Yuval Kedar. The goal, he said, was to prevent investigators from locking onto a single theory and overlooking another possibility. Detectives pursued even the smallest details. Figures appeared in surveillance footage, but none could be identified with certainty, while a person carrying a black-and-green bag prompted investigators to visit bag stores in an attempt to determine who had purchased such an item.
A shoeprint at the scene led investigators to examine two possible shoe models, including shoes made by Nabil. Police even contacted company officials in an attempt to determine where the shoes had been sold and to whom. Other avenues were also explored. People were questioned, including relatives, and those suspicions were ultimately ruled out.
Kani Tal, who joined the case later, said that in hindsight it is easy to see that some investigative paths did not lead to the killer, but that does not mean they should not have been pursued. “You have to understand that at that stage police really had no lead,” she said. “They knew what the scene looked like, they knew what happened, but they had to pull on every relevant thread possible.”
The fact that alternative theories were examined and eliminated later became part of the strength of the prosecution’s case, she said. Rather than facing a claim that investigators had fixated on a single suspect, prosecutors could show that other possibilities had been seriously investigated. “The price is obviously difficult and painful,” she said, but investigators still had an obligation to seek the truth.
For years, the case remained open. Kani Tal said investigators “never let go at any stage.” Cassantini said there is always a fear that the truth will never be uncovered, but looking back he cannot identify one obvious investigative step that, had it been taken earlier, would necessarily have led police to Assaid. Assaid had acted alone and had not shared his plans with others, according to the prosecution. Investigators simply had no direct lead pointing to him.
A second murder creates the breakthrough
The turning point came from an entirely different crime scene. In March 2022, three years after the Kaduri murders, Moldovan worker Ivan Tirnovski was murdered in Jerusalem, while Igor Unoi, who was staying in the same apartment, was seriously wounded. According to the verdict, Assaid entered the apartment carrying a knife and stun gun, stabbed both men in the neck and fled.
Cassantini said investigators initially considered the possibility that the incident had been a fight among the Moldovan workers. At the same time, Assaid was detained after arousing the suspicion of forces near the A-Ram area, and a knife and stun gun were found in his bag. Initially, investigators still did not connect the detained man with the murder scene. Only after detectives reconstructed his walking route from Armon Hanatziv toward the checkpoint did the pieces begin to come together.
Then came the forensic evidence. Blood belonging to Tirnovski and Unoi was found on the knife in Assaid’s possession, and the court found that it was the weapon used in the murder and attempted murder. Then someone looked back at the old case.
Cassantini said one investigator compared the figure documented in the new investigation with a person appearing in footage from the earlier case and suggested to Shin Bet investigators that there might be a match. Kani Tal described it as a “click,” the moment when two cases that had previously seemed unrelated suddenly connected. “That was the moment they suddenly realized we had something here,” she said.
Details only the killer should have known
As the investigation progressed, the picture widened further. Assaid began talking about events from 2019. Before murdering the Kaduris, the court found, he had attempted to murder a Jewish teenage girl who was walking to a bus stop in the morning. He caught up with her on a staircase, tried to slit her throat and fled when she screamed.
During interrogation, Assaid began giving detailed descriptions of the crime scenes. Regarding the Kaduris’ home, he described the apartment’s layout, the rooms, where the couple had been and what he had done inside. He spoke about two refrigerators in the home, the food Yehuda ate before he was murdered, a photograph of a naval officer, taking the key and eating an apple after the killings.
The court found that Assaid was able to describe the crimes “down to the smallest details,” including apartment layouts, furniture, the location of people, where the victims were stabbed and many concealed details that could not be explained merely by exposure to media reports. One detail particularly stayed with Cassantini. Assaid said he had seen a photograph in the apartment of a man wearing a light-colored uniform. Prosecutors reviewed hundreds of crime-scene photographs but initially could not find the picture he described.
Only later did the Kaduris’ daughter explain that her brother had served in the Israeli Navy. For Cassantini, it was precisely the kind of detail that a suspect could provide before investigators themselves were able to verify it. The reconstruction was also significant. Cassantini said Assaid was driven from a distant location and, rather than investigators directing him to the crime scene, Assaid guided them to the neighborhood, street, building and stairwell.
At one point he stopped, checked whether he had reached the correct building, went to an adjacent building and then returned, saying he had identified the right place. He later drew the apartment’s layout almost “like an architect,” Cassantini said. Still, prosecutors decided that even a confession containing numerous concealed details was not enough.
“It wasn’t enough for us,” Cassantini said. “We wanted forensic, scientific evidence that this man was actually there.” Kani Tal said prosecutors knew that statements made in an interrogation room could look very different once a case reached court. A defendant could retract a confession, claim that investigators had fed him details or argue that his statement had not been given voluntarily.
So they kept searching. The decision not to rely solely on the confession was made by attorney Erez Padan, then deputy Jerusalem district prosecutor and now Southern District prosecutor. The prosecution wanted to exhaust every possible avenue for finding independent forensic evidence that would physically place Assaid at the murder scene.
That search eventually led to the storage room behind his mother’s home and to the shoes. The verdict found that blood belonging to Yehuda Kaduri was discovered on the shoes and that, in the absence of a reasonable explanation for how the victim’s blood reached footwear connected to Assaid, the finding was evidence that he was the killer. The shoes also shared class characteristics with footprints found at the crime scene.
Kani Tal put it simply: once investigators had shoes from a storage room used by Assaid with Yehuda Kaduri’s blood on them, together with all the details Assaid had been able to describe, there was no credible way to explain everything as fabrication. That was the value of insisting on independent evidence that did not depend on anything Assaid had told investigators.
The courtroom test
The prosecution’s concern about relying only on the confession ultimately proved justified. At trial, Assaid denied committing the crimes and claimed investigators had improperly pressured him, fed him information about the crime scenes and planted evidence. The court rejected those arguments. It found his confessions clear, coherent, detailed and largely consistent with one another, adding that it was difficult not to be struck by the “sense of satisfaction and pride” with which he described his actions during interrogation.
The trial also produced one unusual scene rarely captured in the dry language of a verdict. At one point, Assaid’s defense attorney asked to withdraw from the case. The court refused to delay proceedings, and during some hearings Assaid questioned witnesses himself. One of those witnesses was the teenage girl he was convicted of attempting to murder.
Cassantini said a partition was placed between her and Assaid and that questions were passed under court supervision. Assaid managed to ask only two questions. “We remember the tension in the room,” Cassantini said, adding that one of the judges wiped away a tear. The questioning was stopped shortly afterward and the girl left the witness stand.
For Kani Tal, the proceedings also illustrated the price imposed on victims and their families a second time. During sentencing arguments, she had to describe the brutality of the crimes and their consequences while members of the Kaduri family sat in the courtroom listening once again to the details of their parents’ murders.
“You feel in a certain sense that you’re causing more suffering, more pain,” she said. “I have to walk out of the courtroom afterward and ask myself, did I do something good? Did I do the right thing?”
Three life sentences and 40 more years
Prosecutors asked the court to classify the Kaduri murders as exceptionally severe. Kani Tal said such a finding is not sought in every murder case and required preparation and approval. In her view, the number of victims, the number of potential victims, the motive and the brutality justified the request.
She pointed in particular to the Kaduri family. “They didn’t lose a father,” she said. “They lost a mother and a father. They lost a home.”
Assaid was ultimately convicted of murdering three people, two attempted murders, additional offenses and active membership in ISIS. The court classified the Kaduri murders as exceptionally severe, ruled that Assaid’s confessions were admissible and found that there was substantial additional evidence proving he had committed the crimes. He was sentenced to three life terms plus an additional 40 years in prison. The classification of the murders as exceptionally severe means he cannot seek an early reduction of the life sentences.
When the sentence was read, members of the Kaduri family sat behind the prosecutors. Cassantini recalled that the judges began by referring to Haim Nahman Bialik’s poem “On the Slaughter.” As the ruling was read, the family could be heard behind them. Kani Tal said she and Cassantini reacted almost instinctively, turning around and reaching a hand toward them.
Three years earlier, the case had been an unsolved double murder: a locked apartment, surveillance footage that could not clearly identify the man appearing in it, shoeprints and investigative leads that went nowhere. Then came another murder, a walking route reconstructed from cameras, a confession, a crime-scene reconstruction, concealed details and finally a few tiny spots of blood on shoes found in a storage room.
Cassantini said he remains in contact with the Kaduris’ daughter. For the family, he said, solving the case, completing the trial and reaching sentencing became “some kind of milestone” from which they might find “some small measure of comfort and continue with their lives and recover.”
After such a long road, that may also best explain the meaning of those drops of blood on the shoe. They were not the moment suspicion was born. They were the moment a case built over years finally gained evidence that did not depend on memory, confession or interpretation. A tiny stain that remained from the crime scene, found far away from it, ultimately connected Yehuda Kaduri to the man the court determined had murdered him and Tamar in their home.

Taiwan Space Agency launches locally developed Maraho rocket

Unknown Publisher

08:09:04 UTC
17:09:04 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) – Taiwan Space Agency said it successfully launched its first self-developed hybrid-propellant sounding rocket the Maraho Saturday morning.
The launch took place at the Xuhai Indigenous Scientific Rocket Launch Site in Pingtung at 7:10 a.m., per Liberty Times. The rocket achieved liftoff thrust of 1,500 kilograms and reached an altitude of 8.1 kilometers during its 432-second flight, the agency said in a statement.
The projectile reached a top speed of 408 meters per second, or Mach 1.2, 20% faster than sound. The launch was a success, as the rocket completed all the planned procedures despite poor weather at sea preventing its recovery, the agency said.
During the flight, communications between the rocket and the base remained stable throughout. The results booked by the Maraho will be used to improve the design of future rockets.
Saturday’s test data and the experience garnered during preparations for the launch will also help reduce the development risks for future rockets and lead to the gradual strengthening of the agency’s research capabilities, Liberty Times reported.
The name “maraho” comes from a species of butterfly also known as the Taiwan broad-tailed swallowtail. The red spots on the endangered species showing similarities to the rocket exhaust also formed the inspiration for the design of the Maraho.

Quick hits: Stunning Shoriful rivals Starc's staggering spell, Hazlewood fumes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
08:08:18 UTC
17:08:18 KST

Australia vs Bangladesh quick hits: Mitchell Starc and Shoriful Islam produce left-arm magic, Matt Renshaw disappoints on return, Josh Hazlewood fumes
Two lethal left arm quicks combine for 12 wickets, Australia comes close to snaring the rarest of dismissals, and a Harrup Park specialist fails on his return to the team.
Here are the quick hits from day one of the second Test between Australia and Bangladesh.
1. Sensational Starc's first-ball strike
We've seen this play before: Four times, in fact.
Mitch Starc steaming in, an opening batter studiously preparing for a lengthy stay at the crease, only to succumb to the very first challenge.
Shadman Islam was the unfortunate batter on this occasion, looking to clip Starc into the leg side but misjudging the pace and sending a leading edge to Cameron Green at gully.
He is, incredibly, the fourth batter to fall to Starc with the very first ball of a Test match.
Sri Lankan opener Dimuth Karunaratne was his first such victim back in 2016.
England's Rory Burns was famously bowled around his legs at the Gabba in the 2021/22 Ashes series.
And then, in 2024 at Adelaide Oval, Yashavi Jaiswal was trapped LBW with a pink ball.
Oh, and he wasn't done there, either.
2. Starc's five-fa comes in just 22 balls
Mitch Starc would not be contained or limited with just one wicket in his first spell.
Incredibly, he took five, tearing through the Bangladesh top order like a cyclone of ill-intent.
Shadman Islam's wicket was the only one to fall in the first over.
But in his second, he took two in the first two balls, accounting for Tanzid and Shanto in consecutive balls.
Mominul survived the first ball of the third over, but shouldn't have let down his guard as he fell later in the very same over to make it 4 in 3 for the big left-hander.
And then, in his fourth over, he made it five, Litton Das falling LBW for yet another duck, his five wickets coming in just 22 balls.
It should have been just 21 balls, had Beau Webster not shelled the sort of ball that you'd toss up to a toddler in the backyard.
It didn't matter though, Starc could not be contained, ending his six-over spell with figures of 5-5 and four maidens, leaving Bangladesh 5-15.
It was the sixth fastest five-wicket haul in Test history, but remarkably, it wasn't Starc's fastest in the format — that came in just 15 balls against the West Indies last year.
3. Obstructing the field?
Fans of obscure dismissals were almost gifted a rare instance of a player obstructing the field in the later stages of Bangladesh's batting innings.
Hazlewood came in and Taskin swiped across the line, sending the ball straight up in the air.
Hazlewood raced towards the ball, as Taskin took off for a run, before he then realised Hazlewood was baring down on him.
Taskin attempted to cover up, Hazlewood barged into him and the ball fell safe.
The crowd in Mackay felt aggrieved and there was more than a small suggestion of obstructing the field.
Hazlewood's eyes were in danger of having to be registered as dangerous weapons such was the ferocity of the daggers he was giving the unfortunate batter, as Pat Cummins engaged in a discussion with umpire Nitin Menon.
There was no appeal though that we could see, and Taskin was reprieved.
Only one player has ever been given out obstructing the field in Test cricket, Len Hutton for England against South Africa at The Oval in 1951.
Incredibly, later in the over, it appeared there was an (inadvertent) case of a double hit too as an attempted pull shot went awry.
4. Renshaw out cheaply on Test return
If Matt Renshaw could have chosen any ground in the world to make his Test return, it may well have been Harrup Park.
The Queenslander is the leading First Class run scorer at the venue, and is the only man to have scored two Sheffield Shield centuries in Mackay.
He's also coming off an impressive domestic summer, during which he scored three red-ball centuries at an average flirting with 50.
And it was under porcelain blue skies and in what looked to be perfect batting conditions that he made his way back to the Test-match crease, with the pitch having flattened out since Starc's new-ball demolition job.
The southpaw made an assured start to his innings, working a few attractive runs through the off-side, but it wasn't long before he was back in the sheds, having edged one into the slips.
Renshaw was out for 8 and Bangladesh, in desperate need of an early wicket after being bundled out for just 64, had their breakthrough.
5. Shoriful's dream day
Forced to sit out the first Test with a side strain, exciting fast bowler Shoriful Islam wasted no time in making an impact in Mackay.
The 25-year-old left-armer is just that little bit quicker than his more workmanlike pace-bowling colleagues, and at over 190 centimetres tall, provides a different challenge in terms of release point.
Coming into the attack at first change, Shoriful took just two deliveries to claim his first Test wicket in Australia.
Pitching on a good length and seaming into Travis Head, the Australian opener was caught trying to play a shot that was never there, and was out chopping on for the third innings in a row.
Three balls later, and Shoriful had his second.
This time, he was aided by thigh pad rather than willow, with the ball rolling onto the stumps after thudding into Marnus Labuschagne.
Labuschagne was in disbelief, Shoriful was in dreamland, and Bangladesh was making a fist of things in Mackay.
And the towering left-armer wasn't done there.
First, he produced a beauty to dismiss Smith, who was well set on 42, LBW midway through the evening session.
Then, he tore through the Australian lower order, conjuring three more moments of magic to dismiss Beau Webster and Cummins for ducks, and Starc for 1.

Lush dahlias without unnecessary hassle: when to plant, what to feed them, and how to protect them from diseases
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
11:02:16 EEST
17:02:16 KST

Lush dahlias without unnecessary hassle: when to plant, what to feed them, and how to protect them from diseases
Kyiv • UNN
Dahlias are planted in spring in a sunny spot and regularly watered and fed. In autumn, the tubers are dug up and stored in a cool place.
Dahlias are among the most popular ornamental garden plants, valued for their large, vibrant flower heads and long blooming period. Depending on the variety, the plants can differ considerably in height, as well as in the shape and size of their flowers. Low-growing dahlias are used for flower beds and borders, tall varieties for creating floral arrangements, while large-flowered varieties are often grown as cut flowers.
With proper care, dahlias can bloom from midsummer until the first autumn frosts. At the same time, these plants are warmth-loving, cannot tolerate frozen soil, and require regular watering and feeding.
When to plant dahlias, how to care for them, and what to do with the tubers in autumn is explained by UNN.
When and where to plant dahlias
Dahlias are planted in open ground in spring, when the threat of severe frosts has passed and the soil has warmed sufficiently. The exact timing depends on the region and the weather, but in most regions of Ukraine, favorable conditions usually occur in May. However, experienced gardeners advise taking both the calendar and air temperature into account.
Choose a sunny location protected from strong winds for dahlias. For abundant flowering, the plants need at least six hours of direct sunlight per day. In deep shade, the shoots may become elongated and the number of flowers may decrease. It is important to avoid low-lying areas and other spots where water remains for a long time after rain. Constant waterlogging is dangerous for the tubers and may cause them to rot.
Before planting, the tubers should be inspected. Severely damaged, soft, or rotten parts should be removed. Tall varieties may require support. It is more convenient to install it immediately during planting so as not to damage the root system later.
The distance between plants is determined according to the variety. Compact dahlias can be placed closer together, whereas tall, spreading bushes need more space for proper lighting and air circulation.
What soil is suitable for dahlias
Dahlias grow best in fertile, loose, well-drained soil. The soil should retain sufficient moisture while not becoming waterlogged after rain or watering.
Before planting, the soil can be enriched with well-rotted compost or other mature organic matter. Heavy clay soils require particular attention to drainage. If water regularly stagnates on the site, it is better to create a raised bed for dahlias or choose another location.
It is undesirable to use fresh manure immediately before planting. An excess of nutrients, especially nitrogen, can stimulate vigorous growth of green mass at the expense of flowering.
How to water dahlias
Dahlias require regular moisture, especially during active growth, bud formation, and flowering. The frequency depends on the temperature, amount of rainfall, soil type, and plant size.
After planting the tubers, excessive watering is undesirable until active growth begins. In cool, wet soil, tubers are particularly vulnerable to rot.
After well-developed shoots appear, water dahlias abundantly, but do not allow the soil to remain constantly waterlogged. It is better to water deeply but less frequently than to moisten only the top layer of soil every day. Water should be directed mainly at the base of the plant.
In hot, dry weather, the need for moisture increases. A layer of organic mulch will help retain it. It also suppresses weed growth and protects the root zone from sharp temperature fluctuations.
What to feed dahlias
Dahlias need balanced nutrition for active growth and prolonged flowering. If sufficient compost was incorporated into the soil when preparing the site, the plants will already receive some of the nutrients they need during the initial stage.
Later, you can use complete fertilizers for flowering plants according to the manufacturer's instructions. After bud formation begins, it is especially undesirable to overuse nitrogen fertilizers. Excessive nitrogen may cause the bush to produce abundant foliage while flowering less profusely.
The condition of the plant also says a lot. Weak growth, changes in leaf color, or poor flowering may be related not only to a lack of fertilizer, but also to improper watering, unsuitable soil, diseases, or root damage. Therefore, increasing the amount of fertilizer just in case is not advisable.
Pruning and Training Dahlias
Training helps produce a stronger bush and control its size. When a young plant has developed several pairs of true leaves, the shoot tip can be pinched out. This stimulates the development of lateral shoots and makes the bush more branched.
Tall-growing varieties must be tied to a support in a timely manner. This is especially important for plants with large flower heads: after heavy rain or strong gusts of wind, their heavy stems may break.
Throughout the season, it is recommended to regularly remove faded flowers. If they are left on the plant, the dahlia will spend resources on producing seeds. Removing spent flower heads helps maintain the bush's ornamental appearance and stimulates the formation of new buds.
Damaged, dried, or diseased leaves should also be removed, and plant debris showing signs of disease should not be left in the flower bed.
Dahlia Diseases and Pests
Among the problems gardeners may encounter when growing dahlias are fungal diseases, rots, and viral infections. The risk of fungal diseases increases with excessive moisture, overcrowded plantings, and poor air circulation.
For prevention, plants should not be planted too close together. When watering, it is advisable to avoid wetting the leaves unnecessarily, especially in the evening. Affected parts of the plant should be removed promptly.
Common dahlia pests include aphids, slugs, snails, and spider mites. Young shoots are particularly attractive to slugs and snails, so plants should be inspected regularly after the seedlings emerge.
The control method depends on the specific pest and the scale of the infestation. When there are only a few insects, mechanical removal or washing them off with water may sometimes be sufficient. If insecticides or other plant-protection products are used, it is necessary to follow the instructions and consider their possible impact on bees and other pollinating insects.
How to Prepare Dahlias for Winter
Dahlias originate from warmer climates, so their tubers are not adapted to severe ground freezing. In Ukraine, they are usually dug up in autumn and stored until the following spring.
After the first frosts, when the above-ground part of the plant turns black and dies back, the stems are cut off. The tubers are carefully dug up, taking care not to damage them with garden tools.
After digging them up, excess soil is removed, the tubers are inspected, and damaged or rotten parts are cut away. Before long-term storage, the tubers are allowed to dry.
In winter, the planting material is kept in a cool, dark place where the temperature remains above freezing. The main task is to prevent both freezing and complete drying out or rotting of the tubers. It is advisable to inspect them periodically throughout the winter.
In spring, the tubers are checked again, divided if necessary, and prepared for planting. With this care cycle, dahlias can return to the flower bed every year and bloom until the autumn cold arrives.

Unions worry Labour’s plan for zero-hours contracts may break manifesto pledge
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
08:00:58 UTC
17:00:58 KST

Trades unions are warning Andy Burnham that Labour’s policy on cutting zero-hours contracts risks failing to live up to the party’s manifesto.
Union leaders are seeking reassurances from the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, amid what the TUC has condemned as “scaremongering” from business groups.
The unions were alarmed by limitations on who will qualify for new guaranteed hours contracts, mooted in Labour’s recent consultation document on the policy.
Joanne Thomas, the general secretary of shop workers’ union Usdaw, said: “The right to a contract that guarantees the hours you normally work is a matter of basic fairness and security. It must be applied to everyone to deliver the government’s manifesto commitment.”
She added that the policy “must apply to everyone up to and including full-time workers. We absolutely cannot have loopholes that make this meaningless.”
Ross Holden, the head of policy and research at the GMB union, said: “We are concerned that without a major rethink there is a risk this policy is not matching what we said in the manifesto.”
He added that unions are worried about whether their concerns are being given sufficient weight. “If the policy development is one-sided then we risk this being watered down.”
Unite raised a separate concern, about a “regularity requirement” – suggested by the government – which the union claimed would exclude a significant number of workers.
“If the government was attempting to create a right which virtually no workers could qualify for or be able to enforce – they could not have done a better job,” a Unite spokesperson said.
Getting rid of “exploitative” zero-hours contracts is a key aim of Labour’s Employment Rights Act. The Act has already become law, but the zero hours changes are not due to be implemented until next year, and many details have yet to be thrashed out.
A consultation document, published when Keir Starmer was still at No 10, included an upper hours threshold. Workers whose existing contract already guarantees them more than the threshold – which could be set at anything from 8 to 48 hours – would not qualify for the new right to a contract that matches the hours they actually work.
Business groups seized on official estimates published by the government last week that showed the most expansive version of the policy could cost companies up to £2.9bn a year. The British Chambers of Commerce called the prospect “a further hammer blow for many firms struggling to keep their heads above water”.
Kate Bell, the assistant general secretary of the TUC, said that 40% of the upper costs estimate was made up of the compensation employers would have to pay out for cancelling workers’ shifts at short notice. “That assumes no behavioural change by employers,” she said. “It assumes they don’t have the creativity and the experience to adapt their model.”
Bell added that the same document showed irregular and unpredictable shifts cost one in three workers on zero-hours contracts about £3,000 a year.
“We keep having to have the same argument time and time again about the real costs of insecurity for workers,” she said. “Most people don’t want to be on these contracts. They’ve been on these contracts for a long time and it has costs for their mental health and their financial security.”
Reynolds returned to the job of business secretary in Burnham’s wholesale reshuffle last month, after being moved out of the post by Starmer. With the zero hours consultation closing next week, the issue will be one of the first he faces back in post.
A government spokesperson said: “We are absolutely committed to ending exploitative zero-hours contracts, where workers bear all the financial risk when hours, shifts and earnings are unpredictable. These reforms will give workers in every postcode greater income security and predictability of hours.”
The spokesperson added: “While no final decisions have been made, we’re consulting with business and trade unions including GMB, Unite and Usdaw, to get the detail right and ensure this works in the real world.”

Meta goes on trial over allegations it hooked children on its platforms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
08:00:58 UTC
17:00:58 KST

Meta’s business can be boiled down to four words that begin with the letter H: hook, hold, harvest, hide, according to a lawyer who is prosecuting the world’s largest social media company.
The owner of Facebook and Instagram “hooks” in users, “holds” them on its platforms for as long as possible, “harvests” their data and then “hides” the truth from the public, she argued.
“Meta’s business model worked especially well for kids,” said Megan O’Neill, a lawyer for the state of California.
Her accusation opened the blockbuster trial against the US tech company on Tuesday in Oakland, California, just north of Meta’s headquarters in Silicon Valley. California has joined 28 other US states in suing the £1tn ($1.36tn) company for allegedly designing addictive products that lead to children being harmed.
Eight jurors heard from O’Neill and attorneys for Meta this week, along with testimony from former employees and a psychologist. The lawsuit centers on allegations that the company violated US federal child privacy laws and state-level consumer protection laws by collecting data on children under the age of 13 without parental permission. Over the course of the trial, the jury is additionally expected to hear from Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg and Instagram CEO Adam Mosseri.
The threat to Meta is existential. If the company is found liable, damages could be as high as $200bn – an amount equivalent to the company’s 2025 annual revenue. The states are also asking that Meta be forced to change the design of its products to make them safer for children, which could have permanent effects on the company’s business model and how its social media platforms operate.
Meta has denied all allegations. Liza Crenshaw, a spokesperson for the company, said: “Rather than sticking to the facts or the law, the states have instead decided to chase an outlandish payout.”
During opening statements, Paul Schmidt, an attorney for Meta, said there is “no dispute” people can struggle with social media, but that Meta had “come up with tools to try and address that”. He added the company does not allow children under the age of 13 to register for accounts on its social networks and that it had disabled more than 1m accounts of those young users.
The trial is expected to last six to eight weeks. The proceedings will be led by attorneys for the states of California, Colorado, Kentucky and New Jersey. The jury’s role is advisory, which means they will give recommendations to the presiding judge, Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers, who will make the final decision on the verdict and damages.
Meta faces thousands of similar US lawsuits brought by families, school districts and other attorneys general. The company lost the first two of those cases to go to trial in March. In the first, the company was ordered to pay nearly $1bn to the state of New Mexico for allowing child sexual exploitation on its platforms; and in the second, it was found liable for deliberately designing addictive products that hooked one young woman and was ordered to pay her more than $4m.
The star witness to take the stand in the trial’s first week was Arturo Béjar, a safety engineer at Meta who worked there in two separate stints between 2009 and 2021. Since leaving, Béjar has been an outspoken critic of the company, testifying before a US Senate committee and serving as an expert witness in other cases that involve social media’s harm to children.
In Oakland, Béjar testified that his motivation for pursuing solutions for harms to children was his own teenage daughter’s treatment on Instagram. He said she received unwanted sexual advances and photos of male genitals as well as misogynistic insults. Later, she told her father that reporting these abuses through Instagram’s established processes was either ineffective or not possible.
“Meta is taking a ‘don’t ask, don’t tell’ strategy” when it comes to child safety, Béjar testified.
Béjar said that his job often included briefing Zuckerberg and that he had spoken with the CEO more than 100 times in the course of his work.
During Béjar’s testimony, attorneys for the government showed the jury an email he sent Zuckerberg in 2021, which outlined a survey he had conducted of teens’ experiences on Instagram. The results showed 51% of users said “yes” to having bad or harmful experiences within the previous seven days and that content was taken down only 0.02% of the time.
Béjar testified he sent that data to Zuckerberg because, “in my experience, when Mark makes something a priority, mountains move.”
“Did he ever respond to you?” the attorney asked.
“No,” Béjar replied. “I didn’t hear back from him.”
Meta fought to bar Béjar from testifying at the trial, filing a series of motions to strike his exhibits and prevent him from taking the stand, all of which were rejected. In an email to reporters on Wednesday, Meta continued to hound him. The company’s statement said Béjar’s testimony was not credible or reliable because he overinflated his role at the company and took credit for work he didn’t do.
After Béjar’s testimony wrapped, the jury heard recorded depositions from Elena Davis and Natalie Troxel – both former user experience researchers for Meta. Jean Twenge, a psychology professor at San Diego State University, also briefly took the stand, with testimony scheduled to continue next week.

Why am I called The Black Farmer? Because there are so few of us in Britain. I’d like that to change | Wilfred Emmanuel-Jones
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
08:00:57 UTC
17:00:57 KST

Who’d be a farmer? Clarkson’s Farm on Amazon is great entertainment but it also gives some indication of the stresses and challenges behind the farm gate. Would anyone who lacked the significant alternative income that Clarkson is lucky to have want that? Well, actually, yes.
I’m an entrepreneur who owns a farm, as opposed to hands-on running the small one I bought 25 years ago, but as I look around the industry, I’m struck by a significant fact: the very reason I can be known as the Black Farmer is because I am such a rarity that it makes me readily identifiable.
Because of what I do, people – many of them British minorities – often ask me how they can be farmers, how they can secure some land and set up for themselves. Don’t be surprised at that: among Britain’s minorities, millions have rural origins in lands abroad. It is a mistake to see people of colour as intrinsically urban – my own origins are in rural Jamaica. But when they ask me, I can’t really help them. There is no obvious route for them to follow, and there is precious little land they could possibly farm. This is the reality. In 2025, when Defra completed its most recent survey of principal farmers and holders in England, it found 99.7% of those who responded self-described as white.
I’m aware of the pitfall here. I know the danger these days of wanting to talk about diversity and being dismissed as woke. I’m hardly woke: in 2010 I fought a rural seat for the Conservatives. But in any other industry, that figure, 99.7%, would prompt some questions.
Here are the problems. If you are black or Asian or a kid from another minority in London, or Manchester, or Birmingham or Newcastle, where do you start? Your parents don’t own even an acre of land. You don’t have the network, or the knowledge that comes from growing up within or adjacent to a farming family and a farming community.
There is the ongoing and emotive debate about inheritance tax and whether farms should so easily be passed down from generation to generation. I’m among those who celebrate the families that have worked the same land year after year, decade after decade. That brings a knowledge and continuity essential to rural communities and our food supply. But as well as inheritance, we have to think about entry. People cannot resolve to make that commitment if they cannot see a way in.
How could that be different? Think about who owns the land. The National Trust, for example, is the country’s largest farm-owner, with more than 1,300 tenant farmers. Think about the Duchy of Cornwall, the crown estate, the Church of England. Universities and local authorities also control large tracts of land. There are people and institutions that could administer properly controlled programmes to allow those from non-traditional farming backgrounds to have a go. They could create starter farms and offer affordable tenancies. They could provide mentoring, pairing experienced farmers with ambitious newcomers, and give access to equipment. Maybe there could be targeted apprenticeships, allowing people to learn the ropes on someone else’s farm – a process that may lead to them owning their own farm. One might cite 28-year-old Kaleb Cooper on Clarkson’s farm, although in that case it is clearly the younger man teaching the older how it is done.
The supermarkets could play a role, as they wield enormous influence over British food and how it is produced. Why can’t they create routes for a new generation of growers, providing a sure path for produce to reach the public? That would be a move towards diversity with a clear economic purpose. Farming could do with new blood: people who question the traditions, people who know about different foods, cultures and business models – people who look at a field and can envision things that previous generations couldn’t.
I think back. I grew up in Birmingham and my first experience with the land was helping my father on his allotment. My route was defiantly non-traditional. I struggled with undiagnosed dyslexia, joined the Parachute regiment and got kicked out, flipped burgers, worked as a chef and then produced cookery programmes for the BBC, which allowed me to buy a farm in Devon. Locals dubbed me “the Black Farmer”. I wish there were many more of us.
I would never want to denigrate those who work so hard, and who may have toiled for generations to run their farms, produce the food we need and sometimes – if they are lucky, if the weather permits, if the stars align – make a profit. But I also want to be just as excited by the prospect of another black kid from Birmingham getting an opportunity, or a minority kid from a council estate in Manchester becoming the first farmer in the family.
Farming is key to the future, and the climate crisis is forcing us to think fast and hard about crops, water, soil and what we do with them. Old timers, new thinkers – we need both.

Huckabee attends screening of ‘The Bridge,’ about Israelis finding joy through music after Oct. 7
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
08:00:14 UTC
17:00:14 KST

The Bridge, a documentary about 10 Israelis whose lives were shattered by the October 7 attacks and who traveled to Los Angeles to rediscover the joy of making music at the legendary Rock ‘n’ Roll Fantasy Camp, was shown at an emotional screening at the Menachem Begin Heritage Center in Jerusalem this week. The audience included US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee and several of the Israelis featured in the film.
Huckabee, an enthusiastic musician who has played bass guitar for decades, said the film moved him deeply. “Music has the power to take our worst moments and help us to put them behind us,” Huckabee said. Songs, he said, express “our struggles, our trials, our tears, and our joys. That is why music is so powerful.”
He thanked the Israelis who took part in the film, as well as David Fishof, Rock ‘n’ Roll Fantasy Camp’s founder and director, who also attended the screening, for allowing the audience “to see the power and the healing that music brings.”
That idea that music can provide a way back into life after devastating trauma is at the center of The Bridge.
The tagline for the movie is, “Ten survivors. One way to rock,” and that captures the essence of the film.
The Bridge, which was produced by Kevin S. Bright (who addressed the audience via video) and directed by Brad Allgood, follows a group of young Israelis affected directly by October 7 as they travel to Los Angeles for the Rock ‘n’ Roll Fantasy Camp, where participants rehearse, form bands, take master classes, and perform with veteran rock musicians. Musicians who performed with bands such as Guns N’ Roses, Van Halen, and Black Sabbath mentored the Israelis.
The movie opens with clips of the October 7 attacks and features interviews with the 10 camp participants about how they survived that day. Among them was Tuval Haim, whose brother, Yotam, also a musician, was kidnapped by Hamas. Yotam managed to escape but was killed in a tragic instance of friendly fire. Another participant, Bar Rudaeff, had to cope with the kidnapping of his father, Lior, on October 7. After the conclusion of the rock camp, Rudaeff learned that his father had been murdered.
Nova survivor describes her emotions after October 7
Raz Shifer, a Nova survivor, spoke in the film about feeling tormented about why she survived when so many around her were killed. Throughout The Bridge, she takes every opportunity to speak out for the release of the hostages, including Romi Gonen, her friend’s sister. Ben King of Kibbutz Be’eri tells about how he survived with his wife in their safe room after terrorists entered their home and set it on fire.
Valeria Dvorkin sat alone in the safe room of her house in Kibbutz Nir Am with her dog for over 24 hours, hearing fighting outside. Many of her friends were killed and kidnapped, including Emily Damari, who was released in early 2025, as well as twins Gali and Ziv Berman, who were ultimately brought home in October 2025. Dov Engel, a reservist, was wounded while fighting in the South on October 8.
All 10 suffered devastating losses, and all had a passion for music prior to the attack, but most said they stopped playing music in the aftermath. Watching them gradually open up to each other and to the musicians and rock-camp participants, and begin to find joy through music again, however haltingly, is incredibly moving.
At the discussion following the screening, Fishof said that one of the most important parts of the experience was not only giving the Israelis a chance to play alongside famous musicians, but putting them in a room with Americans who, in many cases, had never met an Israeli. The camp itself became a kind of bridge in precisely the way the documentary’s title suggests.
“It was just so amazing to see how we changed all these people’s visions about Israel,” Fishof said. “And that these guys could rock out too.”
The trip took place in March 2024, when anti-Israel demonstrations were intensifying in the United States. Fishof and some of the other organizers said they had been genuinely nervous about how the Israeli delegation would be received. But when the group was introduced to the other rock-camp participants, and they told their stories, the response was overwhelmingly warm.
Sam Grundwerg, world chairman of Keren Hayesod–UIA (United Israel Appeal), who helped organize the project and who attended the screening, recalled how the Israelis were embraced by the other campers and by the musicians.
“What we’re hoping that it will do is for people that love music, that genre or any genre, people who are brought in by this human story,” Grundwerg said. “They’re also hearing these stories about real people and about real horrific things that they went through on October 7.”
Fishof said former Skid Row singer Sebastian Bach, who knew little about Israel or October 7 before he met the Israeli delegation, came to love them. Bach subsequently posted publicly in support of Israel, including posting the phrase, “Am Yisrael Chai.”
Israeli film participants discuss the meaning behind the trip
For the Israeli participants, the trip was about reclaiming parts of their lives that had become inaccessible after October 7.
Valeria Dvorkin, one of the participants in the Jerusalem screening, said that after October 7, she found herself unable even to listen to music.
“It was very difficult to hear music after October 7. Even in my car, in my room,” she said.
But the Rock ‘n’ Roll Fantasy Camp experience changed that. “After this experience, I am running on it, full power,” she said. “I’m doing music. It fills me. It makes me happy. So, I think it helps me all the time.”
She has continued making music with Rudaeff, who also attended the screening.
“You appreciate, first, that you live to enjoy this experience, and then, again, that people are fighting for the freedom that we have,” Rudaeff said at the screening. “So even though you experience fighting, you also feel grateful.”
He described how his family discussed what song should accompany his father’s burial, after Lior’s remains were returned to Israel in 2025, since music had always been such an important part of Lior’s life. The family chose Led Zeppelin’s “Stairway to Heaven.” As the last bits of earth were placed on the grave, he said, the final notes of the song were playing.
“It was the way to be buried for him,” he said.
Only after the burial, Rudaeff said, did he feel that he could begin focusing more fully on his own life again. He has since built a music studio in Tel Aviv and returned to creating music.
Fishof said the experience convinced him that it was time to bring Rock Camp to Israel.
“Sam and I, I think our goal is to bring Rock Camp here, and to really have these rock stars come and share their music.”
He said he also hopes to give Israelis affected by the war opportunities to write songs and work directly with professional musicians.
“We want to give this opportunity to people to get into writing songs and meeting these celebrities and change people’s lives through music.”
Fishof spoke about how the recent wave of antisemitism following October 7 had affected him.
“All my life… I never had any problems, I worked with rock stars, never had problems,” he said. “But when I made this film... for the first time in my entire career, I really felt it,” said Fishof, a former sports and music agent who produced many revival tours.
He said he had difficulty obtaining the rights to one song the participants played and hoped to use in The Bridge, adding that the Tribeca Festival rejected The Bridge because its selection committee feared it would be considered too pro-Israel.
But while he has recently encountered some anti-Israel sentiment, he emphasized that others were happy to help with the Rock Camp journey. He recalled that songwriter Linda Perry heard Dvorkin perform one of her songs and allowed the production to use it without charge. Award-winning songwriter Diane Warren contributed a peace song for the Israeli participants to perform, and he said that gestures like these encouraged him.
It all went back to Huckabee’s heartfelt words immediately following the screening: “Music is able to touch us where we are,” he said, “and take us where we need to be.”

Less than two years before the Philippines chooses its next president, Ferdinand Marcos Jnr still has no candidate to carry his banner.

Layers of history: Egypt unearths 6,000-year cemetery spanning Predynastic to Ptolemaic eras
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
08:00:08 UTC
17:00:08 KST

Egyptian archaeologists unearthed an ancient cemetery whose roots stretch back through the Greco-Roman era to the Predynastic period, the Egyptian Tourism and Antiquities Ministry announced earlier this month.
Discovered at the Kom El-Khalgan archaeological site in Dakahlia Governorate, the oldest finds at the site date back to the Lower Egyptian prehistoric cultures, Buto I and Buto II, in the first half of the fourth millennium BCE.
In the cemetery, archaeologists found a group of tombs with simple oval pits carved into the sandy layer, containing remains buried in various funerary positions, indicating the different burial rites of the time.
The tombs were also characterized by the simplicity of their funerary furnishings, such as small handmade pottery vessels and some seashells, even though the density of burials point to the area being heavily populated at the time.
A second group of tombs dating to Egypt’s Second Intermediate Period (circa 1782 to 1550 BCE) to the New Kingdom era, were also found at the site.
Confirms settlement in region during Hyksos’ reign
The finds confirm that the area had been settled during the Hyksos’ reign during the 15th Dynasty given its proximity to Avaris, which had served as the capital city at the time.
Among this group, the there are two styles of tombs: mastabas, which are flat-roofed, rectangular structures with inward sloping sides, and tombs with cornices.
Similar to the earlier group of burials, preliminary research here points to a diverse set of burial positions, varied age groups, and funerary customs.
Funerary furnishings found within these tombs include jewelry, amulets, scarabs, bronze tools and weapons, pottery vessels and Tell el-Yahudiyeh (TEY) style juglets.
A mudbrick tomb containing a collection of pottery vessels and bronze tools and dating back to the early Eighteenth Dynasty was also found.
From the Ptolemaic period, excavations revealed a number of simple burial pits, including the burial of a child inside two amphorae that had been reused as a burial vessel.
Remains of ancient residential buildings also found
Alongside the cemetery, archaeologists also uncovered the remains of residential area dating to the Second Intermediate Period, including mudbrick buildings, grain storage silos, ovens, and hearths.
Surrounding the residential and funerary infastructure, researchers at the dig found a group of sinusoidal (wavy) walls, commonly seen in Egyptian architecture between the Middle and New kingdoms.
As well, the excavations yielded a collection of other artifacts, including pottery vessels, stone tools, and large quantities of fish, bird, and animal bones.
The foundations of a building with thick mudbrick walls, pottery shards, and stone tools dating to the beginning of the New Kingdom were also found.
Tourism and Antiquities Minister Sherif Fathy praised the archaeologists efforts and affirmed the importance of the find.
Dr. Hisham El-Leithy. Egypt’s Supreme Council of Antiquities secretary-general, noted that the discoveries offers insight into ancient settlement patterns, funerary practices, and the way people interacted with nature in antiquity.
He added that excavations at the site are still ongoing.

Three men arrested on suspicion of importing drones from China for use in drug, weapons smuggling

Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
07:59:30 UTC
16:59:30 KST

Three men were arrested on suspicion of importing drones from China for use in weapons and drug smuggling on Wednesday after an extensive investigation uncovered the operation.
The Lahav 433 National Economic Crime Unit conducted the investigation in collaboration with the Tax Authority, Southern Regional Police Headquarters, Ben-Gurion Airport Customs, the Israel Prison Service’s canine unit, and other law enforcement agencies.
The investigation centered on a security company suspected of serving as a cover for the drone-importing operation, committing customs and Value Added Tax (VAT) violations, and transferring the drones to entities involved in smuggling operations in southern Israel.
The company’s owner, an Ashkelon resident in his 30’s, and two employees allegedly served as intermediaries and delivered the drones to individuals involved in smuggling weapons and guns.
Over the course of the investigation, dozens of shipments of drones and drone equipment suspected to have been used as part of the smuggling operation were received by the company.
Police raid company warehouse, confiscate drones
On Wednesday, police raided a warehouse owned by the company after it received a shipment containing dozens of drones. During the raid, the three suspects were arrested, and the shipment was seized.
The suspects are now being investigated for suspected offenses under the VAT Law and the Customs Ordinance, as well as suspected money laundering and criminal conspiracy.
On Thursday, courts granted a police request to extend the detention of two of the suspects until August 25. The court released the third suspect under restrictive conditions.
According to police, the investigation is ongoing, and more arrests related to the case are expected.

Ferguson job losses were entirely avoidable warns Sweeney
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
08:55:30 BST
16:55:30 KST

The decision to place the first phase of the Small Vessel Replacement Programme with a Polish yard rather than Ferguson Marine directly caused the job losses now being announced at Port Glasgow, Paul Sweeney MSP has told the UK Defence Journal.
Ferguson Marine confirmed on Tuesday that it had opened a voluntary redundancy programme expected to see up to 70 employees leave, around a quarter of the workforce, as work on the ferry Glen Rosa winds down.
Mr Sweeney, a former shipyard worker and Labour MSP for Glasgow, said: “This is yet another example of the completely incoherent industrial policy of the Scottish Government over many years. We’ve had over half a billion pounds worth of shipbuilding contracts awarded to overseas shipyards in the last four years, and not a single contract awarded to Ferguson Marine, despite the shipyard being under the ownership of the Scottish Government.”
He said one government agency had excluded another government-owned asset from bidding for work. “Caledonian Maritime Assets Ltd froze out another government-owned asset, Ferguson Marine, from even tendering for the Lord of the Isles ferry replacement recently, and instead shortlisted only overseas shipyards and essentially drafted the tendering qualification requirements to exclude any British shipyard.
“This is completely perverse, and it shows that we are seeing a government risk averse and run by essentially lawyers rather than by people with an understanding of industrial and engineering policy and what will produce good economic outcomes, prosperous jobs, and a thriving competitive industrial base in our shipbuilding sector.”
‘A criminally negligent opportunity missed’
Mr Sweeney was most critical of the phase one award, which went to Remontowa in Gdansk.
He said: “They could have awarded directly to Ferguson Marine the phase one of the Small Vessel Replacement Programme. Instead, they gave it to Remontowa in Gdansk in Poland. That decision alone has directly caused these job losses at Ferguson Marine.
“They could have, and as has been demonstrated by their subsequent stated intention to directly award phase two of the Small Vessel Replacement Programme to Ferguson Marine, shown that all along they could have directly awarded that phase one contract for those relatively straightforward, repeatable series build ferries to Ferguson Marine.
“That would have given them a robust drumbeat of orders and a stable production cycle through the whole shipyard, going right through from steel production and fabrication to outfitting trades, and then the sea trials and so on. So you have every part of the shipyard flowing well, and you’ve got that flowline production model going.”
He said the opportunity to put the yard into what he called ferry factory mode had been squandered. “It’s astonishing, the incompetence around not doing that and not using that opportunity with the Small Vessel Replacement Programme to get Ferguson Marine into basically a ferry factory mode. That could have been the game changer there. And it’s a criminally negligent opportunity missed.”
Why the work has run out
Sweeney set out the immediate cause of the crunch at the yard, pointing to the end of subcontract work alongside the completion of the ferry. He said: “The Scottish Government have been in no rush to verify their ability to award that second phase contract to Ferguson Marine. They’ve been dragging their heels on that now for months, and we’ve now seen the consequences of that. The lack of mobilisation at the yard as Glen Rosa leaves, there’s simply no work coming through. The BAE Systems subcontract for Type 26 has come to a conclusion, so that is why we’re seeing this crunch for the shipyard, and it’s completely avoidable.”
On the loss of skills, he said: “It’s devastating to see that institutional memory being eroded, that critical mass of skills being undermined, because they’re very hard to re-establish once you lose them. It is simply going to make it more expensive, more difficult for that shipyard to be competitive in the medium to long term if you lose that capacity. You can’t just flick it on and off like a light switch.”
The subsidy control argument
Sweeney also said he had put forward a legal route for direct awards and been rebuffed.
He said: “I have repeatedly tried to offer constructive suggestions to the Scottish Government over several years now about how they can get this to work properly. Most recently, I spelled out quite clearly the opportunities in the Subsidy Control Act to directly award using national security provisions, and they simply responded with a load of legalistic guff.
“It has subsequently been made clear by the Treasury and by the Cabinet Office that national security powers can be used to directly award contracts in the shipbuilding sector, and are actively encouraging government agencies to do this. So why the Scottish Government isn’t using this massive opportunity with the verification provided by the UK Government to directly award is beyond me.
They need to get a grip and get a grip quickly, because lives, livelihoods, and people’s wellbeing are at stake here, as well as the future existence of a shipbuilding industry in Scotland. It’s not unexpected news, but it’s certainly something I thought we could have avoided. And the government ministers seem to be completely asleep at the wheel, as this thing unravels on their watch.”
He also pointed to the wider pipeline, noting that the National Shipbuilding Strategy identified a cross-government pipeline of orders over the next 30 years, and that Scotland is seeing what he described as massive leakage of that pipeline overseas.
Defending the yard’s record
Sweeney has also pushed back on the suggestion that Ferguson Marine’s own track record has made it an unattractive prospect for commercial customers, “It successfully completed a major frigate fabrication contract for BAE Systems recently. Many shipyards have had bad contracts in the past and successfully rebounded, but you need some fundamentals to sustain a commercial shipbuilding industry, and state financing is one of them.”
He argued that heavy industry of this kind cannot operate without state involvement anywhere. “Shipbuilding is similar to aerospace, in that the barriers to entry are so high that the state inevitably becomes involved in some way. Even Europe’s most successful shipbuilding firm, Meyer Werft in Lower Saxony, was jointly nationalised by the state and federal governments in 2024, but it then secured a 10 billion Euro contract with MSC Cruises last year. The problem is that the Scottish Government just tinkered with state intervention rather than taking the comprehensive measures necessary to be effective and competitive internationally.”
‘The yard has a record’
Asked publicly on social media whether the yard’s record would deter commercial customers, Mr Sweeney rejected the idea that its history rules it out of future work.
He said: “It successfully completed a major frigate fabrication contract for BAE Systems recently. Many shipyards have had bad contracts in the past and successfully rebounded, but you need some fundamentals to sustain a commercial shipbuilding industry, and state financing is one of them.”
On why the state has a role at all, he said: “Shipbuilding is similar to aerospace, in that the barriers to entry are so high that the state inevitably becomes involved in some way. Even Europe’s most successful shipbuilding firm, Meyer Werft in Lower Saxony, was jointly nationalised by the state and federal governments in 2024, but it then secured a 10 billion euro contract with MSC Cruises last year.”
He said the failure was not intervention as such but the extent of it. “The problem is that the Scottish Government just tinkered with state intervention rather than taking the comprehensive measures necessary to be effective and competitive internationally.”
He has also said the yard cannot win commercial work because Scotland does not provide shipbuilding project finance through its state investment bank, something he says every other shipbuilding nation does, leaving Ferguson Marine dependent on government contracts that have gone abroad.
The government and the yard respond
Stephen Flynn, the Economy Secretary, said the redundancies would put the yard on a more competitive footing and were necessary to help secure a viable future, adding that he was assured they would not affect Glen Rosa and that the intention to directly award four vessels is going through due diligence.
Graeme Thomson, chief executive of Ferguson Marine, said: “Shipbuilding capability relies on continuity and while changes of this nature are difficult, taking proactive action now ensures we protect the long-term viability of the yard and remain lean, modern, and ready to cut steel on the new fleet as quickly as possible.”
The Scottish Government said in March 2026 that it intended to make a strategic direct award to Ferguson Marine covering two ferries for Caledonian Maritime Assets under the Small Vessel Replacement Programme, along with a marine protection vessel and a marine research vessel.

Russia Conducted Missile Drills Near Kuril Islands Following Putin’s Visit and Protests by Japan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
07:53:28 UTC
16:53:28 KST

Russia conducted high-profile missile exercises near the Southern Kuril Islands after Japan lodged a protest over Vladimir Putin’s visit to the occupied island of Iturup.
The Ministry of Defence of the Russian Federation announced the exercises.
During the exercises, the Russian Pacific Fleet deployed a strike group consisting of the missile cruiser Varyag, the nuclear submarine Omsk, and the Bastion coastal missile system.
As part of the exercises, the cruiser Varyag fired two Vulcan anti-ship missiles, and the submarine Omsk launched a Granit cruise missile.
In addition, the crew of the Bastion coastal missile system, deployed on one of the islands, fired an Onyx anti-ship missile.
Russia has been strengthening its military presence in the Kuril Islands for quite some time.
As early as November 2016, the Pacific Fleet’s newspaper Boevaya Vakhta reported on the deployment of the Bal and Bastion coastal anti-ship missile systems on the islands of Iturup and Kunashir.
And in 2021, Russia deployed the Bastion coastal anti-ship missile system on Matua Island.
In late 2017, the Russian military also completed the restoration of an airfield on the island and announced plans to establish a base there for Russian Navy ships.
The Southern Kuril Islands are under Russian control, but Japan considers them its Northern Territories. Tokyo has consistently opposed the strengthening of Russia’s military presence on these islands.
The Japanese prime minister then called the Russian president’s visit ‘absolutely unacceptable.’
The missile drills took place against the backdrop of a new escalation in relations between Moscow and Tokyo. Russian President Vladimir Putin recently visited Iturup Island, prompting protests from Japan.
The territorial dispute over the Kuril Islands has been ongoing for more than 80 years, ever since the Soviet Union established control over the four islands. Japan claims them and demands their return, while Russia considers the islands its territory. Due to this unresolved issue, Moscow and Tokyo have yet to sign a full-fledged peace treaty following the war.

Russian attacks on Ukraine kill 2 people a day after deadly shopping mall drone strike
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
07:53:02 UTC
16:53:02 KST

Russian and Ukrainian attacks kill 10 people, a day after deadly shopping mall drone strike
KYIV, Ukraine (AP) — Russian drone and missile strikes killed at least seven people in Ukraine, officials said Saturday, while a Ukrainian drone attack on Russia’s Krasnodar region killed three people there.
The attacks came a day after a Russian strike on a Ukrainian shopping center killed at least 16 people and wounded some 130.
Moscow’s forces have recently intensified their ballistic missile attacks on Kyiv, exploiting Ukraine’s chronic shortage of U.S.-made Patriot air defense interceptors, the sole weapon in its arsenal able to shoot down the missiles.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that one person was killed and another wounded in the latest attacks when ballistic missiles hit railway infrastructure in the capital, Kyiv, overnight.
Russia’s Defense Ministry said that its forces had hit a locomotive depot.
In a separate attack, local authorities said two people were killed Saturday afternoon in a Russian ballistic missile strike on the Kyiv region, which surrounds the capital.
Russian drone strikes also killed one person overnight in the Zaporizhzhia region, local officials said Saturday, and a daytime attack killed three others and wounded 15. Zelenskyy said that three people were also wounded in an attack on a minibus in the regional capital, also called Zaporizhzhia.
In Russia’s southern Krasnodar region, authorities said that three people, including two children, were killed and two adults were wounded in a Ukrainian drone strike.
A day on from a deadly attack on a shopping center
The latest attacks came a day after Russian drones struck a shopping center in the city of Kryvyi Rih in central Ukraine.
Dnipropetrovsk regional head Oleksandr Hanzha said in the early hours of Saturday that the death toll had risen to 16. Later on Saturday he said four people remain missing after the attack, which wounded a further 130.
Kryvyi Rih is the hometown of Zelenskyy, who described the attack as a double-tap strike, in which an initial wave of drones hit the area followed by a second wave as rescue workers responded. The Ukrainian leader said the fire, which spread across 9,000 square meters (around 97,000 square feet), had been extinguished and rescue efforts were underway.
Kryvyi Rih has been hit multiple times during the 4½-year all-out war between Russia and Ukraine, with one of the deadliest occurring in April 2025, when 20 people were killed, including nine children.
Large-scale Russian strikes have become a regular occurrence this summer, with Friday’s attacks landing just 24 hours after Russia pounded Kyiv with scores of missiles and drones in a nighttime assault that killed 16 people. The United Nations said last week that Kyiv was one of the hardest-hit cities in July, with at least 54 civilians killed and 202 wounded.
Ukraine pounds Russia with long-range strikes
At the same time, Ukraine has shifted the war onto Russian soil through long-range drone strikes on oil facilities that have caused fuel shortages across Russia. It also has unsettled the Russian public by striking warehouses of Wildberries, the country’s biggest online retailer.
The Russian online news outlet Astra reported Saturday that a Ukrainian drone set ablaze an oil refinery in the Samara region. Local officials said that damage was recorded at an unidentified “industrial facility” and a logistics center for Ozon, a competitor to Wildberries.
Zelenskyy said Saturday Ukrainian forces struck the Novokuibyshevsk oil refinery in Samara, noting it is some 620 miles (1,000 kilometers) from the front line.
Russian President Vladimir Putin said in remarks to state TV reporter Pavel Zarubin, who posted them Saturday on his Telegram channel, that strikes on civilian targets “cause economic damage to our country” and “lead to losses,” but that “no turning point” in the conflict had been reached and that Kyiv “will never gain any advantage.”

Rescue workers search for people under rubble of Kryvyi Rih shopping centre – Zelenskyy
Rescue workers are continuing to clear the rubble and search for people at the site of a Russian strike on a shopping centre in Kryvyi Rih. So far 16 people are known to have been killed and 130 injured.
Source: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy
Details: Zelenskyy reported that the fire, which covered an area of 9,000 sq m, has been extinguished. Emergency rescue teams from seven oblasts and specialist dog handlers have been deployed to the site.
Of the 130 people injured, 23 are children.
Zelenskyy also said Russia's missile and drone strikes started in the evening and went on throughout the night across Ukraine.
In Kyiv, ballistic missile strikes damaged railway infrastructure, killing one person and injuring another.
In Zaporizhzhia, a Russian FPV drone attacked a fixed-route minibus, injuring three people.
Odesa, Dnipropetrovsk, Kharkiv, Donetsk, Sumy, Kherson, Chernihiv and Mykolaiv oblasts also came under attack.
Background: On 21 August, Russian forces mounted two drone attacks on a shopping centre in Kryvyi Rih.
