Putin issued another batch of statements about Russia&apos;s war against Ukraine - Center for Strategic Communications responded
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
18:40:22 EEST
00:40:22 KST

Putin issued another batch of statements about Russia's war against Ukraine - Center for Strategic Communications responded
Kyiv • UNN
Putin issued another round of threats while claiming that he was allegedly ready for dialogue. The Center for Strategic Communications responded.
Kremlin chief Vladimir Putin issued a new batch of statements, including about Russia’s war against Ukraine. The government’s Center for Strategic Communications responded, UNN reports.
Details
In an interview with one of the Russian media outlets, Putin stated, in particular, that "we are always ready for dialogue, but only on the basis of the realities taking shape on the ground." Putin spoke of Ukraine’s proposals for peace as "exotic" and "unacceptable" to Moscow, but refused to clarify what he meant. Putin also commented on Ukrainian strikes against Russian infrastructure facilities, threatening that "you will get a response."
The Center for Strategic Communications’ response
"On August 22, the Kremlin dictator repeated familiar narratives about Ukraine’s "failure," Russia’s "response," and Kyiv’s alleged unwillingness to negotiate," the Center for Strategic Communications pointed out.
"Putin produced a new batch of fantasies: five claims that do not correspond to reality," the Center for Strategic Communications emphasized, dissecting the five main manipulations:
-  Fake No. 1: «Ukrainian strikes against Russia did not lead to any turning point.» 
"In fact, Ukrainian long-range strikes forced Russia to redeploy air defense systems, restore damaged logistics facilities, and acknowledge the damage to its own infrastructure. Just days ago, Putin himself admitted that Ukrainian attacks were causing damage to Russia, although he attempted to downplay their effect," the Center for Strategic Communications noted.
-  Fake No. 2: «Kyiv has not gained and will never gain any advantage.» 
"In fact, the aim of Ukrainian strikes is to weaken Russia’s military potential, logistics, and defense industry. The Ukrainian campaign has already forced Moscow to change its system for protecting strategic facilities and spend additional resources eliminating the consequences of the attacks," the Center for Strategic Communications pointed out.
-  Fake No. 3: «Ukraine provoked the situation itself and is now asking Russia for a way out of it.» 
"In fact, it was Russia that launched the full-scale war against Ukraine in 2022. Attempts to shift responsibility onto Kyiv are one of the basic narratives of Kremlin propaganda, intended to justify the aggression," the Center for Strategic Communications emphasized.
-  Fake No. 4: «The massive strikes against Ukraine are a response to Zelenskyy’s "40-day campaign."» 
"In fact, Russia has systematically attacked Ukrainian cities, energy infrastructure, and civilian infrastructure throughout the full-scale war. The latest massive strikes against Kyiv alone resulted in numerous civilian casualties and the destruction of residential buildings and social infrastructure facilities," the Center for Strategic Communications pointed out.
-  Fake No. 5: «Kyiv opened the "Pandora’s box" itself, and therefore is receiving strikes against its economy.» 
"In fact, the Kremlin is trying to present deliberate terror against civilian infrastructure as supposedly a "legitimate response." This is informational cover for attacks that Russia has been carrying out for more than four years, despite numerous violations of international humanitarian law," the Center for Strategic Communications noted.

Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22

Russian "Banderole" crashed in Belarus - media
Kyiv • UNN
The "Banderole" reportedly crashed near Kopatkevichi in the Gomel region, likely due to a lack of fuel. Ukrainian channels reported 12 drones.
One of the "Banderol" missile drones fell near the settlement of Kopatkevichi in the Petrikovsky District of Belarus’s Gomel Region, reports the Belarusian service of "Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty," UNN writes.
Details
As stated, Ukrainian sources claim that it ran out of fuel and fell into a field. The Belarusian authorities, as noted, have not commented on this information.
Several Ukrainian monitoring channels that track the movements of drones and missiles from Russia during Russian attacks reported that, on the morning of August 22, at least 12 Russian "Banderol" drones entered the territory of Belarus. According to Ukrainian channels, a military aircraft was scrambled from the airfield in Baranovichi. At the same time, there is no information on how the Russian drones were neutralized—whether they were shot down or hit by electronic warfare systems.

Texas seeks federal probe of airport washing facilities, Muslim group denounces move
- Texas Governor Greg Abbott requested a federal investigation into ritual washing facilities at Dallas-Fort Worth and George Bush airports, alleging discrimination.
- The Council on American-Islamic Relations (CAIR) called the move an "anti-Muslim political stunt" and defended the facilities as inclusive accommodations.
- Following Abbott's referral, Dallas-Fort Worth airport halted plans to add ablution stations, amid broader concerns about rising Islamophobia in the US.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – Texas Governor Greg Abbott on Aug 21 sought a federal probe into airport facilities for ritual washing before Islamic prayers, a move that a Muslim advocacy group called an “anti-Muslim political stunt”.
In a letter to the Department of Justice, Abbott called on the department to immediately review the ablution facilities at Dallas-Fort Worth International Airport and George Bush Intercontinental Airport, casting them as discriminatory.
“Because the airports receive federal funds, they are subject to numerous conditions attached to that funding – including the requirement to comply with all applicable laws prohibiting discrimination,” Abbott’s office said in a statement.
Many Muslims wash their faces, arms and legs before daily prayers.
“These are not ‘Muslim-only’ spaces any more than a nursing room or an interfaith prayer room is ‘Christian-only’ or ‘mothers-only’,” said the Texas chapter of the Council on American-Islamic Relations (CAIR), an advocacy group.
“They are accommodations, open to any traveller, that happen to be used mostly by the Muslim community. That is not discrimination.
“That is what accessible public infrastructure looks like,” CAIR-Texas said in a statement.
Last week, Abbott referred the airports to US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy for investigation and threatened to revoke state funding.
Following that referral, he said, Dallas-Fort Worth International Airport abandoned its plans to install more ablution facilities. The airport said this week that officials had “determined the originally anticipated benefit may not be achieved” if the stations were built.
There are about 4.5 million Muslims in the US, including more than 300,000 in Texas, the World Population Review says.
US rights advocates say Islamophobia has risen since the Sept 11, 2001 attacks on New York and the Pentagon, and more recently because of anti-immigration policies, white supremacy and the fallout of Israel’s war in Gaza.
Rights advocates have also documented a spike in anti-Muslim messaging and rhetoric in US political campaigns as Muslim American politicians have risen to prominent offices and roles.
Republican governors in Florida and Texas have cast CAIR, which has opposed Republican President Donald Trump’s crackdown on immigration and pro-Palestinian protests, as a terrorist group.
CAIR and other civil rights groups have denounced the allegations and also said Republicans have attempted to stoke fear against Muslims. REUTERS

European wildfires reveal a hidden danger: buried bombs and mines from WWI and WWII
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
06:23:02 UTC
15:23:02 KST

Wildfires expose — and detonate — buried bombs and mines from WWI and WWII
ELSENBORN, Belgium (AP) — The wildfires burning across Europe this summer have exposed a potentially deadly threat lurking beneath the blackened landscape: rusty bombs and mines from World War I and II that threaten crews responding to the flames.
Some of the weapons have exploded in the intense heat. Blasts have been reported in France, Belgium, Germany and the Netherlands, where a bomb-disposal team was dispatched to check a forest threatened by flames near a site of fierce fighting in the Limburg province in 1944.
Fueled by climate change, the fires and explosions show that the continent’s “climatic luck” is running out, said Sarah Njeri, a peace and conflict scholar at London’s School of Oriental and African Studies. Steady temperatures and predictable rainfall once ensured that most buried weapons stayed dormant.
“Climate change is now doing the work of unburying and reactivating what was previously stable,” Njeri said. Fires can ignite old munitions but can also burn away the scrub and brush that hides them.
This wildfire season was supercharged by heavy rains in January that spurred vegetation growth, which became kindling when the summer heat arrived. Those temperatures, combined with drought conditions, low humidity and stiff winds, offered an ideal environment for fire, according to a study issued last month by the World Weather Attribution group.
Flames chewed up old battlefields and set off buried explosives
As they advanced, the flames moved over territory that has long been known to hold unexploded weapons, a lethal legacy that lingered long after the guns fell silent.
In a forest in tinder-dry France, a massive wildfire outside the southwestern city of Bordeaux uncovered a cache of what is believed to be World War II-era ammunition.
In the eastern Belgian province of Liege, Gov. Hervé Jamar said “a few sporadic detonations” were recently heard and that emergency services were adapting to account for munitions buried in a fire area. He said no fire crews were in danger, but local media published photos of a firefighter handling a rusted bomb.
During World War II, booby traps, bombs and mines were sprinkled throughout the province’s dense peat-bog forest known as the High Fens. In the first four years after Germany’s surrender in 1945, the munitions killed six civilians, said Bernard Collard, a local historian who runs the Truschbaum Museum near Belgium’s border with Germany that houses a collection of found objects from the war.
“When you go into a forest like this, you are not sure where the explosives are,” he said. He remembers his father detonating a found bomb in a quarry.
The fire in the High Fens, which stretches across the border with Germany, is smoldering atop a much-bloodied battlefield where Nazis fought Allied troops. The Battle of the Bulge was fought in and around the High Fens.
The fire is even closer to the sites of two lesser-known skirmishes along Elsenborn Ridge and in the Hurtgen Forest, which lasted 88 days and killed about 33,000 American and 28,000 German troops.
Every year, Belgium responds to thousands of calls about explosives
Collard is authorized to scan with a metal detector the former battlefields, now forests, pastures and farmland. He has found mortar shells, machine guns, helmets, cigarette cases, and once, a human skeleton.
“You never know what you might come across, and you shouldn’t take it lightly,” Collard said while standing in a field that was once a blood-soaked site. Nearby, blueberry bushes cover old foxholes, trenches and deep craters from artillery fire.
He frequently works with the Belgian demining squad. “It’s part of our history. We live with it,” Collard said.
Unexploded ordnance is even more dangerous around wildfires because heat can trigger the explosives, said Jonas Tepe, a spokesperson for North Rhine-Westphalia, just across the border in Germany.
The Belgian Ministry of Defense said it receives requests from the region about every week to assist in disarming explosives, yet it does not consider the area a “hot spot” compared to elsewhere in Belgium. Such requests are even more common in the west, where farmers in towns such as Ypres — infamous for harrowing trench warfare in World War I — call the annual tilling of the soil “ the iron harvest ” because it turns up so many war remnants.
Every year across the nation, Belgium’s Explosive Ordnance Disposal and Destruction Service responds to more than 3,000 calls and disposes of 200 to 250 tons of munitions left over from both world wars.
Flames are not the only threat
Drought has also helped to lay the past bare by shrinking rivers and lakes to reveal old weapons.
In Slovakia, the Danube River fell and exposed two naval mines that police pulled out of the water and buried in a trench for a controlled demolition. Authorities in Hungary closed Budapest’s Margaret Bridge after a bomb dating from World War II emerged at its base in receding water.
As the Rhine dried up, German authorities also found a WWII-era bomb.
Christina Greene, a researcher at the University of Arizona who, with Njeri, wrote an article on Europe’s wildfires and unexploded ordnance risk, said “the legacy of war keeps creeping up” because of climate change.
“It’s reliving the legacies of war and conflict in a way that we haven’t had to deal with in a while in certain places.”
___ Associated Press writers Mike Corder in The Hague, Netherlands; Sylvain Plazy in Brussels; Angela Charlton in Paris; Kirsten Grieshaber in Berlin; and Stanislav Hodina in Prague contributed to this report.

MINSK, 22 August (BelTA) – Suggestions have been made to introduce a ban on online ads of gambling establishments in Belarus. The relevant bill has been drafted by the Antimonopoly Regulation and Trade Ministry, the ministry’s press service told BelTA.

Trump calls Hormuz ‘American territory’ as ships go dark
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
06:15:28 UTC
15:15:28 KST

U.S. President Donald Trump has described the Strait of Hormuz as “American territory,” although ship-tracking data show that most vessels whose routes could be identified were using the corridor designated by Iran rather than the route backed by Washington.
Speaking at a campaign rally in Myrtle Beach, South Carolina, on Aug. 21, Trump said: “I view the Strait of Hormuz as an American territory right now. It’s an American territory.”
Trump previously said the United States had “total control” of the waterway and shared a map on social media labeling it “new U.S. territory.”
The strait runs between Iran and Oman and normally carries about one-fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas shipments.
Data from maritime intelligence company Kpler recorded 236 vessels entering or leaving the Gulf between Aug. 1 and 19.
Of the 88 ships whose routes could be identified, 83 used Iran’s northern corridor, three took the Omani route backed by Washington and two followed the prewar central route.
The remaining 148 vessels were classified as dark or unidentifiable, meaning their routes could not be reliably established.
Among 112 oil and gas carriers, 21 used the Iranian corridor and two took the Omani route, while 89 were dark or unclassified.
The figures do not establish where most vessels sailed. They show, however, that the Iranian corridor accounted for nearly all traffic whose route could be identified.
Before the conflict, ships generally used established traffic-separation lanes through the central part of the strait.
Iran now directs authorized vessels along a northern corridor near Larak and Qeshm islands, while Oman has promoted a route closer to its coast with U.S. support.
Some operators have limited or switched off their Automatic Identification System signals, making commercial tracking more difficult as Washington and Tehran seek to enforce competing rules in the waterway.
Iran says it will not fully reopen the strait unless the United States lifts its naval blockade and oil sanctions, releases frozen Iranian assets and ends military operations.
Washington is preparing further economic pressure.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Aug. 20 that the United States would impose its toughest sanctions yet, targeting Iran’s oil sales, financial transfers and ship-to-ship trade.
Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei rejected the planned secondary sanctions as an attempt to impose U.S. rules beyond its jurisdiction.
Bessent is expected to provide details of the measures on Monday.

GTA VI publisher files subpoenas in bid to unmask leaks surrounding eagerly anticipated video game
- Take-Two Interactive obtained court orders to subpoena Microsoft and Discord to identify the source of recent Grand Theft Auto VI leaks.
- The leaks, attributed to an account named Cyberleek, expose copyrighted game content and disrupt the game's extensive marketing campaign.
- The subpoenas seek data on three suspect accounts and forum members, with Microsoft and Discord required to respond by Sept 4.
AI generated
SAN FRANCISCO – The publisher of Grand Theft Auto VI obtained court orders on Aug 21 requiring Microsoft and Discord to turn over data in an effort to identify the source of recent leaks surrounding the eagerly anticipated video game.
Two federal judges in New York approved the subpoena requests, which had been filed a day earlier, according to court documents reviewed by AFP.
In order to obtain the injunctions, Take-Two Interactive, the American parent company of GTA VI developer Rockstar Games, had to assert that the videos posted online reproduce material for which it holds the copyright – a claim it has never publicly confirmed.
According to the court documents, “the copyrighted material includes but is not limited to audiovisual content, artwork, images, dialogue, or other creative elements”.
The leaks are attributed to an account with the pseudonym Cyberleek, whose author or authors claim to be acting to expose the industry’s business practices.
Take-Two subsidiary Rockstar Games has been criticised for pre-selling a GTA VI version with additional content at higher prices, and for offering the game only in a digital format.
Neither Rockstar nor Take-Two have commented on the leaks, which continued on Aug 21 with a new clip showing a game character stealing a sports car.
The leaks are seen as undermining the group’s extensive marketing campaign, which began nearly three years ago with an initial trailer.
Following the global buzz generated by the start of pre-orders in late June, the promotion ramps up with an exclusive presentation on Netflix on Aug 27, more than two months ahead of the worldwide GTA release on Nov 19.
The sixth installment of the flagship series, which takes place in a region inspired by the US state of Florida, has had players around the globe waiting for more than 13 years since the release of GTA V, which is the second-best-selling game in history.
The subpoenas seek data held by Microsoft, owner of the GitHub developer platform where the leaks were allegedly posted, and by Discord, a communication platform widely used by gamers where the “infringing content” was shared in several chatrooms.
Take-Two is requesting data that would identify three accounts suspected of being the source of the leaks, as well as information on all members of the forums where the leaks circulated.
The two companies must respond by Sept 4. AFP

In a communication to technical institutions and admission authorities, AICTE said the graduates could be considered only for “relevant and closely aligned” disciplines (Representative image)
NEW DELHI: Four-year BSc (honours or honours with research) graduates may now seek admission to select ME and MTech programmes, with AICTE opening a new bridge from undergraduate science to postgraduate engineering. The move has, however, prompted calls for GATE-based admissions and limits on institutions allowed to use the route to prevent dilution of MTech standards and protect enrolment in MSc courses.In a communication to technical institutions and admission authorities, AICTE said the graduates could be considered only for “relevant and closely aligned” disciplines or specialisations in which MSc degree-holders are already eligible. It is, therefore, not a blanket opening for every BSc graduate or every MTech programme. Three-year BSc degree-holders are not covered.The decision follows the UGC’s Minimum Standards of Instruction Regulations, 2025, notified on March 26 last year, which sought to enable greater academic mobility under NEP 2020. The regulations recognise a four-year undergraduate honours or honours-with-research degree carrying 160 credits and allow graduates in relevant subjects, including physics, biology and mathematics, to enter two-year ME or MTech programmes.
Until now, BE and BTech degrees have been the principal route to postgraduate engineering. MSc graduates are also admitted to select programmes in areas such as computer science, biotechnology, mathematics and applied sciences. AICTE’s decision extends that limited pathway to four-year BSc graduates without requiring them to first complete an MSc.S Vaidhyasubramaniam, vice-chancellor of SASTRA University, Thanjavur, called for tighter guardrails. “To balance PG degree enrolment in technology and science, this new policy should be implemented only in top 100 NIRF universities or top 50 engineering institutions, and admissions shall be through GATE scores only,” he said.The director of a govt engineering college, who did not wish to be named, said: “Everything is now happening under the NEP 2020 canvas and not all are correct. AICTE should also ensure that this new policy is not misused by private universities for whom AICTE approval is not necessary.”Under the framework, institutions may set minimum marks or CGPA, demand GATE or another entrance-test score, assess domain knowledge and prescribe prerequisite or bridge courses. Candidates must possess the subjects or credits required for the MTech specialisation concerned.
AICTE said that academic standards must not be diluted and said the new provision would “supplement and shall not replace” the existing BE/BTech pathway. Admissions must remain within the approved intake and comply with reservation policies and other statutory requirements.The council will separately publish a discipline-wise mapping linking eligible four-year BSc courses to corresponding ME and MTech programmes. The mapping will determine the actual scale and reach of the change. It has asked institutions, universities and state and UT admission authorities to incorporate the provision in admission notifications and prospectuses.

CANBERRA, Aug. 22 (Xinhua) -- Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said on Saturday that the Australian Capital Territory (ACT) will join a gun buyback scheme in response to December's fatal mass shooting at Bondi Beach.
Albanese said in a statement that the ACT has agreed to introduce a gun buyback scheme as part of a push to strengthen Australia's firearm laws.
The federal government introduced laws for the gun buyback in January after 15 people were killed at a Jewish festival at the iconic Sydney beach on Dec. 14, 2025, in Australia's deadliest mass shooting since 1996.
The ACT government initially committed to join the scheme, but had remained in negotiations with the federal government over how it would be funded.
Under the final agreement, the federal government will fund 75 percent of buyback and administrative costs and 100 percent of firearm destruction costs.
"National gun reform is an important part of making sure an antisemitic terrorist attack like we saw at Bondi can't happen again," Albanese said.
"I thank the ACT government for their collaboration as we work to take guns off our streets in order to better protect Australians."
It makes the ACT the second of Australia's eight states and territories to join the buyback after the east coast state of New South Wales (NSW) did so earlier in August.
Albanese said that there are currently around 23,000 firearms in the ACT and more than 7,000 people with firearms licenses.
The NSW government said it will pay up to 1,000 Australian dollars (717 U.S. dollars) for guns that are handed in during the first phase of its buyback, which begins on Nov. 2, and up to 10,000 Australian dollars (7,170 U.S. dollars) for higher-value firearms handed in during phase two from early 2027. ■

Squid take over North Sea: what's behind the squid boom
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
06:05:19 UTC
15:05:19 KST

In the North Sea, cephalopods are appearing in growing numbers. Fishermen are landing more squid and octopus, a trend likely tied to rising sea temperatures.
When people think of the North Sea, they think of prawns, plaice or cod. But that picture is changing: cephalopods are increasingly spreading there. Researchers have observed that several species are now permanently present in the North Sea which used to appear there only as occasional visitors.
The North Sea is becoming a habitat for cephalopods
Rising water temperatures play a key role. Cephalopods have comparatively short life cycles and can therefore adapt quickly to changing environmental conditions. According to the Thünen Institute, various species have expanded their range over the past decades. The Thünen Institute is a German federal research institute that conducts research, among other things, on agriculture, forests, fisheries and the seas and provides scientific advice to the federal government.
According to the institute, some squid are now reproducing in the North Sea and forming their own stocks there.
Species such as the short-finned squid Illex coindetii were still rare vagrants around 100 years ago. Today they live permanently in the North Sea and reproduce there.
This fits in with a fundamental change in these waters: 2025 was the warmest year since BSH measurements began at the Federal Maritime and Hydrographic Agency in 1969. The average surface temperature was 11.6 degrees, around 0.9 degrees above the long-term average.
The summer of 2025 was also exceptionally warm: with an average of 15.7 degrees, it was the warmest North Sea summer since records began. In parts of the western and south-western North Sea, temperatures were at times more than two degrees above the long-term average. Official data for this summer are not yet fully available, but the high temperature readings are expected to continue.
More cephalopods, fewer classic North Sea species?
The changes are not limited to cephalopods. As the water warms, cold-loving species such as cod come under pressure and shift their distribution areas. At the same time, squid are changing the food web: these voracious predators prey on fish such as herring, sprat, whiting and also cod.
Researchers are therefore investigating the extent to which growing squid stocks are affecting commercially important fish species.
It is not only squid that are benefiting from the warmer North Sea: octopus are also being sighted and caught more frequently. Recent reports from 2026 speak of significantly more octopus in the southern North Sea, especially off Belgium. Fishermen there report sometimes large catches.
In the German Wadden Sea, a live curled octopus (Eledone cirrhosa) was still a rarity in 2017.
Today the curled octopus is still rare in the German Wadden Sea, but no longer completely unknown: BeachExplorer, a scientifically curated online database in which finds of animals, plants and other organisms on the coasts of the North Sea and Baltic Sea are documented, describes the species as "widespread in the North Sea", with individual records on the Wadden Sea coast.
The most important difference is that squid have ten arms and octopus eight. Squid also have an elongated body with fins and an internal gladius, while octopus have a rounded body without fins and without a gladius.
A gladius is a hard, calcareous or horn-like supporting structure inside a cephalopod's body. It gives the animal stability and helps it maintain its body shape.
Fishermen discover a new line of business
Squid fishing has now become one of the more important cephalopod fisheries in the North-East Atlantic. As traditional fish stocks change and fishing opportunities for other species have been restricted, fishermen are looking for new sources of income.
According to the Thünen Institute, squid landings in the North Sea have roughly tripled in the space of about 40 years. Up to 3,000 tonnes are now landed every year.
There are currently no specific catch quotas for North Sea squid, and the scientific basis for such regulation is still being developed.
At the same time, there is a problem: fishing for cephalopods has so far not been regulated in the same way as for many traditional commercial fish species. Researchers are therefore working on options for sustainable management.
Possible measures could include catch limits that are regularly adjusted to stock trends, supplemented by closed seasons or protected areas for key spawning grounds. This would require better data on stocks and on the impact of fishing on the ecosystem.
Even the spawning grounds are not yet sufficiently known. On one research cruise, for example, egg masses of squid were found. Exactly where the animals regularly spawn in the North Sea and which areas are particularly important for their reproduction has not yet been fully clarified.
No classic "invasion"
Describing the development as an "invasion" would not be entirely accurate. Cephalopods are indeed increasing significantly in the North Sea, but the trend is part of a broader ecological shift.
Cephalopods are therefore, in a sense, among the winners of the warming North Sea. What still seems unusual today could in future become a normal sight in Germany's coastal waters.

TikTok has agreed to pay $400 million to settle a US Justice Department lawsuit alleging the company violated federal children’s privacy laws.
The Justice Department said on Friday that TikTok will pay $300 million immediately and another $100 million after an order vacates an earlier consent decree against its predecessor, Musical.ly.
“This settlement is a major victory for American children and parents,” US Associate Attorney General Stanley E. Woodward Jr. said in a statement.
The department said the settlement would strengthen protections for children and hold companies responsible for safeguarding users’ personal information.
Lawsuit over children’s data
The 2024 lawsuit alleged that TikTok and ByteDance violated a federal law requiring apps and websites aimed at children to obtain parental consent before collecting personal information from users under 13.
It also alleged that the companies failed to honour requests from parents seeking to have their children’s accounts deleted and did not delete accounts even when they knew the users were under 13.
TikTok has undergone major changes since the lawsuit was filed, including changes to the ownership structure of its US operations.
In January, TikTok signed agreements with investors including Oracle, Silver Lake and Emirati investment firm MGX to form a new TikTok US joint venture.
TikTok representatives did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Friday.
The settlement comes as social media companies face increasing legal scrutiny over children’s safety and privacy, while a growing number of countries move to restrict young people’s access to social media platforms.
Meta Platforms, the parent company of Instagram, is also currently on trial in federal court in Oakland, California, over allegations that it violated the 1998 Children’s Online Privacy Protection Act, or COPPA, as well as various state laws.

Estonia may end automatic school payments for out-of-district students
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
06:01:00 UTC
15:01:00 KST

Estonia may end automatic school payments for out-of-district students
The Ministry of Education and Research wants to end automatic payments between local governments when children attend schools outside their home municipality.
Under the current system, if a student enrolls in public school in another municipality, the student's local government of residence must automatically help cover that school's operating costs — even if it has already offered them enrollment at its own local school.
The costs cover expenses not funded by the state's education grant, including school building maintenance, utilities and other day-to-day operations.
The ministry has submitted a bill for review that would end the automatic payment requirement, leaving it up to local governments to agree among themselves on how school operating costs are shared.
Association of Estonian Cities and Municipalities (ELVL) executive director Veikko Luhalaid said local governments have discussed the proposed change with the ministry several times.
Not everyone benefits
He said the current system can leave municipalities on unequal footing. For example, families may choose larger schools in neighboring municipalities over smaller local schools.
The municipality where a student lives, however, must still maintain its own schools, even with fewer students.
"That's a double burden," Luhalaid pointed out.
He said local governments could instead agree via contracts on student admissions and how costs are shared, avoiding automatic payment obligations altogether.
Municipalities, however, are divided on the proposal. Some benefit from the current system because schools near municipal borders tend to attract students from neighboring areas.
"Teachers' salaries are paid from the funding that comes with those students," Luhalaid explained.
For municipalities losing students to larger neighboring schools, however, many operating costs remain even as enrollment falls, leaving them with fewer students but little relief from the cost of maintaining their schools.

Battery fires at recycling centres are costing UK £1bn a year, figures show
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
06:00:57 UTC
15:00:57 KST

Fires at recycling centres caused by wrongly discarded lithium batteries such as those found in vapes are occurring at the rate of more than 10 a week, according to new figures.
Experts say the sheer volume of battery fires now occurring at waste facilities has reached a crisis that is putting lives at risk, costing £1bn a year and frustrating fire chiefs.
In figures shared with the Guardian, the Environment Services Association (ESA), the trade body for waste management companies, said its members had reported 1,518 fires in the year to March 2026. At least 541 of these fires were directly attributed to lithium ion batteries, the survey found. There were a further 216 battery fires in bin lorries.
The ESA said the reported number of battery-related fires underestimated the scale of the problem, because in most incidents it was impossible to determine the cause of the blaze. A spokesperson said: “We know 40% of fires at recycling centres are caused by batteries, but we think the actual number is more like 70%.”
It estimates that annual cost of these fires has increased from £150m in 2021 to £1bn today. The cause of this week’s blaze at a recycling centre in Deptford, south-east London, has yet to be determined. It was the latest in a series of fires at recycling centre and bin lorries, many of which have been blamed on batteries, particularly those in vapes. They include: Ilford in east London; Caerwent in Monmouthshire; Widnes in Cheshire; Glasgow; Costessey near Norwich, and Dereham in Norfolk.
Fire chiefs have been alarmed by the rise in this type of blaze and the resources needed to put them out.
After the Ilford fire, which took 25 firefighters to control, a spokesperson for London fire brigade said: “We’ve seen a growing number of fires at waste disposal sites that are believed to have been caused by a lithium battery.”
“Fires that we attend at sites like recycling centres and scrap yards can be very time consuming for our firefighters and often require a high level of resources to put the fire out. We’ve also seen the detrimental environmental and societal impact these fires can have on local communities.”
Dr Francesco Restuccia, a fire expert at King’s College London, said: “There has been exponential increase in fires at recycling centres, mainly because we are using and discarding lithium batteries in everyday objects like smartphones, children’s toys, toothbrushes and vapes. If they are not disposed off properly there’s a high chance of ignition.”
Explaining what happens when a lithium battery gets crushed, Restuccia said: “If the separator is pierced – which happens a lot at recycling centres – it creates a lot of internal short circuits in the battery, causing the temperature to increase until it reaches ignition point.”
The ESA commissioned the Health and Safety Executive to test what happens when a vape battery is punctured while next to paper and card. Video of the experiment, shared with the Guardian, showed the vape igniting like a sparkler and setting alight the paper and card. Temperatures of the vape reached more 750C in the experiment and became hot enough to ignite paper for two minutes.
The ESA hopes the experiment will demonstrate the need to safely dispose vapes to policymakers and the public. The waste management company Biffa said it has recovered 500,000 vapes at its facilities this summer alone.
The ESA is calling for a £5 deposit scheme on the sale of all vapes to ensure that vape users have an incentive to return used devices to retailers for safe disposal.
Patrick Brighty, the head of recycling policy at the ESA, said: “Battery fires are reaching epidemic proportions across Britain’s recycling and waste industry, placing workers at risk and threatening vital infrastructure upon which we all rely every day.
“It only takes a single battery hidden in household rubbish or recycling to cause a huge fire and decimate a facility. The total cost of battery fires now exceeds £1bn a year, with huge knock-on implications for insurance costs.
“Vapes are among the biggest culprits because they’re cheap, abundant and typically have a short use-life. ESA and others across our industry are calling on the government to implement a mandatory deposit scheme for vapes to incentivise users to return them safely back to the point of purchase so they can be recycled properly and away from other waste.”

Island hopping through stone-age history in Ireland, Wales and the Isle of Man
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
06:00:57 UTC
15:00:57 KST

The guide was adamant. “I’ve picked human teeth out of there and I’m not doing it again.” The small group of tourists looked suitably aghast, except the boy. He was jiggling the wellington boots on his feet and singing to himself. He looked about 14. I sensed that he was the catalyst, the one to make things happen.
“So, if anyone is planning to leave human remains in this ancient place,” went on the guide, throwing the boy a stern look, “I say, DON’T.”
We had arrived on the visitor centre bus from nearby Knowth, the first stop on our tour of Newgrange Neolithic site, 30 miles (50km) north of Dublin. I was on a circuit of the Irish Sea, a ferry and road trip to see the best ancient sites that ring this salty mere at the heart of these islands. It was here, around 5,100 years ago, that a new people arrived and, capitalising on the sea as a cultural superhighway, constructed a dazzling array of stone monuments. Some of Europe’s finest Neolithic passage tombs are here, notably at Newgrange, the only one you can enter. But as the guide was sternly pointing out, some modern folk are irresistibly drawn to leave the ashes of deceased relatives inside, especially at Newgrange.
The plush visitor centre had been informative but had not conveyed the deep atavistic intensity that drives such tributes. There was magic here. I wanted to feel it. I had a hunch this boy was in touch with it.
“As for pets,” said our guide, “I want no dog or cat ashes either.”
The boy was drumming his hands on his knees, hearing an unheard rhythm. We were about to walk up to the hallowed tumulus with its 19-metre-long passageway that leads to the central chamber, but our guide was determined to get that boy’s attention. “There,” she shouted. The boy’s head shot up. She was pointing at a set of wheelie bins in the corner. “I can promise you,” she went on, grimly, “that if I find your granny’s remains inside my Neolithic chamber, then her last resting place will be that green wheelie bin.”
There was a stunned silence among the tourists. But not the boy. He immediately ran over to the bin, opened the lid and stared inside.
“Nothing,” he reported, slamming it down. “She’s not there.”
The guide looked nonplussed, then marched away towards the hill that is a tomb. “Follow me,” she commanded. “Do not leave the path.”
Everyone obeyed, except the boy. He ran in a great arc off the path, arms flapping like shamanic wings.
We had started our huge circular journey around the Irish Sea at Pentre Ifan, a magnificent tomb from 3500BC, sited on the same Pembrokeshire ridge that provided the bluestone for Stonehenge. I was travelling with my partner, Sophie, and our dog, Stevie, who had gone through complex hoops to prove he was not carrying either rabies or tapeworm into Ireland. He liked the first ferry, from Pembroke Dock to Rosslare; it had an excellent pet lounge, but what fascinated him was the sea. He could not stop staring. His reaction made me pay more attention to him. Could dogs, I wondered, also help connect us with the deep past? After all, their wolf heritage is 30,000 years old, yet they relive it every minute of their lives. If anyone could remember the Neolithic age, it was Stevie.
He had been well cared for initially. We stayed near Wexford, in a dog-friendly hotel, Marlfield House, with superb gardens. Then we toured the ruins of the greatest Irish saint of them all, Kevin. His sixth-century seat at Glendalough, in County Wicklow, is now a busy pilgrimage site. Twelfth-century Trim Castle in County Meath was next, followed by the Hill of Tara with its ancient standing stone, the Lia Fáil. Here all the pagan kings of Ireland were crowned, so the legend goes.
At its base, visitors had laid a collection of apples, flowers and coins. That puzzled me. Were the apples significant? Or had that gang of girls carrying hurling sticks just donated their unwanted snacks? Some people, it was clear, wanted such places to mean something, not simply be dusty artefacts.
I persuaded Stevie to lie down on a nearby grassy mound. Under us was the Mound of the Hostages, a chambered tomb that was already ancient when the Great Pyramid was built. Time slipped away. Those Neolithic people are so distant and mysterious. What we know for certain is almost nothing. They had cows … and dogs. I opened one eye. Stevie had gone. He’d given up communing with the stone age and gone after the hurling sticks.
That night, we stayed in another excellent dog-friendly hotel, Bellinter House, and visited Marcie Regan’s in Trim, a vibrant, dog-loving pub. Not until Newgrange did we meet the dreaded sign, NO DOGS. I’d been forced to leave him in the car, my dæmon, my conduit to the ancient.
Our guide stopped us at the entrance to the great megalithic structure, a turf-topped hill walled with white quartz. Discovered largely intact in 1699, the entrance was guarded by the same five-tonne stone that sits there now, covered in mysterious swirling patterns. Behind was a narrow entrance and a passage that lay under 200,000 tonnes of stone and earth.
“If you get claustrophobic,” said the guide, “you can leave at any time. Do not touch the carvings.”
Out the corner of my eye, I saw the boy come running. He had done a lap of the monument, chanting to himself, his little sister close behind. The guide bowed her head and disappeared inside. The boy ran his fingertips over the carvings and followed. I went in next. My unsatisfied desire for stone age magic was about to be fulfilled.
The tunnel is slightly kinked and rises imperceptibly. You don’t see the final chamber. The mystery grows. There are patterns on some stones. A deep silence descends. I thought of Stevie back in the car. They found the bones of a dog in here, and its DNA showed traces of wolf from both Europe and Asia. Stevie’s Neolithic moment, however, would have to wait.
At the end of the corridor, we arrived in a small chamber. Above, the roof was made of massive stones. In more than 5,000 years, it has not leaked. It looks haphazard, but is perfect, a Rolex assembled by Flintstones. The most impressive thing, however, was not understood until Prof Michael O’Kelly came and stood in this chamber on 21 December 1967. Our guide was now going to recreate that event, and what has happened at dawn on every winter solstice since about 3150BC.
We were in complete darkness. The boy had pressed himself into a niche where a huge stone basin sat. Human remains, ancient ones, had been found there. And then, the guide touched a hidden switch and a golden light came creeping up the passageway towards us, finally illuminating a triple spiral of megalithic art carved into one giant stone. It was like hearing a deep harmonic chord, or the haunting cry of a night bird, something profound and enigmatic. I forgave the bus, the tickets, the gift shop – all the paraphernalia of the tourism business – and saw the genius of this recreation.
Light slowly filled the chamber. We were all dumbstruck, except the boy. He spoke out loud and bold. “Question. Are there aliens here?”
The guide shook her head impatiently. “I won’t have any talk of aliens.”
The boy nodded and turned to his little sister. “That means there are.”
Then he was gone, scurrying down the tunnel in a half crouch, humming to himself.
A huge storm came in that night, downing trees and flooding roads. We drove through it to Belfast and hunkered down in our hotel.
Next day, thankfully in calm weather, we sailed for the Isle of Man. Landing here was like travelling back in time, to around AD1950. Manx ancient monuments do not come with visitor centres and guides, they come only with a cast iron sign, “Ancient Monument”. We climbed the highest peak, Snaefell, visited several fabulous Celtic crosses and spent ages in the wonderful Manx Museum.
Then, one afternoon, we left the car and walked through fields to the island’s most important Neolithic monument, Cashtal yn Ard. It was in a tussocky field behind a kissing gate and a small sign. No ticket required, only some imagination and, if possible, a stone age scent hound. Behind were ranged the dark hills. The monument itself is a collapsed passage tomb that has left the ghostly imprint of its shape in rows of pale stones, marking the entrance, the tunnel, and finally, a low portal into what is left of the central chamber. Nevertheless, Stevie seemed to know the layout. He ran to the entrance, bounded down the tunnel, dodged through the portal and stopped dead. We lay on our backs and watched the skies. After a few minutes, I sneaked a look at the dog. He was curled up asleep at the exact centre of the vanished chamber.
Travel was provided by Discover Ferries, the industry body for 12 ferry companies. Irish Ferries sails Pembroke to Rosslare from £190 for car plus two (pets travel free). Isle of Man Steam Packet Company sails Belfast to Isle of Man from £179.50 for a car plus two (pets in cars free, pet-accessible cabins £75). Taking a dog to Ireland requires micro-chipping, rabies jab and tapeworm treatment (Stevie’s documents were checked at Rosslare).

‘We fear lessons will not be learned’: Chloe Moffat’s parents on their fight to hold Treasury to account
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
06:00:56 UTC
15:00:56 KST

When a coroner ruled this month that the Treasury “materially contributed” to Chloe Moffat’s death, her parents breathed out in bittersweet relief. For a year, David and Anne Moffat had been forced to become detectives in the worst case any parent could have to solve: why their daughter took her own life.
Chloe, 26, went to her job as a personal assistant at the Treasury on a Monday last May “happy as Larry” after a weekend she’d told her friends was a “10 out of 10”. She was planning a holiday with her sister, Alice, and arranging for friends to come for a dinner party the next weekend. She was, according to her father, living “the best life”.
That afternoon, however, she was sent to a surprise disciplinary meeting with her manager and her manager’s manager, which the coroner found left her distressed and convinced she was going to lose her job. The following morning, Chloe was dead.
Anne, 64, who is retired and used to work as the head of care at a children’s hospice, said: “When she first did it, we had to question Chloe. We had to question what might have driven Chloe to this.” She paused, and David added: “Criminality? Fraud? All sorts of things. Because why would somebody take their own life if they were the person that we expected?”
Anne interjected: “Are they on drugs? Are they in debt? Everything. And so we searched and questioned our own daughter.”
None of this was the case. After trawling through emails, talking to Chloe’s friends and colleagues and holding the Treasury to account in a gruelling, multi-day coroner’s court hearing, they found out their daughter had been mistreated by her employer.
“After our investigations, it was clear it was literally that one-to-one meeting,” Anne said. “Chloe never recovered. She walked out of that meeting absolutely destroyed and never recovered and went down a black hole.”
Speaking from their house in the French Alps, which they bought to be near Alice, who lives there and recently had a daughter, the couple seem exhausted. If the Moffats had not fought their daughter’s case, it is likely the coroner would have explained Chloe’s death with one word: suicide. Instead, she made a narrative finding, explaining the circumstances that led up to the death and laying blame partly at the Treasury’s door.
Since that finding two weeks ago, the Moffats have had no contact from the Treasury to offer condolences or an apology. “Now that the inquest has said that the coroner has found them responsible for Chloe’s death, we would have expected for them to have written to us,” David said.
Chloe was described as cheerful, popular and funny, and a person who took her job seriously. “I think Chloe was always looking to serve,” David said. Anne added: “I didn’t realise, but people like Chloe, who are bright, confident perfectionists, when they’re given a piece of shocking news such as they might lose their job, can be very vulnerable.”
The young woman was blindsided after being presented with anonymous complaints that she had shared confidential information at work, which she denied. She was not reassured that her job was safe even though she was unlikely to be dismissed, or offered a third party in the meeting to give her support or advice.
“If Chloe had known that it shouldn’t have happened, if she’d known her rights, she could have walked in and said: ‘I’m not having this meeting’, and walked out. But of course she didn’t. She didn’t know that, she was a people pleaser,” David said.
The coroner found Chloe was denied her rights at work, such as being told what the likely outcome of the disciplinary process would have been, which was a written warning, and that she could bring a supporter with her. Instead, she felt ambushed and was convinced she would lose the job she had worked so hard for.
Anne said: “I don’t know about the original complaints about Chloe, if they were malicious or to bring her down a peg or two – she was a big personality in the office.”
Her parents are considering suing the Treasury for wrongful death, particularly as they have had no response from the ministry since the finding. “If that’s the only way we’re going to get recognition, it’s a possibility,” David said.
The Treasury is obliged to give the coroner a response to the prevention of future deaths report she issued to the civil service. The coroner found there was a risk of further deaths at the Treasury because of how the department handled disciplinary cases.
The department brought a team of lawyers to the inquest, who pushed for Chloe’s death to be recorded as an unexplained suicide.
“We definitely want to be in touch with the Treasury because we do want Chloe remembered for the Chloe that she was,” Anne said. “And be that a bench in her name or whatever, but we want her to be remembered, but we do fear that she is going to be brushed under the carpet and lessons will not be learned.”
Unusually for an inquest, the small, drab room in Surrey was full of young people in their early to mid-20s – Chloe’s friends and colleagues, who wept throughout. Those who attended from the Treasury were not given bereavement leave to attend the inquest into their friend’s death. “They didn’t get any time off from the Treasury or support for that horrible ordeal they had gone through,” Anne said.
The couple said they hoped the Treasury acknowledged Chloe and issued a satisfactory response to the prevention of future deaths report, so this nightmarish chapter could be closed and they could begin to grieve.
“We need to grieve. And I’m not sure that we have. I think the inquest has delayed that,” Anne said.
David said: “The hole it’s left in our lives is just enormous. We’re only still coming to terms with that. Sometimes we don’t feel we can attend family events because we’ve got something missing. We are a tight-knit family, we’ve all holidayed together. But now we don’t have Chloe.”
They said they hoped Chloe’s case could help prevent other parents from going through the same experience. And they wanted to remember their daughter as the grinning, popular, confident, adventurous woman she was.
“We have got so many happy memories. So that’s what we have to be positive about,” Anne said. “I think: ‘At least she didn’t have cancer,’ you know, and suffer. She was literally happy up until that meeting.”
David said: “I think for sure we will continue to want to ensure that we spread the word of what we have learned from all this.”
A Treasury spokesperson said: “Our deepest sympathies continue to be with Chloe’s family, and the department continues to mourn Chloe’s death.
“We are taking all concerns extremely seriously and are considering the coroner’s findings carefully. We have introduced improvements to guidance, support and wellbeing arrangements but recognise we must continue to take action to prevent this happening again.”

A bridge too far? Why link to Sicily is still a dream despite 2,000 years of plans
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
06:00:56 UTC
15:00:56 KST

For more than 2,000 years, it has been an obsessive dream: a plan to link the Mediterranean Sea’s largest island to mainland Italy. It began with the Romans, who, according to Pliny the Elder, built a bridge of boats and barrels across the strait of Messina in 251BC to transport 140 war elephants captured from the Carthaginians.
Centuries later, the fascist dictator Benito Mussolini embraced the same vision, followed by rightwing prime minister Silvio Berlusconi, who made the bridge a flagship project. Then, in 2022, after being appointed Italy’s infrastructure minister, Matteo Salvini revived the mythic ambition, claiming that the ferry crossings “cost people more in a year than it would cost to build the bridge”.
Since then, however, there have been more promises than action. Salvini’s stated goal of breaking ground on the €13.5bn project in 2024 slipped to early 2025 and then early 2026. In February, with opponents openly mocking the repeated delays, the leader of the far-right Lega insisted construction would finally begin by this summer.
But in Torre Faro, the neighbourhood on Sicily’s north-eastern tip where work is supposedly due to begin, there is still no sign of construction. In streets lined with homes earmarked for expropriation, families are still there.
“You’re surprised I’m so unfazed. Why should I worry?” said Mariolina De Francesco, a 76-year-old retired university lecturer whose villa is among more than 400 properties that have been slated for compulsory purchase. “If they didn’t build the bridge before, why would they now? It’s all talk. They’ll never build it.”
According to the official plans, the bridge from Torre Faro to Villa San Giovanni in Calabria would be the world’s longest suspension bridge, with a central span – the distance between the two main supporting towers – of 3.3km. Its deck would carry six traffic lanes, two service lanes and two railway tracks. No suspension bridge with a comparable span exists. (The closest is Japan’s Minami Bisan-Seto Bridge, opened in 1988, with a main span of 1.1km.)
The delays in construction have been driven by various mounting obstacles: concerns raised by public bodies over the project’s environmental impact, a corruption investigation by prosecutors in Rome, an intervention by Italy’s court of auditors, which is scrutinising its cost, and a long series of requirements filed by Italy’s Higher Council of Public Works.
In interviews with the Guardian, leading engineers, seismologists and environmental experts all expressed scepticism that the dream of the bridge would ever become reality.
“You might be able to build it,” said Antonino Risitano, a former dean of engineering at the University of Catania. “But you cannot guarantee its long-term safety.” Risitano said there was no technology currently available to test suspension cables of that size and length for a single-span bridge. “If you cannot test the suspension cables, you cannot build it. Given today’s scientific knowledge, the current project is not technically feasible.”
Webuild, which is leading the Eurolink consortium contracted to design and build the infrastructure, declined to comment but said the issues raised by Risitano had already been addressed and refuted in a 2025 technical report by the Strait of Messina company.
The document said Risitano’s concerns about the main suspension cables were not supported by the historical performance of suspension bridges worldwide. It also noted that full-scale fatigue testing of main suspension cables is not standard engineering practice.
One of the other big concerns over the bridge is that it would be strikingly vulnerable to seismic activity traversing the strait of Messina, one of Europe’s most tectonically active regions.
“More than 5,000 low-magnitude earthquakes have been recorded within a 40km radius over the past 40 years,” said Carlo Doglioni, one of Italy’s leading geologists and former president of the National Institute of Geophysics and Volcanology. “The strait is also slowly widening, with Sicily and Calabria drifting 2-3mm apart each year.”
The area is crossed by three fault systems capable of producing magnitude 7 or greater earthquakes, like the one that hit Messina in 1908, killing more than 80,000 people. “Although it is impossible to predict when, the region will inevitably experience further major earthquakes,” said Doglioni.
“An earthquake of the magnitude expected here could affect not only the tower foundations but also the cable anchor blocks,” said Federico Massimo Mazzolani, professor emeritus of structural engineering at the University of Naples Federico II. “Vertical ground motion could reduce cable tension and destabilise the bridge, while horizontal shaking could permanently rotate a tower foundation, leaving the structure damaged and potentially unusable.”
Webuild insists “the bridge has been designed to withstand extreme conditions”. They say seismic studies show it would remain structurally safe during earthquakes of up to magnitude 7.1. Pietro Ciucci, chief executive of the Strait of Messina company, said the bridge’s foundations had been positioned to avoid active faults.
Tremors aside, opposition to the bridge is also building on other fronts. Last October, Italy’s court of auditors blocked the project, saying the government had failed to demonstrate its financial sustainability and ordering revised cost estimates before it could proceed.
In June, Rome prosecutors opened a corruption investigation into allegations that a lawyer and a businessman sought to influence court of auditors judges by promising support for future public appointments in exchange for approval of the project. The businessman is a former board member of Strait of Messina plc, the Italian state-owned company responsible for managing the bridge’s design, construction, and operation.
Both men deny any wrongdoing and rejected the allegations, saying they never sought to influence the court or offered favours in return for decisions.
The court of auditors also raised concerns about compliance with EU environmental rules. The Strait of Messina company insists that environmental protection and biodiversity are “at the heart of the project”. But, once again, experts disagree. The WWF argues the bridge would threaten the strait of Messina, a vital migration corridor for millions of birds and marine mammals.
“The strait of Messina is one of the world’s 28 most important bird migration routes,” says Gaetano Benedetto, WWF Italy’s vice-president. “A 2006 study commissioned by the bridge company estimated that 4.3 million birds crossed the proposed bridge corridor in just six weeks of spring migration.”
In early August, Italy’s Higher Council of Public Works said the bridge could only go ahead if the government addressed more than 100 requirements, with particular attention to seismic risk and the testing of construction materials – a process likely to force designers to substantially rewrite the project.
Even greater than the risk of the bridge being built, however, is the risk it will be started and abandoned halfway through, leaving the landscape permanently scarred, added Benedetto. That fear is shared by the founders of the No Ponte Capo Peloro campaign.
“I’m convinced the bridge will never be built,” said Mariella Valbruzzi, who has campaigned against the project for a decade with her husband, Daniele Ialacqua. “What worries me is that work on the roads and viaducts could begin anyway, leaving this protected landscape buried under concrete, with or without the bridge.”
Webuild says the project would generate more than €23bn for Italy’s economy, more than €10.3bn in tax revenue and more than 100,000 direct and indirect jobs.
Opposition parties argue the money would be better spent upgrading Sicily’s ageing road and rail network, among the weakest in Europe. Travelling the 265km between Syracuse and Trapani by rail takes 11 to 14 hours and usually requires three changes – enough time to fly from Rome to New York and clear passport control.
Since Roberto Vannacci, a far-right former army general, left Salvini’s League to launch his own party, the bridge project has become increasingly tied to the infrastructure minister’s political fortunes. With Lega slipping in the polls and Vannacci’s new party rising, it has taken on added significance for Salvini. An EMG survey puts Futuro Nazionale (National Future) on 7.2%, just 0.5 percentage points behind Lega, fuelling speculation that Salvini’s leadership within the rightwing coalition could come under growing pressure.
“The bridge will never be built. Salvini has failed. He should resign,” said Angelo Bonelli, an MP and leader of the Green-Left Alliance (AVS).
Rosa Cattafi wishes she could be so certain the bridge will never happen. The 66-year-old’s villa is another home earmarked for expropriation. “I bought this house 12 years ago, when the bridge seemed to have been abandoned,” she says. “No one can give me absolute certainty it will never be built. Until it is definitively declared unbuildable, I’ll have to live with that uncertainty.”

India joins China and South Korea in push for Arctic shipping routes
With Middle East sea lanes choked by conflict, melting polar ice offers Asia a seasonal two-week short cut to European ports
4-MIN READ4-MIN
6
 Listen
Climate change and conflict are conspiring to open up the Arctic to Asian commercial shipping, with China, South Korea and India all eyeing the icy short cut to Europe.
Last Saturday, Chinese shipping company Sea Legend launched the first scheduled weekly container service across the top of the world, marking the realisation of Beijing’s long-held ambition to build a “Polar Silk Road”.
It will not sail alone for long, however. This Sunday, South Korea’s PanStar Group plans to send its own pilot vessel from Busan through Russia’s Northern Sea Route (NSR) towards ports in the UK, the Netherlands and Poland.
India is also preparing to dispatch its first cargo ship along the same corridor next year.
“In 2027, we are planning to have the first pilot vessel running through the Northern Sea Route. We are seeing huge possibilities,” S. Venkatesapathy, a joint secretary in India’s shipping ministry, reportedly told the Arctic-Regions Forum in Arkhangelsk, Russia, on August 13.
Two crises are pushing Asian shippers north. The first is climate change: warming sea temperatures mean that the Arctic ice pack is no longer impassable in summer, opening a navigable window running roughly from July to October.

Components crunch: China’s carmakers face rising costs to keep intelligence edge
Smart vehicle makers scramble for key parts PCBs and MLCCs as AI demand soaks up supply, leaving margins under siege
3-MIN READ3-MIN
1
 Listen
Daniel Renin Shanghai
Chinese smart vehicle makers have been hit by another setback as a global components shortage collides with surging prices of raw materials, driven by the artificial intelligence boom.
It would take at least a year for the global supply chain to ramp up production of printed circuit boards (PCBs) and multilayer ceramic capacitors (MLCCs) – two key parts that make vehicles intelligent – to meet rising demand, according to industry officials and analysts.
“The components, though small, play a key role in the automotive industry’s effort to make millions of cars more autonomous and smarter,” Chen Jinzhu, CEO of the consultancy Shanghai Mingliang Auto Service, told the South China Morning Post on Wednesday.
“Market demand for electric vehicles [EVs] is falling, but component supply remains a thorny issue for leading players since they focus on intelligence to make their cars attractive to consumers.”
Industry officials said the global auto sector was facing a 20 to 30 per cent shortage of components, with prices more than tripling over the past year.
The crunch stems from explosive AI growth and the rapid buildout of AI data centres worldwide.

Iran's defence equipment production doubled in a year
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
06:00:11 UTC
15:00:11 KST

Iran's defence ministry spokesman said that weapons and equipment production doubled over the past year, with the country now targeting a threefold increase as it deepens self-reliance in the face of sanctions.
Brigadier General Reza Talaei-Nik, speaking to state television, said production had doubled after the 12-day war. Some strategic products with wartime priority had seen output increase more than threefold during the latest imposed war, contrary to claims by U.S. and Israeli leaders that Iran's defence production would be halted.
"We use our own equipment and simultaneously continue producing. This simultaneous production, together with strategic reserves built over years and daily, uninterrupted production in a broad network, has given the defence industry high capacity," he said.
He said more than 9,000 private and knowledge-based companies now work in the defence supply chain, up about 20 percent in one year. Seventy-six percent of research projects in the past year reached product completion. Some Iranian weapons are produced at one-tenth or even one-twentieth the cost of foreign equivalents, he added.
Talaei-Nik said Iran now builds more than 1,000 types of advanced systems and weapons, compared with just 31 basic items before the Islamic Revolution. He said the country ranks among the top ten in missile power and among the leading states in drones.
He cited Imam Khomeini and the late Leader Ayatollah Seyyed Ali Khamenei as the architects of this path, with hundreds of documented orders on defence ranging from missile range to strategic doctrine.
The spokesman said public unveiling of some systems had been deliberately limited to protect military secrets and surprise the enemy, but commanders were fully briefed on production and upgrades including ballistic and cruise missiles, drones and air defence systems.

Renouncing Russian citizenship many times more expensive than previously
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
05:56:00 UTC
14:56:00 KST

Renouncing Russian citizenship many times more expensive than previously
Renouncing Russian citizenship has become several times more expensive since August. Interior Minister Igor Taro said it is too early to assess whether the price increase will also lead to a decline in the number of applicants.
Former Russian citizen Andrei Malaškin began the process of applying for Estonian citizenship in 2022. He said the entire process took nearly three and a half years and was only completed last year.
"When the war started, I began to think that Russian citizenship was no longer convenient for me," Malaškin said.
According to Malaškin, renouncing his Russian citizenship took the most time.
"I remember I was in the queue for the Russian consulate for about four months. Then I went there and some of my supporting documents had expired, so I had to get back in line and that took another three months or so," Malaškin said.
At the time, renouncing his Russian citizenship cost him just over €300. Since August this year, the same procedure in Estonia has cost €2,376.
"I've heard about it. I didn't believe it was true. People can't spend that much money on a document," Malaškin said.
Interior Minister Igor Taro said the price increase is due to the difficult situation in Russia.
"I think Russia doesn't have the money to maintain its foreign missions. Secondly, the number of people renouncing their citizenship has probably increased and they don't have enough staff to handle it properly. Under the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, no one may take measures to prevent people from renouncing their citizenship. Looking at that general principle, Russia is currently violating the declaration to some extent," Taro said.
Taro said it is still too early to assess whether the high fee will reduce the number of applicants.
"Unfortunately, when it comes to Russian state fees, the Estonian state can't do anything about them. The amount is certainly large, but if someone really has a strong need to renounce their citizenship, I think they can find the money," Taro said.
Interest among Russian citizens in obtaining Estonian citizenship has remained high in recent years. A total of 465 applications were submitted to the Police and Border Guard Board last year. As of July this year, 217 applications had been submitted.

Canadian Vice Admiral: Unity Is the Strength of Ukrainian Society During the War
Ukrainian Society Demonstrates Remarkable Resilience Amid the Protracted War Because Every Citizen, Not Just the Military, Is Taking Part in Resisting the Occupiers
This view was expressed in an interview with Ukrinform by Mark Norman, former Vice Chief of the Defence Staff of Canada and a retired vice admiral.
“The strength of Ukrainian society lies in the fact that everyone is experiencing the war together. I hope that when it comes to reintegration, the cultural and social dimensions will not be as difficult as they have been in other countries, precisely because of this sense of a cohesive, unified Ukrainian community: everyone is part of the war effort, regardless of whether they are in uniform or not,” Norman said.
According to him, “this was precisely one of the historical failures of reintegration in the West: people feel isolated.” “So if Ukraine remembers this, it will have much greater success in reintegrating people from a societal perspective,” the vice admiral said.
He added that, from a material perspective, the most important task would be to restructure Ukraine’s economy for postwar conditions, “which will require the same level of mobilization that we saw during the war, but directed toward rebuilding the economy.”
Read also: Ukraine Can Help Strengthen Allied Armies – Canadian Vice Admiral
“Former military personnel should not simply return to their previous lives; they should have a role in rebuilding Ukraine that is just as important as their role in defending it,” Norman concluded.
As reported, Canada has announced its readiness to work with Ukraine to establish a Veterans Support Fund.

NHL referee Garrett Rank wins his 4th Canadian Men’s Mid-Amateur golf title

The 38-year-old Rank, from Waterloo about 40 miles north, closed with a 3-under 69 for a one-stroke victory. He finished at 18-under 270. Third-round leader Evan Nachtigall of Brandon, Manitoba, bogeyed the last for a 72 to drop into second.
“As soon as I saw my ball was on the back of the green, I knew it was a good time for lag putt to try and two putt, and luckily enough I was able to make the 6-footer at the end to win,” said Rank, who worked his first Stanley Cup Finals as a referee this year.
Rank’s previous Canadian Men’s Mid-Am wins came three years in a row from 2014-16. He has five national titles, also winning the 2012 Canadian College/University Individual Championship.
“It’s a huge honor,” Rank said. “Winning a golf tournament is never easy. To do it four times is pretty special. I think it’s been 10 years since I last did it so to do it close to home in a place like Brantford is something that I will remember for the rest of my life.”
Rank received a spot into the U.S. Mid-Amateur Championship at Sand Valley Resort in Nekoosa, Wisconsin, in late September and early October.

IndyCar drivers amazed at downtown DC course: ‘It’s stuff that you dream of’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
05:53:02 UTC
14:53:02 KST

IndyCar drivers amazed at downtown DC course: ‘It’s stuff that you dream of’
WASHINGTON (AP) — Even for well-traveled IndyCar drivers, a track with the U.S. Capitol in the background is a little awe inspiring.
“We get to race at a lot of cool cities, but this one is by far the best that we’ve ever had, and I can say that very truthfully,” Kyle Kirkwood said Friday. “Going by the Capitol building, the views here, all the architecture of all the buildings around here, all the museums, it’s stuff that you dream of.
“It’s a serious honor and privilege.”
This weekend’s Freedom 250 Grand Prix is the second big sporting event staged by President Donald Trump in Washington as part of the nation’s 250th birthday celebration. The first was a UFC fight card on the White House’s South Lawn in June.
IndyCar racing — an open-wheel counterpart to NASCAR — doesn’t have quite the same association with the right-wing “manosphere” or the MAGA movement, but series owner Roger Penske received the Presidential Medal of Freedom from Trump in 2019 and led the effort to put together this race in the District of Columbia.
For the drivers, it’s a welcome moment in the spotlight.
“What’s been the coolest part of this week? Honestly, the media covering us,” Kirkwood said. “It’s cool to see IndyCar in this light. We don’t get these opportunities very often outside of the Indy 500, and to have an event that is sought after as much as the 500 is something that’s special.”
Washington has little history with high-level motorsports. In 2002, the parking lot at RFK Stadium on the city’s east side was transformed into a course for an American Le Mans Series event.
The Freedom 250 is downtown in one of D.C.'s prime tourist areas. If you’re not in a race car, it’s not the greatest weekend to be driving around the area given all the road closures, but if the weather holds up, the setting has the potential to be spectacular.
“As a boy from the Netherlands that just got his green card, it is really cool,” said Rinus VeeKay, who has six top-10 finishes this season. “We didn’t get too much U.S. history in school ... but learning so much about it here, seeing all the monuments and museums and just how every building kind of has a special purpose here around the city, is very cool. Getting to see the White House, this is stuff you see in movies.”
The White House is not part of the D.C. course, although after Turn 1, the track does include a lengthy straightaway along Pennsylvania Avenue, heading northwest away from the Capitol. Then there’s a sharp left turn between the National Archives and the main Justice Department building, followed by a couple quick 90-degree turns as the track navigates the city’s grid system.
After a straightaway takes drivers across the National Mall, they turn left onto Independence Avenue, passing the Smithsonian’s National Air & Space Museum. and the Eisenhower Memorial before heading north on 3rd Street to the finish line, which is just west of the Capitol.
“I think it’s more exciting when you actually get on the grounds and see what you’re about to do. I mean, when is this ever going to happen again?” said Josef Newgarden, a driver for Team Penske. “I hope it’s great visibility. That’s probably the biggest thing that it could bring to us — is visibility to people that aren’t maybe as familiar with IndyCar racing.”
IndyCar practice and qualifying are scheduled for Saturday, along with an IROC race. The IndyCar race is Sunday and set for 250 miles (147 laps) — the second-longest street circuit race in IndyCar history.
The 1.7-mile track includes seven turns in all. The Air & Space Museum and National Gallery of Art are both inside the course’s perimeter, with a fan zone between them. The track is shorter and has fewer turns than several others on the IndyCar schedule, but it’s not much different from the 1.6-mile, nine-turn circuit used in downtown Detroit.
“It’s short and snappy, but you know what? We don’t know. We haven’t driven on it yet,” driver Marcus Armstrong said. “We’ll find out tomorrow. It might even be wet tomorrow. There’s a lot of crosswalks, a lot of paint on the track, so that could be super slippery.”

US court strikes down Trump visa ban affecting South Asian nations
Federal judge calls 75-country suspension ‘patently unlawful’, ruling officials cannot block visas based on nationality
A US judge has struck down a Trump administration policy suspending the issuance of immigrant visas to applicants from 75 countries, saying that the policy exceeded Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s statutory authority.
“The Policy, which categorically prohibits the issuance of immigrant visas based upon the nationality of the applicant, represents a direct abrogation of this statutory scheme,” she wrote.
The State Department’s suspension that also took effect in January affected applicants from Latin American countries including Brazil, Colombia, and Uruguay; Balkan nations such as Bosnia and Albania; South Asian countries Pakistan and Bangladesh; and those from many nations in Africa, the Middle East and the Caribbean.
The State Department said applicants from those countries were “at a high risk for becoming a public charge and recourse to local, state and federal government resources in the United States”. The department did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the ruling.
